title: Every Settings visit leaks its whole SettingsScreen via an un-unsubscribed theme_changed_signal subscription
trigger: Every Settings visit builds a new SettingsScreen (non-reusable route), and on_mount subscribes it to app.theme_changed_signal. Nothing releases it until a theme publish.
cost:
Setup: booted app, isolated profile. Probes: scratch/second-lens-screen-tour/probe_f3.py (N=26 Settings<->Library visits) and probe_leak.py (N=8). The F4 ContextVar pin can also hold these screens, so in probe_f3 it was neutralized with a Worker._run_threaded shim that resets the ContextVar token.

26 visits:
- Without the F3 fix: 26/26 SettingsScreens alive, all 26 still keys in app.theme_changed_signal._subscriptions. Growth from visit 3 to 26 was +63,961 objects per visit; maxrss went 419 -> 639 MB (about +9.6 MB per visit). A full gc.collect took 1,041 ms with 2.35M objects.
- With on_unmount unsubscribe on SettingsScreen and ThemePicker: 1/26 alive, and that one is the designed survivor held by _PermissionSummaryWrite. Growth was +15,982 objects per visit (unrelated residue); maxrss 421 -> 470 MB; full gc 475 ms with 1.23M objects.

So F3 alone retains about 48k objects and about 7-8 MB per Settings visit. 26 retained screens exceeds F4's 22-thread cap, which shows the growth is unbounded.

Nothing publishes the theme signal periodically. The only theme assignments are user actions: theme_catalog apply/undo, the theme editor, and the first-run wizard. So pruning never happens in normal use.

probe_leak.py (N=8): the baseline had 8/8 alive and all 8 in the signal. With F3 fixed but F4 not fixed, 8/8 were still alive, with Worker referrers. That confirms the verifier's caveat: a leak test must neutralize F4 or use N>22, or it will pass or fail for the wrong reason.
fix: In SettingsScreen.on_unmount add `self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)`, and add the same to ThemePicker (an on_unmount with unsubscribe). The repo already has the pattern at console_selection_menu.py:593 and console_session_switcher_modal.py:563. Add one leak test: visit Settings twice, gc.collect(), and assert the first instance's weakref is dead.
fix_notes: Add `self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)` to SettingsScreen.on_unmount, and an on_unmount with the same call to ThemePicker. Unsubscribe is idempotent (pop with default), so this is safe. Caveat for the proposed weakref leak test: SettingsScreen has 37 `thread=True` worker sites, so the F4 ContextVar pin can still keep an instance alive after this fix. The test should force a follow-up thread worker, or allow for F4, or it will flake.
evidence:
settings_screen.py:4187 self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)
4188 self.app.theme_changed_signal.subscribe(self, self._refresh_appearance_theme_summary)
4213 def on_unmount(self): ... (no theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe)
settings_theme_picker.py:363 self.app.theme_changed_signal.subscribe(self, lambda _theme: self.refresh_catalog(rescan=False))
# textual/signal.py: _subscriptions = WeakKeyDictionary(); value closure captures `node` -> key never dies; pruned only on publish()
reason: settings_screen.py:4187-4190 on_mount unsubscribes, then subscribes `self._refresh_appearance_theme_summary`. on_unmount (line 4213) stops the timer and fences results but never unsubscribes. In textual/signal.py (Textual 8.2.8), `_subscriptions` is a WeakKeyDictionary whose value list holds a `signal_callback` closure that captures both `node` (non-immediate branch: `node.call_next`) and the bound-method callback. The value therefore strongly references the key, so the entry never dies. Pruning happens only inside publish(), which needs a theme change. Textual has no auto-unsubscribe on removal: the only unsubscribe in the package is screen.py:1308 for its own layout signal. The same leak exists at settings_theme_picker.py:363 (a lambda closing over the picker, with no on_unmount in that file). Settings is non-reusable (screen_registry.py:149), so every visit leaves a new instance on the app-owned signal. Repo-wide grep: these are the only two theme_changed_signal subscribers, and neither unsubscribes on unmount.

title: Departed PersonasScreens pinned by Textual thread-worker ContextVar (active_worker never reset on pool threads)
trigger: Every visit to a non-reusable screen that runs a Textual thread worker (Personas, and also Settings, MCP and others) pins that screen instance to one executor thread until another Textual thread worker runs on that thread.
cost:
Setup: booted app, isolated profile. Probe: scratch/second-lens-screen-tour/probe_leak.py with 8 Personas<->Library visits.

Results:
- Baseline: 8/8 PersonasScreens alive after gc, each with Worker referrers (plus CCPCharacterHandler and PersonasConversationsController).
- F3 fix only: 7/8 alive.
- Worker shim added (run_callable does `token = active_worker.set(self); try: work() finally: active_worker.reset(token)`): 0/8 alive. This confirms the thread-worker ContextVar is the only retention path for Personas.

Cost: about 60k objects retained per Personas visit (+72k objects per visit at baseline vs +12.5k with the fix). The same pin also held all 8 SettingsScreens once F3 was fixed. After a full 8+8+8 Home/Settings/Personas tour, a full gen2 gc.collect took 630 ms at baseline vs 423 ms with all fixes (1.89M vs 1.34M objects, under load 40+).

Why P1 and not P0: the default executor had 22 threads (max_workers 22) in every run, so at most about 22 screens are retained, about 1.3M objects in the worst case. Pins also decay whenever another Textual thread worker lands on the same thread: in the F3-only run, Settings pins dropped after the Personas visits. Retention is bounded and self-healing, but it inflates every automatic gen2 pause by hundreds of ms.
fix: Upstream a one-line Textual fix: `token = active_worker.set(self); try: return work() finally: active_worker.reset(token)`, or run the callable in `contextvars.copy_context().run`. Until that lands, either add a small shim that wraps `Worker._run_threaded`'s callable runner, or move these two sync loaders to `asyncio.to_thread`, which copies the context per call. Also making Personas reusable (F6) would cap retention at one instance.
fix_notes: The upstream Textual fix (a reset token in run_callable/run_awaitable) is the right root fix. A local shim over the private `Worker._run_threaded` is version-fragile. Textual is pinned >=8,<9, so add a version guard and a test that fails if upstream changes the runner. Moving the two loaders to asyncio.to_thread fixes only these two sites (235 thread=True sites remain) and drops Worker semantics (exclusive/group cancellation, state events). The two cited loaders use generation and attempt tokens rather than get_current_worker(), so they would tolerate the switch. Making Personas reusable (F6) caps retention for Personas only.
evidence:
textual/worker.py:306 def run_callable(work):
    active_worker.set(self)   # set in the executor thread's persistent context, never reset
    return work()
leak probe referrers of a departed PersonasScreen: Worker(name=load_character_1 group=ccp-load-character state=SUCCESS) <- hamt_bitmap_node (contextvars)
Worker(group=personas-conversations state=SUCCESS) <- hamt_bitmap_node
reason: textual/worker.py `_run_threaded` defines `run_callable`, which does `active_worker.set(self); return work()`, and dispatches with `loop.run_in_executor(None, runner, self._work)`. run_in_executor does not copy or run in a fresh Context, so the set lands in the executor thread's persistent context and is never reset. The Worker keeps `_node` and `_work` (a partial over a bound method), and Textual never clears them after completion. I verified the mechanism with a standalone script: an object passed through run_in_executor + ContextVar.set stays alive after gc and is visible to the next work item on that thread, while asyncio.to_thread (copy_context().run) does not retain it. The cited sites are real: ccp_character_handler.py:470-476 (`run_worker(partial(self._load_character_sync...), thread=True)`) and personas_conversations_controller.py:309-317. Personas is non-reusable. Retention is bounded by the number of default-executor threads, and any later Textual thread worker on the same thread overwrites it; there are 235 `thread=True` sites repo-wide. So this is capped rather than unbounded, and P1 (not P0) is right.

title: Reused Home screen full-recomposes on every visit (even after the user left) and its query_one cache pins the discarded trees
corrected: tldw_chatbook/UI/Screens/home_screen.py:411 (call_from_thread; cited :402 is inside the worker body), tldw_chatbook/UI/Screens/home_screen.py:413-415 (whole-screen recompose), tldw_chatbook/UI/Screens/home_screen.py:376 (dispatch from on_screen_resume)
trigger: Every Home visit (reusable route, so on_screen_resume runs each time), whenever the adapter exposes refresh_chatbook_artifact_snapshot.
cost:
Setup: booted app, isolated profile. Probes: scratch/second-lens-screen-tour/probe_f5.py (12 Home<->Library cycles) and probe_leak.py (8 cycles x 3 variants).

Recompose cost: _refresh_after_chatbook_artifact_snapshot ran on 13 of 13 visits, so the whole-screen recompose fires on every Home visit. Each recompose took 115-132 ms wall (median) and 70-74 ms loop CPU (median) under load 40, and rebuilt 55 widgets. Home-phase loop CPU was about 225 ms (median).

Clearing HomeScreen._query_one_cache alone released every detached tree (-46k objects, about 4.2k per tree). Clearing app._query_one_cache released nothing more. So the verifier's retention chain is confirmed. The cache held 59 entries after 12 cycles (about 5 per visit), so the LRU(1024) cap takes effect only after about 200 visits (about 0.8M objects). That makes it bounded, not P0.

Corrections:
- 'Often after the user has left' did not reproduce on an empty profile. The callback ran while Home was current 13 of 13 times at a 2 s dwell and 6 of 6 times at a 0.3 s dwell; the worker finishes in under 0.3 s. It may happen with large DBs.
- A skip-when-not-current guard (tested as FIX5) changed neither the cost nor the orphans. The fix must replace the recompose with the targeted sync_state path, which removes both.
- Correct location: home_screen.py:411 (call_from_thread) and 413-415 (recompose).
fix: Replace the whole-screen recompose with task-282's targeted HomeRail/HomeCanvas.sync_state path. At minimum, skip it when `self.app.screen is not self` and set a dirty flag that on_screen_resume consumes. If a recompose is kept, call `self._query_one_cache.clear()` after it so detached trees are released. Task-282 (Done) made sync_state targeted, but this callback predates Home becoming reusable.
fix_notes: The preferred fix is the targeted `_sync_triage_surface`/sync_state path the content-snapshot worker already uses. A `self.app.screen is not self` skip is enough on its own, because on_screen_resume re-dispatches the worker on the next visit, so a dirty flag is optional. Avoid `self._query_one_cache.clear()`: it is a private Textual attribute, and retention is already bounded by the LRU. Removing the recompose makes the clear unnecessary.
evidence:
home_screen.py:376 on_screen_resume: self._refresh_home_chatbook_artifact_snapshot()  # @work(thread=True)
402     self.app.call_from_thread(self._refresh_after_chatbook_artifact_snapshot)
413 def _refresh_after_chatbook_artifact_snapshot(self):
414     if self.is_mounted:          # True for a suspended installed screen
415         self.refresh(recompose=True)
reason: home_screen.py:360-378 on_screen_resume dispatches `_refresh_home_chatbook_artifact_snapshot` (a @work thread worker) on every visit. Home is reusable (screen_registry.py:73-83, TASK-24452). The worker ends with `self.app.call_from_thread(self._refresh_after_chatbook_artifact_snapshot)` at line 411, which does `if self.is_mounted: self.refresh(recompose=True)` (lines 413-415). A suspended installed screen stays mounted, and Widget.refresh(recompose=True) schedules `_check_recompose` via call_next, which recomposes regardless of whether the screen is current. So the rebuild runs even after the user has left. The recompose re-mounts BaseAppScreen's MainNavigationBar, whose on_mount runs the synchronous attention query (F7) and starts a new 0.5 s interval. The retention claim is real but bounded: Textual's DOMNode._query_one_cache is LRUCache(1024) keyed on `_nodes._updates`, and is cleared only on the node's own removal (widget.py:4535), so stale-generation entries pin old widgets until 1024 newer entries evict them. title: Every MainNavigationBar mount runs a synchronous ChaChaNotes attention query on the loop
trigger: Every MainNavigationBar mount: each visit to a non-reusable destination and each Home whole-screen recompose.
cost: Code path verified; costs not re-measured. The finder measured 5.4–28 ms per visit (39–64 ms on a cold Home) under load average 13–18. That straddles the P1 per-visit threshold, and unloaded it is likely under 10–20 ms typical, so P2 stands.

fix_notes: Prefer offloading (asyncio.to_thread or a thread worker) over dropping the call. The runtime's recompute is designed for off-loop callers and marshals its publish back through call_later. A mount-time fresh read may exist to catch durable marks written without a runtime recompute, and removing it outright could leave a stale badge. Also consider pushing the limit into SQL (LIMIT, plus an index on mark_type or a non-LIKE prefix range). Today the query fetches all rows before truncating.

main_navigation.py:511 def on_mount(self):
    self.apply_console_attention()
    ...
    recompute = getattr(runtime, "recompute_console_attention", None)
    if callable(recompute): recompute(force_projection=True)
console_runtime.py:1519 marks = tuple(list_marks())  # under self._attention_operation_lock (threading lock)
reason: main_navigation.py:511-520 on_mount applies the cached `app.console_needs_attention` twice, then synchronously calls `runtime.recompute_console_attention(force_projection=True)`. console_runtime.py:1495-1520 takes `_attention_operation_lock` (a threading lock), then calls `list_console_unseen_marks()`. conversation_local_marks_service.py:634-658 opens `self.db.transaction()` (deferred, so no write lock) and runs `SELECT ... WHERE mark_type LIKE ? ORDER BY updated_at DESC` with fetchall() over every matching row before applying the limit in Python. on_mount runs on the loop, and every BaseAppScreen composes a MainNavigationBar (base_app_screen.py:385). So every non-reusable screen visit and every Home recompose (F5) runs this query on the loop, and can block on a lock a worker thread holds. The recompute is written to be thread-safe: it publishes through app.call_later and explicitly avoids call_from_thread deadlocks. No open task covers it.

title: No GC policy: 660k-object boot heap makes each automatic gen2 collection a 130–370 ms UI stall; gc.freeze() after boot measured ~0 ms
trigger: Automatic generation-2 collections fire during allocation-heavy screen switches. CPython 3.12 runs a full collection once long_lived_pending exceeds long_lived_total/4, which a ~660k-object boot heap plus per-visit screen rebuilds and the F3/F4/F5 retention will keep reaching.
cost:
Same isolated in-app tour, with gc.callbacks timing every generation-2 collection.

Boot heap: 578-585k tracked objects (fresh profile), and a full collection right after boot took 143.6 ms. The finder's 660k and 133-151 ms are the same order.

BASE arm:
- Automatic gen2 fired inside 4 of 5 non-reused Personas visits (243, 325, 283, 401 ms wall) in run 2, and 5 of 6 (192-427 ms) in run 1.
- It also fired on the cold Library visit (203-296 ms).
- It fired on zero warm (reused) Library visits.
- After the tour, a full collection took 316-414 ms on 1.01M objects. After gc.freeze() it took 0.0 ms, so the lever is real.

REUSE arm (personas made reusable): gen2 fired only on the two cold visits, then never again in the warm tour. The pause frequency is driven by non-reusable-screen allocation churn (F6) plus retention (F4).

FREEZE arm (gc.collect() then gc.freeze() after boot settle):
- The first post-freeze gen2 took 16.7 ms.
- Pauses climbed back to 78-117, then 105-153 ms within 2-4 Personas visits, because each non-reused visit retains about 90k objects (491k unfrozen after the tour).
- gen2 fired about twice as often, since the smaller long_lived_total trips CPython's 25% rule sooner.
- Total gen2 wall per Personas visit fell only from 243-401 ms to 131-284 ms.

So the finding's '~0 ms after freeze' holds only immediately after the freeze. It is a real, measured, cheap P1 mitigation that removes about 140 ms of boot-heap scan from every automatic full collection. It is not a standalone fix: with F6/F4 churn, pauses above 100 ms return within a few visits. Sequencing stays as the finder wrote it: fix F6/F4 first, and TASK-31966 AC#2 needs an ADR.

The no-GC-policy claim was not re-grepped here; the first verifier's grep stands.
fix: Write the ADR that TASK-31966 AC#2 requires, then call `gc.freeze()` once after `_ui_ready` and the deferred-startup settle (app.py ~16160 / 16333), optionally preceded by `gc.collect()`. This is new evidence for TASK-31966, whose scope is Console activation at 79 ms: the cost appears on any switch, is 2–4× larger, and has a measured fix. Fix F3, F4 and F5 first, because they keep feeding gen2 with post-boot objects.
fix_notes: TASK-31966 AC#2 requires an approved ADR first. Run gc.collect() before gc.freeze(). Frozen objects are never scanned again, so boot-time objects that later become cyclic garbage (the splash, first-run and wizard trees, and any boot-mounted non-reusable screen) become permanent. Freeze only after those are torn down. Fix F3, F4 and F5 first so post-boot retention does not keep re-inflating gen2. Re-check under Python 3.13+, where incremental GC changes the cost model.
evidence:
gcfreeze.py (in-app, after boot settle): tracked objects 662,052; full gen2 136.2 / 141.8 / 133.2 ms
after gc.freeze() (657,429 frozen): 0.0 / 0.1 / 0.0 ms
# grep: no gc.freeze / gc.set_threshold anywhere in tldw_chatbook
reason: Grep over tldw_chatbook finds no gc.freeze, gc.set_threshold or gc.disable. The only gc use is import gc in Embeddings_Lib and PDF_Processing_Lib for explicit collects. app.py:16160 (`self._ui_ready = True`) and 16326 (`_schedule_deferred_startup_work`) are real candidate hook points. TASK-31966 (To Do) owns GC pauses but is scoped to Console character-switch activation (a 79 ms gen2). Its AC#1 already names a 'frozen baseline' comparison and its AC#2 requires an ADR for any global GC policy. The finding adds new evidence: automatic gen2 pauses fire on ordinary destination switches (Settings, Personas, Home, Notes) at 130–370 ms, larger than the task's 79 ms, and the freeze lever is measured. title: Scheduler tick resolves the emergency-stop path (get_user_data_dir admission) on the loop every 30 s; residue of Done TASK-31507

title: Per-connect storage admission makes Library/Notes/Home/Console connection churn expensive on worker threads (GIL pressure during visits)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite.py:1517 (admission); tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite.py:1878 (prepare_in_helper per connect); tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite_process.py:366 (helper subprocess Popen, cap 4 at :159); churn sources: tldw_chatbook/Chat/chat_conversation_scope_service.py:193, :404; tldw_chatbook/Notes/notes_scope_service.py:1965, :2101
trigger: Visits to Library (reused), the Notes alias, Home and Console run scope-service list and count reads through `asyncio.to_thread` or thread workers. Each read opens a fresh connection and closes it. The finder's recorder shows 8-13 connects on warm visits, all on worker threads and none on the loop except for 2 on the first cold Home visit.
cost:
In-app tour, same isolated profile. Wrapped private_sqlite._connect_registered_sqlite and prepare_in_helper, and captured a stack per connect.

Warm, reused Library visit (15 visits over 3 runs):
- 9-17 connects per visit, all on worker threads, none on the loop.
- Each connect spawns a `python -I -S private_sqlite_helper_entry.py` interpreter (private_sqlite_process.py:366, called from private_sqlite.py:1878). Helper spawns equal connects in every window.
- Child CPU was 450-845 ms per visit, about 45-50 ms per helper.
- Parent worker-thread CPU inside connect was 270-518 ms per visit, about 25-30 ms per connect. My scratch data path is about 12 components deep, and the verifier found admission scales +17 opens per path component, so a real ~/.local/share path is cheaper here: roughly 6-10 ms per connect.
- The slowest single connect took 450-885 ms wall under load, bounded by the 4-helper cap.
- The loop is not blocked: loop CPU on a warm Library visit was 150-290 ms per 2.5 s window, the largest loop callback was about 22 ms, and navigation took 2-5 ms.

The cost is about 0.8-1.3 s of process-plus-child CPU and several hundred ms of data-population latency on every warm Library visit, a common per-visit path, so P1 stands.

Root cause is wider than the 4 scope-service sites the verifier named:
- Backup_Recovery/participants.py:42-105 `run_finite_local_worker` deliberately closes every chachanotes/media/prompts connection a finite worker opened. It has 26 uses across 9 files, including library_screen.py:13009-13014 `invoke_service_in_worker`.
- Explicit closes remain at notes_scope_service.py:2098-2103 and chat_conversation_scope_service.py:191.

Observed connect sources per warm visit: count_prompts (x2, the same count fetched twice), count_notes (x2), list_notes, list_media_items, search_media, library_content_evidence, collections list_page, list_conversations, and the study/quiz counts.

Non-reused Personas visits also opened 1-14 connects (character list/page/count, conversations, world books, dictionaries).

Aside for TASK-31501: console_trace_maintenance run_batch pays a helper spawn every time it connects, 0-2 times per 2.5 s idle window.

The fix needs sign-off from the quiescence/ADR-029 owner, because run_finite_local_worker's close-on-exit is intentional.
fix: Hold connections (the held-connection idiom from TASK-15466) so each visit stops re-connecting, and amortize the admission per store per generation instead of per connect. New evidence for TASK-24457: every connect carries a 600–1600-open admission, so the churn costs far more than the plain connect cost.
fix_notes: First remove the per-read `close_connection()` in the scope services so pool-thread connections are held. That is rung 2: the held-connection idiom already exists, and the pool threads are long-lived. Before doing that, find out why the closes were added. They probably exist so backup/recovery quiescence can drain (`_core_closing`, `retiring_threads`, and `participant.drain` refuse live borrowers), and a connection held on a pool thread must still be retirable when capture pauses storage. Consider one dedicated long-lived DB thread per store instead of the shared pool. Any cache of the helper's prepare verdict per (path, inode, admission generation) must be signed off by the private-path/ADR-029 owners. TASK-24457 AC#3 requires the policy check on every logical open, so update that AC rather than silently skipping it. Medium risk.
evidence:
admission recorder (thread side, warm round):
library r2: private_sqlite.py:1517 admitted <- :1928 connect_private_sqlite  n=12  1349 ms
notes r2:   same site n=11  1928 ms
home r2:    same site n=8    696 ms
chat r2:    same site n=5    137 ms
reason: private_sqlite.py:1517 is `lease = acquire_storage(Path(database))` inside `_with_storage_admission`. private_sqlite.py:1928 is `connect_private_sqlite` → `_connect_registered_sqlite`. The finder missed the dominant cost. On POSIX, every file-backed connect also calls `prepare_in_helper` (private_sqlite.py:1878), which starts a subprocess (private_sqlite_process.py:366, `[sys.executable, "-I", "-S", private_sqlite_helper_entry.py]`). That is a fresh Python interpreter per connection. Transient helpers are capped at 4 process-wide (private_sqlite_process.py:147/159), so bursts are serialized. TLDW_TEST_MODE does not affect this path. The churn does not come from screen construction as TASK-24457 assumed: Library is now reusable (screen_registry.py:114, TASK-31521), and the finder's own admit2.json still shows 13 connects on the reused warm Library visit (and 11 on Notes, 8 on Home, 4 on Chat). Textual's thread workers and `asyncio.to_thread` share the default pool, so without those closes the pool threads' connections would be reused. TASK-24457 is open and covers Library connection churn, but it prices each connect as PRAGMAs plus a file open. This finding adds real scope (Notes, Home, Console, Personas), the actual root cause (close-after-read in the scope services), and a much higher per-connect cost.

trigger: Every Console send while world books are active (frozen_inputs world_enabled), through asyncio.to_thread. This is per send and scales with entries x keys x scan-text length.

I ran the real WorldInfoProcessor (construct + process_messages) in the isolated env at audit tree 840ed2ca58, with 3 keys per entry, scan_depth 3, and a few injected hits. Script: scratch/second-lens-f2f5/bench_wi.py. Per-send cost as min ms, original vs a `key in text` prefilter:

- 8.6 KB scan text: 25 entries 4.6 vs 0.4; 50 entries 9.3 vs 0.8; 100 entries 18.2 vs 1.6; 200 entries 40.6 vs 3.2; 300 entries 64.4 vs 4.5; 500 entries 109.9 vs 9.1; 1000 entries 222.6 vs 15.2.
- Match counts were identical in every case. Processor construction is only 0.07 ms at 25 entries and 2.8 ms at 1000.

The mechanism is real, but P1 overstates it.
1. It runs off the event loop: `_apply_world_info` wraps the applier in `asyncio.to_thread` (console_chat_controller.py:23286/23307). It is called exactly once per send path: submit :10808, retry :19702, continue :19859, regenerate :20003, edit-resend :21051 and speculative voice :9356. None of these loops.
2. It only runs when the user has attached world books to the conversation (`capture_prompt_transform_inputs`, :1250-1287). For everyone else `self.entries` is empty and it returns immediately.
3. It passes the ~20 ms P1 bar only with lorebooks of about 100-200+ entries and long history. The cost is added before a provider call whose time-to-first-token is hundreds of ms or more.
4. The claim that it contends with the UI loop is generic to any worker thread, not specific to this code. Measured median 1 ms-tick lateness: ~14 ms during this workload, 13.9 ms for a plain pure-Python 100 ms busy thread, 1.2 ms idle. It lasts only as long as the work, and the loop is never frozen.

Two sub-claims are refuted:
- **The '>512 keys re-cache thrash'** is minor. Per-key cost only rose from 0.061 ms (300 keys) to 0.074 ms (3000 keys). The dominant cost is the unanchored sre scan: the leading `\b` defeats sre's literal-prefix search.
- **Chat_Dictionary_Lib.match_whole_words** is negligible: it scans only the current message. Measured 0.07 ms at 20 entries, 0.33 ms at 100 and 1.17 ms at 300 (P3 at most).

The fix remains a trivial, exactly equivalent one-line quick win. Add `if keyword not in text: return False` in `_keyword_in_text` (world_info_processor.py:602-606); it is 11-15x faster. Do not add a per-revision processor cache: construction is under 3 ms, so it is YAGNI.

For Chat_Dictionary_Lib.match_whole_words, which uses re.IGNORECASE, a .lower() substring prefilter is not strictly equivalent for some Unicode case folds. Either apply casefold() to both sides or prefilter only ASCII keys. Precompiling per-key patterns once per processor is also safe. Skip the per-revision processor cache: construction measured under 1 ms, and caching adds invalidation risk when books are edited (YAGNI).

title: Audiobook generator accumulates audio with bytes += per stream chunk and per segment (quadratic memcpy)
trigger: STTS window 'Generate audiobook' (STTS_Window.py:1188 posts STTSAudioBookGenerateEvent) → App @on handler awaits the full generation. Per-chunk += runs for every TTS stream chunk (8 KB OpenAI, 1 KB ElevenLabs), and the combine runs once per chapter, all on the UI loop.

For the combine, use `silence.join(segments)`, which gives exactly the same bytes as the current interleave (silence between segments, none after the last). This is trivially safe. Note that naive byte concatenation of MP3 or WAV files is itself format-dubious (WAV headers), but that is out of scope. The bigger issue is that the whole pipeline (decode, normalize, ffmpeg `subprocess.run` without a timeout) runs on the loop. That was flagged P1 in the tier2 review and has no open task, so consider filing it.

title: Semantic chunker calls sklearn cosine_similarity once per adjacent sentence pair
trigger: PDF ingestion with default settings (chunk_method 'semantic') plus any explicit semantic chunking: once per sentence pair, in the ingest worker.
cost: Measured 442 µs per pair (5,000 sentences, 15-word TF-IDF rows = 2.21 s) including the two CSR row slices, against 1.5 ms for all pairs vectorized (`V[:-1].multiply(V[1:]).sum(axis=1)`). A 10k-sentence book PDF spends ~4.4 s here. The finder estimated 50–100 µs per call.
fix: Normalize sentence_vectors once and compute all adjacent similarities with a single sparse row-wise multiply-sum before the loop.
fix_notes: TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized by default, so `sims = np.asarray(V[:-1].multiply(V[1:]).sum(axis=1)).ravel()` equals cosine_similarity for each pair. Zero rows give 0 in both. Compute it once before the loop and index `sims[i]`. The per-pair try/except fallback to 1.0 becomes moot; keep a whole-array fallback if the multiply raises. Low risk; the chunk boundaries are unchanged.

next_vector = sentence_vectors[i + 1:i + 2]
similarity = cosine_similarity(current_vector, next_vector)[0, 0]

The finder under-rated both cost and reach. `DEFAULT_MEDIA_INGESTION_CONFIG['pdf']['chunk_method'] = 'semantic'` (config.py:756), and local_file_ingestion.py:1150-1161 resolves the chunk method from those defaults, so every default PDF ingest runs this strategy (registered as 'semantic' in Chunking/engine/strategies/__init__.py:23 and chunker.py:378). It runs in the ingest pipeline, which is sync and not on the UI loop, but it is GIL-bound and scales with document length. Upgraded to P2.

title: Diarization alignment compares every transcription segment against every diarization segment (O(T×D)) and sorts overlaps per segment
trigger: Local ingestion with diarization plus transcription, once per file (Step 7 at :796-802), off the UI loop.
cost: Estimated. T×D after merge (for example 1,500 × 300 = 450k iterations at ~0.4 µs) is ~0.2–0.6 s per long recording. The per-segment `overlaps` list is tiny, so the sort is negligible. Small next to model inference.

fix_notes: A two-pointer or bisect sweep needs diarization segments sorted by start. `_detect_overlapping_speech` (:785) can emit OVERLAPPING segments, so a strict two-pointer that advances past ended segments must scan a window rather than one pointer. Use `max(overlaps, key=...)` instead of sort, but note the tie-break: sort is stable and keeps the first-seen maximum, and `max` also returns the first maximum, so behaviour is the same.
reason: The code matches: diarization_service.py:1440 `for trans_seg in transcription_segments`, :1444 an inner loop over all `diarization_segments`, and :1456 `overlaps.sort(...)`. The caller is the sync `diarize()` (:690) at :800, after `_merge_segments`. The diarization list is therefore post-merge, which cuts D substantially, and it runs in the ingest pipeline off the UI loop. The cost is negligible next to embedding and clustering inference, so P3 hygiene is correct.

title: check_dependency's cache is write-only: missing optional deps re-run the import search on every call
trigger: Cold and per-event only: once per Markdown widget compose (Library media/notes preview), once per image-preview decode, once per TTS backend initialize, once per chunker construction or language list, once at image-protocol warm-up. No per-keystroke, per-tick or per-chunk caller exists. The hot-ish callers (Persona Buddy rendering, meeting capture numpy) already memoize themselves.
cost: Measured in an isolated scratch env with no tldw import. A present module costs about 0.05 µs for the `__import__` hit and about 9 µs with the loguru f-string debug record through a TRACE sink. The real app adds forwarding to stdlib handlers on top. A missing module cost about 188 µs per failed `__import__` in my setup; the finder measured 32.8 µs, and the gap comes from sys.path and cwd. Either way it is well under 1 ms per call, on cold paths only.
fix: Return `DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[feature_name]` when the key is present, keeping the kokoro and Windows special case, and log only on the first probe.
fix_notes: The proposed fix is UNSAFE as written. DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE is pre-seeded with False for about 90 keys (optional_deps.py:16-104), including pillow, PIL, textual_image, onnxruntime, omnivoice_tts, jieba, fugashi, lxml, sentence_transformers, pydub, chatterbox and kokoro_onnx. So 'return DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[feature_name] when the key is present' would return False forever without ever probing. That would permanently disable image previews, graphics images, OmniVoice (the default TTS engine), CJK chunking and more. A second problem: keying by feature_name collides when two modules share one feature key. omnivoice.py:124 checks both onnxruntime and tokenizers under 'omnivoice_tts', so the tokenizers probe would silently return the onnxruntime result. A correct memo needs its own probed-set keyed by module_name, for example a private `_PROBED: dict[str, bool]` or @functools.cache on an inner `_probe(module_name)`. It must still write DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[feature_name] on every call, must be cleared in reset_dependency_checks (optional_deps.py:~1427), and must keep the kokoro_onnx Windows special case. Also check the 17 test files that reference check_dependency or DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[...], because tests that simulate absence by patching imports would then need a reset. Cheapest safe alternative: only log on the first probe of a module. Given the cold callers, 'leave as is' is also defensible.
evidence:
"""Check if a dependency is available and cache the result."""
    ...
        module = __import__(module_name)
        MODULES[module_name] = module
        DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[feature_name] = True
        logger.debug(f"✅ {module_name} dependency found. ...")
reason: The code is as quoted at tldw_chatbook/Utils/optional_deps.py:614-652, and `__import__(module_name)` is at line 639. check_dependency writes DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE and MODULES but never reads them back, so every call re-runs `__import__` plus an eager f-string logger.debug. I traced all callers: 70 `check_dependency(` sites, plus 28 more through get_safe_import/require_dependency at optional_deps.py:1007 and 1029. None of them is on a hot path. The finder's 'repeated' sites run once per event: front_matter_parser_factory once per Markdown widget compose (library_media_content.py:325, library_notes_canvas.py:2912), image preview once per decode (library_media_image_preview.py:132 and 226, where the decode itself costs milliseconds), terminal_utils.py:62 once at warm-up, language_chunkers.py:210-212 only in get_available_languages, omnivoice.py:648 once per backend initialize(), and kokoro_languages.py:73 only while the frontend is not yet cached. The callers that could be hot already memoize on their own side: Persona_Buddy/rendering.py:43 uses @lru_cache and Audio/meeting_capture.py:53 uses a _NUMPY global. title: ModelCapabilities double-caches is_vision_capable with a method-level lru_cache that pins retired instances and survives invalidation

The trigger is re-verified:

- run_reply builds a new _ModelCallLifeline per turn (console_agent_bridge.py:6509), and each fleet child builds one too (:3308).

Give each long-lived thread one handle for its whole lifetime.
- In `_ModelCallLifeline._run`, wrap `self.loop.run_forever()` in `operation_owned_connection(chachanotes_db)` and prime it with `db.get_connection()`. Every nested owned op then borrows (base_db.py:66-67), and the handle closes once at run end. Do the same for fleet child lifelines, and add an initializer on `_provider_trace_settlement_executor`.

- Remove `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` from the per-op `close_connection` path and let `wal_autocheckpoint` do its job; keep TRUNCATE for shutdown or maintenance only.

The held handle also pins a storage lease for the whole run. That is acceptable, because the run's own trace writes need that lease anyway.

Dropping `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` from close is a separate, riskier change (WAL growth, backup capture assumptions); do it after the lifeline fix, not with it.

Do not make a singleton app-lifetime loop part of this fix. It reworks the PR3a-1 teardown and orphan-child guarantees for little extra gain once the handle is held.

title: The UI-stall watchdog and diagnostics drain threads wake at 10 Hz each, forever, when idle
trigger: Always on by default. The watchdog runs from heartbeat install (at boot) and the drain from the first diagnostic (the first send). Both run until process exit.
cost: About 20 thread wakeups per second while idle, each with a GIL reacquire and a trivial compare. Well under 0.1% of a core (estimated). A battery and idle-wakeup tax, not CPU.
fix: In the watchdog, sleep until `last_heartbeat + limit` and re-arm from the heartbeat, or wait on an Event set by `heartbeat()`. In the drain, use a blocking `get()` with a close sentinel instead of a 0.1 s timeout.
fix_notes: Watchdog: sleep until `beat + limit - now`, recheck, then re-sleep against the newest heartbeat. That gives about one wakeup per heartbeat and keeps the same detection moment, since the stall sample is taken at beat+limit either way. Drain: a blocking get() needs close() to enqueue a sentinel. The queue is bounded at 64, so close() must use put with a timeout or drop an item to make room, or the sentinel can be lost when the queue is full. Keep the existing `_diagnostic_closed` check as a fallback.

app.py:7961-7965  UIResponsivenessMonitor(enabled=get_cli_setting('diagnostics','ui_responsiveness_enabled', True), heartbeat_interval_seconds=1.0)

With the default threshold of 250 ms (constructor line ~46) that is 0.1 s, so the watchdog runs `time.sleep(poll)` in a loop until close, at 10 Hz. It is started by arm() at app.py:11942 when the heartbeat timer is installed, and the monitor is enabled by default at app.py:7961-7966. The drain thread (ui_responsiveness.py:122-128; the get is on line 125, not 124) loops on Queue.get(timeout=0.1) and continues on Empty. It is spawned by the first recorded diagnostic, and console_send_stage is recorded on every send, so it runs for the rest of the process. Neither thread is gated on idle. TASK-32920 (Done) added the watchdog and describes it as 'polls cheaply', but no task tracks the idle wakeup rate. Both threads run off the loop and each wakeup does only a float compare or an Empty exception, so the cost is idle wakeups and battery, not CPU.

TASK-32804.1's AC#2 ("the handshake is amortised per derivation") is unmet for load_settings, and TASK-32804.3 and TASK-24454 both collapse into this fix. Steps:
1. Mirror `_warm_config_cache_hit`. Rename the guarded body to `_load_settings_guarded` and add it to the config_participants.guarded allowlist.
2. Make `load_settings(force_reload=False)` unguarded: return `_SETTINGS_CACHE` lock-free when `_SETTINGS_CACHE is not None`, `_SETTINGS_CACHE_SOURCE == _get_effective_config_path()` and `_warm_config_cache_hit() is not None`. Otherwise fall through to the guarded path.

3. Give the get_*_db_path helpers an optional precomputed user_data_dir.
4. Needs sign-off from the owner of private_paths/ADR-126, because it changes when the hardening walk runs.
fix_notes:
The memo-plus-leaf-lstat revalidation weakens ADR-126's per-call walk. A leaf lstat does not detect an ancestor directory being swapped or re-permissioned, which secure_private_directory/_secure_default_data_dir exist to catch. It needs sign-off from the owner of private_paths/ADR-126 (TASK-32562 is active in exactly this code).

Lower-risk first step with most of the boot win: resolve get_user_data_dir once in TldwCli.__init__, pass it into the _wire_* helpers, and add an optional user_data_dir parameter to the get_*_db_path accessors. Freshness semantics at other call sites stay unchanged.

The memo key must also cover a users_name/data_dir change (a profile switch) and the storage-pause state.

title: resolve_sensitive_context calls get_user_data_dir 19 times; agent file/git/patch tools and @-reference expansion build it once or more per call/token
trigger: Every file/git/patch agent tool invocation (1-3 resolves each), and every @-reference token in a Console send, before the provider call.
cost:
Script: scratch/second-lens-cfgreads/bench_f3.py and gil_lag.py (isolated profile). Calls were counted exactly with a profile hook on the inner code objects; timings were taken with the profiler off.

Per-call counts and cost at depth 11 / depth 19:
- resolve_sensitive_context: exactly 19 get_user_data_dir calls. 32,737 / 48,545 opens, which extrapolates to about 15k at real depth. CPU min 1.56 s / 2.61 s.
- local_tool_impls.read_file on a 2-byte file: 2 resolves, 38 get_user_data_dir calls, 65,475 opens. CPU 2.65 s / 5.6 s.
- resolve_reference per @token: 1 resolve, 19 calls, 1.55 s.
- expand_references with 3 @refs: 57 calls, 98k opens, 4.3 s CPU at depth 11.
- build_console_reference_resolver: 2 calls, because _resolve_sandbox_config computes the get_user_data_dir default unconditionally.

At real depth:
- Per resolve: about 0.4 s (two-point fit) to 0.85 s (19 x 44 ms).
- read_file: about 0.8-1.7 s.
- Per @-reference: about 0.4-0.9 s added before the provider call.

It is off the event loop: console_chat_controller.py:10120 uses asyncio.to_thread, and agent tools run on the worker thread. Measured GIL contention with a resolve loop on a background thread moved the UI ticker's p99 lateness from 6.9 to 11.7 ms and its max from 15 to 29 ms. That is latency and contention, not a UI freeze.

So P1 stands, though it sits near P0 for agent-heavy sessions (tens of seconds of overhead per multi-read run). Fixing F2 also collapses this cost.
fix:
1. In resolve_sensitive_context, call get_user_data_dir once. Derive the 13 DB paths as `_get_custom_database_path(name) or udd / profile_paths.database_leaf(name)`, and pass udd into _sensitive_skill_trust_dir, _sensitive_single_file_paths, _direct_child_rule_container_dirs and default_rag_profiles_dir. That takes it from 19 calls to 1 with identical values.
2. local_tool_impls.read_file (and the write paths): build one context and pass it to both resolve_workspace_path and sensitive_exclusions_under.
3. build_console_reference_resolver: build the context once per expansion and pass `context=` into is_sensitive_path.
4. _resolve_sandbox_config: compute the get_user_data_dir default only when [tools].file_sandbox_root is unset.
5. Keep the per-call freshness contract: do not cache across calls.
fix_notes:
Step 1 as written is unsafe: re-deriving the DB paths inside sensitive_paths as `_get_custom_database_path(name) or udd / database_leaf(name)` is wrong in two ways.
- get_scheduled_tasks_db_path passes expand_before_validation=False, which a generic re-derivation drops.
- It bypasses tests that monkeypatch individual accessors (Tests/Utils/test_sensitive_paths.py:253 patches get_chachanotes_db_path).

Instead, add an optional user_data_dir parameter to each accessor (shared with F2) and call accessor(user_data_dir=udd). Do the same for _sensitive_skill_trust_dir, _sensitive_single_file_paths and _direct_child_rule_container_dirs.

Steps 2-4 (one context per read_file, context= per @-expansion, lazy sandbox default) are low risk. Keep the documented no-cross-call-caching contract.

title: Every new SQLite connection now spawns a Python helper subprocess, and the UI offload wrapper forces a new connection on almost every Library, Notes and media call
corrected: Add tldw_chatbook/DB/base_db.py:38 (operation_owned_connection) and tldw_chatbook/Chat/console_chat_controller.py:11482/11513 (Console durable calls pay the same re-open, 2x per send at :12069 and :12475)

A pool thread only keeps its connection when a non-owned to_thread caller left it there, and most sites now use the owned seams.
cost:
Pin 840ed2ca58, isolated scratch profile, load avg 28-39 on 18 cores. Scripts are in scratch/second-lens-dbui/ (bench_f1.py, bench_f1_owned.py, bench_send.py).

(1) Cost of one open:
- connect_private_sqlite takes 87.0 ms wall median (p10 75.6, p90 102). Reaped helper CPU per open is 47.0 ms (user+sys, RUSAGE_CHILDREN).
- For comparison, raw sqlite3.connect is 0.13 ms and a bare `python -I -S -c pass` spawn is 17.4 ms.

(2) Every owned seam pays exactly 1.00 helper spawn per call, counted by wrapping HelperLease.start over 30 sequential calls. The same seams on the main thread with a warm connection take 0.04-0.06 ms per read.

| Seam | Median per call | Child CPU per call |
|---|---|---|
| run_owned_db_call (chacha read) | 79 ms | 48 ms |
| run_owned_db_call (IMMEDIATE txn) | 95 ms | not recorded |
| to_thread(run_finite_local_worker, chacha read) | 77 ms | 46 ms |
| to_thread(run_finite_local_worker, media read) | 67 ms | 47 ms |

(3) Library-like fan-out: a gather of 4 finite calls takes 133 ms with 4 spawns. A gather of 8 takes 214 ms with 8 spawns, because the 4-helper cap splits it into two waves.

(4) NEW, a real send: 12 sends through ConsoleChatController.submit_draft on a file-backed CharactersRAGDB with a fake gateway.
- Steady state is 3 helper spawns per send, all off-loop, not the 2 the first verifier counted.
- The spawns come from: the library-policy read (console_library_policy_coordinator.py:78 owned_call → console_library_policy_repository.py:44), commit_durable_turn and cas_state. Each spawn takes 58 ms median.
- Each durable call takes 138 ms median, which adds about 283 ms of sequential latency per send before provider dispatch.
- At about 35-47 ms per spawn when idle, the 3 spawns alone are about 105-140 ms.

(5) Minor contributors: asyncio.run per isolate_in_worker call costs 0.54 ms median, which is small next to the spawn. Call-site counts reproduce: 75 isolate_in_worker=True, about 88 _run_library_service_call, 32 _run_folder_repository, 21 _call_local_leaf.

Caveat: in the real app, a pool thread already warmed by a non-owned to_thread caller would borrow its connection and skip the spawn. Tests pin registered_connection_count()==0 after sends, so the send path itself warms nothing.

Verdict: the finding is real and larger than filed. It stays P1 because the cost is off-loop latency and the UI does not freeze. The send slice does cross the P0 100 ms number as pre-dispatch latency; promote only that slice if dispatch delay counts as a stall. The same seams cover prior audit PERF-09 and TASK-24457.
fix: (1) Verify each (path, st_dev, st_ino) with the helper once per process, then reuse that proof. The existing `verify_expected_named_identity` stat check covers later opens, and the helper re-runs only when the identity changes. This keeps the private-path policy on every logical DB, which is TASK-24457 AC#3. (2) Stop retiring pool-thread connections per call in run_finite_local_worker. Either keep them, since the pool size bounds the count, or route each DB's sync work through one long-lived backend thread, as writing_scope_service `_ThreadOffloadedBackend`/`_run_on_backend_thread` already does. (3) Replace `asyncio.run` per call in `_run_library_service_call(isolate_in_worker=True)` with that same backend thread. Pin the result with a probe that counts helper spawns per Library visit.
fix_notes: (1) Caching the helper proof per (dev, ino) weakens the guarantee the helper exists for: the parent never opens unverified inodes, and private_sqlite.py:1395 notes that the stat-only identity check still has a pathname race. This is a security-policy decision for the owner, and TASK-24457 AC#3 requires policy enforcement on every logical open. A lower-risk variant keeps one retained helper process (the protocol already has 'retained' leases for TTS) and sends prepare requests over its pipe instead of spawning per open. (2) The per-call retirement in run_finite_local_worker and operation_owned_connection is deliberate ADR-126 maintenance-quiescence design: backup and restore drains must be able to retire handles. Long-lived pool-thread connections would break that. Prefer a dedicated long-lived per-DB backend thread wired into the maintenance participant drain, as writing_scope_service does with _maintenance_close_admission/_maintenance_drain/_close_settled_core_cache. (3) Include the Console durable-call seam, not just Library, Notes and media. (4) The 4-helper cap plus a 5 s reserve budget means parallel gathers queue, and under sustained contention they can hit HelperTimeoutError. Pin the fix with a spawn-count probe per Library visit and per send.

title: The Console turn-terminal persist and dispatch settle run a synchronous write transaction on the loop for every send
trigger: Yes. Once per completed Console send. The completion path at :27275, plus the other mark_message_complete / finalize_variant_stream call sites the finder named, run in the send coroutine on the UI loop.
cost:
Measured with bench_send.py and bench_txn_tax.py on the same real-send harness: submit_draft, file-backed DB, 9 KB streamed reply, a 1 ms heartbeat to catch loop stalls, load avg about 30.

(1) On-loop terminal persist: mark_message_complete takes 18.9 ms wall median (p90 31.9) and 16.1 ms of main-thread CPU per send. cProfile shows about 86% of it is Backup_Recovery storage admission, not SQLite. The call chain is settle_with_assistant → _core_operation → acquire_storage → admission_authority → 245 posix.open.

(2) Per-transaction tax. The table shows a warm main-thread db.transaction(immediate=True) running SELECT 1, against a raw BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT.

| Case | Median |
|---|---|
| db.transaction(immediate=True), SELECT 1 | 17.7 ms (16.0 ms CPU) |
| Raw BEGIN IMMEDIATE / COMMIT | 0.004 ms |
| Read with no transaction | 0.035 ms |

- Each transaction makes about 850 syscalls: 245 open, 243 close, 253 fstat, 73 lstat, 36 stat.

title: The Buddy speech 1 Hz poll reads the persona profile from sqlite on the loop every tick
corrected: Also cite tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_speech.py:202 (_capture stamp, once per candidate), :216 (owner_current re-stamp through revalidate/validators), and :123 (revalidate each tick); tldw_chatbook/Character_Chat/local_character_persona_service.py:1175 (the in-memory read); tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/chat_source_participants.py:413 (guarded) and :260-:330 (operation(): the deepcopy of every persona cache plus storage admission), which is where the cost is.
trigger: Yes. The 1 Hz asyncio task runs on the app loop while Buddy speech is enabled, the Buddy is open, and it is bound to a persona session (a workspace binding pays this per persona session in the workspace). Each tick makes 2 guarded profile reads, or 3 while an item is queued or playing, and the TTS lifecycle validator re-runs `owner_current` at its checkpoints.
cost: Measured in an isolated scratch profile with a real file-backed CharactersRAGDB and persona JSON store. `get_persona_profile` had a median of 14–22 ms per call (p95 ~20–27 ms). The same lookup without the guard took about 0.15 µs. cProfile showed about 812 `posix.open` calls per call, from `acquire_storage` / `admission_authority` / `pinned_directory` walks. A path-depth sweep gave medians of 22.4, 35.7 and 50.2 ms at depths 10, 18 and 26, which is about 1.7 ms per path component. Extrapolated to production depth (~5–6 components), that is ~6–10 ms per call. A larger store adds deepcopy time: 19.9 ms at 20 profiles and 2,000 memories versus 13.9 ms for a tiny store. That makes a ~12–30 ms loop stall every second while the feature is on, roughly 1.2–3% of a core, and it causes keystroke jitter. This is far above the finder's 0.2–1 ms sqlite estimate. I upgraded it from P3 to P2 rather than P1 only because it is opt-in and applies to persona-bound sessions only. If it were on by default, the per-tick magnitude would make it P1.
fix: Stamp using the persona version already on the session (identity_revision), or cache the profile version keyed on the persona-service revision. Do the read only when that revision changes.
fix_notes: Replacing the stamp with `session.identity_revision` alone is unsafe. The persona read exists to catch persona deletion, deactivation and version bumps, which live in the persona store rather than on the session, so that change would silently drop the revocation check. Safe, cheap options: (1) Memoize `_session_stamp` per session within a single `refresh()`, which takes the tick from 2–3 reads to 1. (2) Add a monotonic revision counter to LocalCharacterPersonaService, bumped in `_persist_personas` and `_load_personas` and on restore, and re-read the profile only when it changes. The real root cause is broader than Buddy. `guarded` runs the full admission walk plus a deepcopy rollback snapshot on read-only methods, so every LocalCharacterPersonaService, LocalChatDictionaryService and ChatConversationService read pays about 6–20 ms. Skipping the deepcopy for non-mutating methods, or caching the admission proof, needs backup and maintenance owner sign-off (ADR-126 pause and drain semantics), so file it as its own finding rather than folding it into this fix.

title: Chatbook import scans notes/conversations by title per item (no title index)
trigger: Chatbook import, local wizard or local_chatbook_service.import_chatbook. One notes scan per imported note and one conversations lookup per conversation, plus one scan per suffix candidate on a RENAME conflict. The only callers are in chatbook_importer.py. Less frequent path.
cost: Measured on a copy of the finder's notes_big.db (6k notes, 36.9 MB content, no sqlite_stat1), under load average ~50. A miss lookup does a SCAN of notes and took 2.2 ms (min of 25) to 3.7-8.8 ms (medians). With a BINARY (deleted, title) index the plan is SEARCH (deleted=? AND title=?) at about 0.0 ms. The conversations half is minor: 0.21 ms on 300 conversations via idx_conversations_archive (archived=?, deleted=?). Loading all active titles once takes 4.7 ms. So cost is O(K×N) at about 2-4 ms per imported note at 6k notes, e.g. about 2-4 s for 1k notes. P2 is right: moderate cost on a less frequent path that scales with data.
fix: Load the existing active title sets once per import (SELECT title FROM notes WHERE deleted=0) and check in memory, including suffix generation. If an index is preferred, add (deleted, title COLLATE NOCASE) with a stat1-absent plan pin.
fix_notes: 1) The index alternative as written is wrong. An index on (deleted, title COLLATE NOCASE) cannot serve `title = ?` under BINARY collation: the measured plan is `SEARCH notes USING INDEX (deleted=?)` only. It must be a plain (deleted, title) index. It also taxes every note save, so the in-memory approach is better for an import-only lookup. 2) A bare title set is not enough for the conflict path, because the resolver needs the existing row (existing_conversations[0] ordered by created_at DESC, and the notes `existing` dict). Use the set as a negative filter: skip the DB lookup on a miss and fall back to the existing query on a hit. 3) Add every inserted or renamed title to the set as the import goes, so later items in the same chatbook see it. Keep the conversation check at archive_scope='all' semantics (non-deleted, archived included). 4) Separately, the wizard running the whole import on the event loop (run_worker of a coroutine) is the larger UI cost and is worth its own finding.

SELECT * FROM conversations WHERE title = ? AND deleted = 0 ... -> SCAN conversations

The unfiled COUNT(*) that runs on every page adds 4-5 ms regardless. An expression index ON notes(deleted, julianday(last_modified), id) gives `SEARCH n USING COVERING INDEX (deleted=?) | USE TEMP B-TREE FOR LAST TERM OF ORDER BY` at 0.15 ms for newest and 0.09 ms for oldest, with the same rows as the unindexed query. It also needs a notes-table rebuild to change the DEFAULT, which is SQLite's no-ALTER-DEFAULT case and carries FTS and trigger risk. That normalisation belongs to TASK-32803. The low-risk perf fix is one expression index that keeps julianday() semantics: CREATE INDEX ... ON notes(deleted, julianday(last_modified), id). It serves both newest and oldest (measured 0.09-0.15 ms), and date functions without 'now' are allowed in index expressions; the repo already has idx_console_trace_retention_expiry on julianday(). The fix needs the migration plus a VALID_TABLES/EXPECTED index census entry and a stat1-absent plan pin in scripts/index_plan_pin_census.tsv. OFFSET ?`. The frequency is higher than claimed: 'newest' is the DEFAULT sort, not an opt-in. title: No DB tunes cache_size / mmap_size / temp_store (2 MB page cache, file temp b-trees)
trigger: Any scan-shaped query on the larger DBs: Library LIKE and FTS searches, the notes tree default 'newest' sort, and chatbook title lookups, on every connection. Connections are thread-local, so every worker thread's connection sees the same effect.
cost: Measured min-of-25 on a copy of notes_big.db (37 MB content, load average ~50). A LIKE scan went 26.7 ms default to 20.1 ms with mmap 256 MB, and 25.8 ms with cache_size=-32000 alone. The placement newest page went 20.4 to 10.7 ms with mmap and 19.6 ms with cache alone. A title-lookup miss went 2.2 to 1.1 ms with mmap. temp_store=MEMORY changed nothing measurable. All three together match mmap alone. The finder's direction and rough magnitudes hold, but the gain belongs to mmap, not cache_size.
fix: In the single per-connection setup of ChaChaNotes and Media (and optionally Subscriptions): PRAGMA cache_size=-32000 (32 MB), mmap_size=268435456, temp_store=MEMORY. That is 3 lines per DB; keep them out of Chunking Lab / recovery.
fix_notes: Set only PRAGMA mmap_size (e.g. 256 MB). It delivers the whole measured gain and lives in the shared OS page cache. Drop cache_size=-32000: it gave no measurable gain here, because the scan working set exceeds 32 MB, and it is PER CONNECTION. Connections are threading.local, so every asyncio.to_thread pool thread can hold one per DB, and a long session could grow RSS to 32 MB × threads × DBs. Drop temp_store=MEMORY: no measured gain, and it moves large content-bearing sorter spills into RAM. Known mmap caveats: an I/O error or a file truncated by another process surfaces as SIGBUS instead of SQLITE_IOERR, avoid it on network filesystems, and the WAL file is not mapped. Keep it out of Backup and recovery validation connections, as the finder says.
evidence:
conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;")
conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")
# no cache_size / mmap_size / temp_store anywhere except Backup validation
reason: Confirmed at ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3502/3509/3511 and Client_Media_DB_v2.py:1143/1151/1152. The per-connection setup is only journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=NORMAL and foreign_keys=ON. A case-insensitive grep over every .py file finds cache_size, mmap_size or temp_store only in Backup_Recovery/sqlite_validation.py:223-224, so app DBs run with SQLite defaults: about 2 MB page cache, no mmap, and file-backed temp. No backlog or Docs/Design item mentions mmap_size or cache_size. The benefit is real but modest and comes almost entirely from mmap. It applies to every scan-shaped query, most of which already run off-loop.

title: TldwCli.__init__ opens and schemas five feature DBs before first paint (~340 ms every boot)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/app.py:8117-8120, tldw_chatbook/app.py:8287, tldw_chatbook/app.py:10004 (ensure_default_workspace; Console dependency), tldw_chatbook/app.py:10395 (pre-loop boundary capture, by design), tldw_chatbook/app.py:15027 (on_mount reads ScheduledTasksDB synchronously)
trigger: Every launch. app_entry.py:606 constructs TldwCli() before run(), and __init__ calls _wire_library_collections_services (8117), _wire_workspace_registry_services (8118), _wire_watchlists_and_notifications_services (8120) and _wire_evaluation_services (8287) unconditionally and serially.
cost:
Scripts: scratch/lens2-godmod/bench_f1.py, bench_f1b.py. The machine load average was 32-40, so absolute times run about 1.3-1.9x the earlier unloaded runs (330-341 ms).

**Measured (isolated profile, each constructor timed after one warm-up private open):**
- Reopening all five DBs costs 613-673 ms serial: LibraryCollectionsDB 135-157, WorkspaceDB 120-123, SubscriptionsDB 128-136, ScheduledTasksDB 62-130, EvaluationOrchestrator 139-158 ms. Each spawns exactly 1 helper.
- A split run with prepare_in_helper wrapped came to 418-491 ms in total. Of that, 277-317 ms (65-70%) is helper time and 126-199 ms is schema/PRAGMA work.
- First creation costs 1,307 ms; ScheduledTasksDB alone takes 739 ms with 8 spawns.
- One connect_private_sqlite plus close has a median of 65-79 ms, against 0.17-0.22 ms for plain sqlite3.

**Severity.** The cost is real, serial and pre-paint on every boot: app_entry.py:606 runs TldwCli() before run(), and __init__ calls the wire methods at app.py:8117-8120 and 8287 after the parallel pool joins at 8021-8049. Cold boot to _ui_ready is 2.7-2.8 s (Docs/Design/2026-09-04-holistic-perf-review.md:61), so these five DBs are about 12% of launch latency. It delays the first frame but never freezes an interactive UI, so it is P1, not P0.

**Overlap with F3.** About two thirds of F1 is F3's per-open helper cost. Dedupe them in the fix plan.

**Traps the fix plan must know:**
- **Thread-local connections.** LibraryCollectionsDB._thread_local (Library_Collections_DB.py:494/584), WorkspaceDB._thread_local (Workspace_DB.py:349/421), SubscriptionsDB._local (:588) and EvalsDB._local (Evals_DB.py:184) all hold one connection per thread. The open in __init__ therefore warms the main/loop thread's connection. Deferring construction to a worker, or into the parallel pool at app.py:8021, leaves the first loop-side sync use paying a fresh ~65 ms helper open on the loop. One concrete case: the sync 0.1 s timer _deferred_wire_collections_capture_services calls legacy_recovery.list_collections on LibraryCollectionsDB (app.py:9828).
- **ScheduledTasksDB.** Its _get_connection opens a fresh, caller-closed connection on every operation (scheduled_tasks_db.py:216-248). Its __init__ open is pure pre-paint cost, and on_mount's sync reconcile_stale_automation_runs (app.py:15027 -> transaction()) spawns one more helper (about 65 ms) on the event loop at every mount.

**Coverage.** TASK-21105 (Done) deferred six other stores and left these five, so this is new scope. No open task covers it.
fix:
1. Extend the TASK-21105 template (Done; it covered research, notifications, event/sync state, writing and kanban, but not these five). Make `local_library_collections_db`, `local_workspace_db`, the watchlists `SubscriptionsDB`, `ScheduledTasksDB` and `evaluation_orchestrator` lazy, lock-guarded properties, following the `_rag_admin_services_lock` / `meeting_session_owner` precedent at app.py:8286 and :18051.
2. Alternatively, construct the DBs with a deferred-connection shape like ClientNotificationsDB.
3. Open them on first use in a worker. Schedulers that need them are already armed post-ready via `_schedule_deferred_startup_work`.
4. Add a boot guard: count `connect_private_sqlite` calls during `TldwCli()` in the startup perf test.
fix_notes:
- **Use TASK-21105's own shape, not lazy app properties.** Its plan rejected app-level lazy properties because Tests/ProductionApp AST-pins the _wire_* calls in __init__, and the app_factory harness patches get_*_db_path only during construction, so path resolution must stay eager. The right shape is the in-class deferred schema: the BaseDB initialize_schema=False seam, with a single-flight _ensure_schema at the connection chokepoint, and eager path resolution.
- **Deferral targets.** Do LibraryCollectionsDB and EvalsDB first (safe). Leave WorkspaceDB eager, or open it on a worker before the Console needs it.
- **Subscriptions.** Keep the boundary-capture invariant: it must be captured before the scheduler worker starts.
- **Scheduled tasks.** Move the on_mount reconcile at app.py:15027 into a to_thread worker before deferring ScheduledTasksDB.
- **First use must happen off the loop.** Otherwise a deferred open (~60-70 ms with a spawn) lands on the event loop on the first Library or Evals visit.
- **Maintenance access.** runtime_maintenance.py:252/333 reads app.evaluation_orchestrator directly and needs a peek accessor, so maintenance does not force construction.

title: Every POSIX private-SQLite connection open spawns a Python helper subprocess (47 ms vs 0.09 ms)
trigger:
Every file-backed connect_private_sqlite on macOS and Linux:
- **Boot:** the F1 DBs plus the parallel futures.
- **Library visit:** 8 opens (TASK-24457).
- **Hybrid RAG search:** 2 opens per search.
- **Personal Context:** opens outside operation().
- **New threads:** each new worker thread's first thread-local connection.
cost:
Script: bench_f3.py, 12 opens per shape. Load average was 41-54, so absolute times are inflated.

**Measured per open (isolated profile):**

| Shape | Open (median) | Open (min) | Close (median) | Popen per open |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain sqlite3 | 0.10 ms | | 0.014 ms | 0 |
| connect_private_sqlite, writable (db.evals) | 82.8 ms | 65.3 ms (p90 127) | 0.64 ms | 1.0 |
| Read-only, rag.chachanotes_keyword_leg | 68.9 ms | 63.9 ms | 0.34 ms | 1.0 |

- **Close is not the cost.** It stays under 1 ms, so the per-open helper spawn is the whole expense.
- **Concurrent shapes.** Two parallel read-only opens (the hybrid RAG leg shape) take 99 ms wall (median). Eight parallel opens (the Library-visit shape, queued through HELPER_ADMISSION) take 232 ms wall (median).
- **Where the time goes.** A bare `python -I -S -c pass` takes about 15-20 ms, so roughly 45-60 ms per open is the helper's imports, IPC and validation.

**Mechanism.** private_sqlite.py:1864-1878 runs a Popen per open on non-Windows platforms (via prepare_in_helper -> private_sqlite_process.py:366), with no reuse. There are 93 call sites in 51 files (grep -c, untruncated).

**Triggers traced:**
- **RAG keyword legs.** rag_service.py:2069 run_in_executor -> _chacha_fts_rows -> :2266 opens a fresh read-only connection and closes it per search. The prompts leg does the same (:2549 -> :2706). Both run off the loop but add about 70-100 ms of wall time to each hybrid search.
- **ScheduledTasksDB.** It opens a fresh connection on every operation (scheduled_tasks_db.py:216). That includes on_mount's sync reconcile at app.py:15027, which puts one helper spawn (~65 ms) on the event loop at every mount.
- **Boot and Library.** About two thirds of F1's boot cost, and TASK-24457's Library-visit cost.

**Severity.** Almost all of this is off-loop latency or pre-paint time. The only on-loop instance is once per mount, about 65 ms. The finding holds, but it is P1, not P0.

**Coverage.** Partly known as TASK-24457 for the Library opens. The per-open cost itself has no open task. Any fix needs an ADR-125 amendment (see the verifier's notes).
fix:
1. Needs an ADR and a security review; the helper exists to validate artifacts without opening inodes in-process.
2. Option (a): keep one long-lived retained helper per process. HelperAdmission already accounts for four retained leases. Send `prepare` frames over its pipe instead of exec'ing per open.
3. Option (b): memoize a successful prepare per (path, st_dev, st_ino, st_uid, st_mode, st_nlink), and re-verify in-process with the existing `verify_expected_named_identity` fstat check before skipping the helper.
4. Independently, hold connections where calls repeat: a per-thread pool for the RAG ChaChaNotes and Prompts legs (the media leg already pools); wrap Personal Context request flows in `repository.operation()`; fix TASK-24457 by reusing screen-lifetime connections.
fix_notes:
- **Option (b) contradicts ADR-125.** Memoizing a prepare per stat identity is the 'one-time permission stamp' the ADR rejects, and its Alternatives section rules out metadata-only checks as incomplete. Treat it as off the table without an ADR amendment.
- **Option (a) needs an amendment.** A retained per-process helper conflicts with the ADR's 'No listener, daemon' clause. Only the four TTS owner permits are sanctioned as retained today.
- **Do the ADR-compatible part first.** Cut open counts rather than per-open cost: a held per-thread read-only connection for the RAG ChaChaNotes and Prompts legs (the media leg already pools), repository.operation() around Personal Context request flows, and screen-lifetime connections for TASK-24457.
- **Four transient HELPER_ADMISSION slots** mean bursts of parallel opens queue for a slot.
- **Measure close cost too.** TASK-32260 recorded 1.15 s cumulative for closes.
evidence:

                 1877  else:
                 1878      prepare_in_helper(request, reservation=envelope, deadline=deadline)
private_sqlite_process.py:366  lease._child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-I", "-S", ...helper_entry.py])
rag_service.py:2266  conn = self._connect_chacha_readonly(db_path)   # per search, closed after
reason:
The cited code is as quoted:
- private_sqlite.py:1864-1878: Windows runs _prepare_artifact in-process; every other platform calls prepare_in_helper.
- private_sqlite.py:1377: prepare_in_helper -> HelperLease.start.
- private_sqlite_process.py:366: subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-I', '-S', helper_entry]) runs once per lease, with no reuse.

The helper block covers every non-memory target, read-only included. I measured it independently in an isolated profile:
- **Writable open** (`connect_private_sqlite('db.evals')`): 61.8-163.8 ms, median 69.4, 10/10 spawns. Plain sqlite3.connect is 0.115 ms.

The RAG legs are confirmed as open-per-search: _chacha_fts_rows (rag_service.py:2217/2266) and _prompts_fts_rows (:2676/2706) each open a fresh connection per search, run via loop.run_in_executor (2069/2549). They are off the loop but add about 50-70 ms of wall time to every hybrid search, which is per-send when Console RAG is on. Personal_Context/repository.py:531 opens fresh outside operation(). There are 93 call sites in 51 files.

The cost is not a known open task. ADR-125 accepted 'connection acquisition gains process/IPC cost' but required that 'existing performance ceilings are not raised'. TASK-32260 (Done) profiled 12 helper connects at 1.02 s and 12 closes at 1.15 s on a Library open, and judged the cost not worth removing only because the work overlapped in workers. TASK-24457 (open) prices Library churn from before the helper existed.

title: First TLDWAPIClient build imports a 1,257-model schema surface (575-854 ms) on the event loop
trigger: Server-mode sessions, every boot: a set_timer(0.1 s) callback after _ui_ready -> _activate_collections_capture_authority -> build_client() -> import tldw_api.client on the event loop (app.py:16341-16344, 9873-9874, 9881, 9915). Also: a runtime switch to server (app.py:11548), and the first Server*Service call from a coroutine worker.
cost:
Script: bench_f4.py.

**Measured.** In a warm process (app and chat_screen already imported, tldw_api.client confirmed not resident), `from tldw_chatbook.tldw_api import TLDWAPIClient` took 775, 795 and 850 ms at load 41 and added 56 modules. The first build_runtime_api_client after that took 0.1 ms, so the whole cost is the import. The bootstrap.py:192 comment itself cites about 450 ms unloaded.

**Exhaustive trace of the deterministic on-loop trigger:**
1. app.py:16341-16344: _schedule_deferred_startup_work runs `self.set_timer(DEFERRED_COLLECTIONS_CAPTURE_WIRING_DELAY_SECONDS, self._deferred_wire_collections_capture_services)`. The delay is 0.1 s (app.py:795) and the callback is sync, so it runs on the loop.
2. :9874 ensure_collections_capture_services -> _wire_collections_capture_services. This also runs legacy_recovery.list_collections synchronously.
3. -> :9849 _activate_collections_capture_authority.
4. When runtime_state.active_source == 'server': :9909 get_active_context, then :9915 provider.build_client().
5. -> server_context.py:334 build_runtime_api_client -> bootstrap.py:195 imports tldw_api.client.

active_source is persisted state (source_state.py:109), downgraded to local only when no server is configured (bootstrap.py:425-427). A server-mode user therefore hits this on every boot.

**Nothing earlier absorbs the import:**
- Every Server*Service.from_config and from_server_context_provider factory stores client=None plus a provider (for example server_evaluations_service.py:32-56).
- The import at server_context.py:16 is TYPE_CHECKING-only.
- The build_runtime_api_client calls at app.py:10923/10929 sit inside a lazy factory closure.
- The screen pre-import thread starts at 0.2 s (app.py:834), after the 0.1 s timer, and does not import tldw_api.
- No open backlog task covers this (grep).

**Result.** In server mode, every boot freezes the event loop for about 0.45-0.85 s, 0.1 s after the first frame. That is a ≳100 ms freeze on boot, so P0 stands.

**Scope caveat.** Only sessions whose persisted source is server are affected; local-only default users never import this module. Secondary triggers are handle_runtime_backend_changed (app.py:11548) and the first Server*Service coroutine call.
fix:
1. Quick fix: when a server target is configured, import `tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client` on the existing background pre-import thread after `_ui_ready`, as one extra entry beside the screen routes.
2. Belt-and-braces: have `ServerContextProvider.build_client` / `LegacyConfigServerClientProvider.build_client` resolve the class via `await asyncio.to_thread(import_module, ...)` on first use.
3. Structural fix, the decomposition seam for this god class: split TLDWAPIClient into per-namespace delegates (the MCPUnifiedClient precedent already in the package), each importing only its schema submodule. First-call cost drops from 1,257 models to the few dozen a namespace needs. TASK-285 (Done) moved this cost off boot but left it on the first call.
fix_notes:
- **The quick fix alone is insufficient.** A background pre-import after _ui_ready races the 0.1 s capture-wiring timer. If the thread is mid-import, the loop's import blocks on the module import lock for the remainder.
- **Make the build off-loop.** Also move the server branch of _activate_collections_capture_authority, and _deferred_wire_collections_capture_services as a whole (it also runs legacy_recovery.list_collections synchronously), into asyncio.to_thread. Alternatively, give ServerCollectionsCaptureService the provider and build the client lazily inside an awaited to_thread.
- **Fix #2 as worded does not fit.** 'await asyncio.to_thread(import_module)' cannot go inside the sync build_client(); the callers need an async ensure step.
- **Per-namespace delegates** (the MCPUnifiedClient precedent) are the right structural fix. That is a large refactor of a 16.7k-line module with a size-ratchet row.

title: No gc.freeze() after boot: every automatic full GC scans the 250k-object import heap (~62 ms)
trigger: Automatic gen-2 collections during the session. CPython 3.12 runs a full collection once pending long-lived promotions exceed 25% of the long-lived heap. TASK-31966 captured one in Console activation (79 ms).
cost:
Script: bench_f5.py (isolated; load average 40).

**Heap and full-collection cost.** After importing app and chat_screen there are 250,738 tracked objects. An explicit gc.collect(2) has a median of 72.4 ms (min 69.0; the finder measured 62.3 unloaded).

**Frequency simulation:**
- One 559-widget re-mint (Static/Label/Vertical, unmounted, so a lower bound) adds 30,752 tracked objects.
- 40 simulated visits, keeping the last two visits alive and releasing older ones: **14 automatic gen-2 collections** (about 1 per 3 visits), with pauses of 59-92 ms.
- The same run after gc.freeze(): 16 automatic gen-2 collections at 6-64 ms (median about 25 ms), and a full collect of 11 ms (250,876 objects frozen).

**What freezing saves.** About 50-60 ms per automatic full collection, which is the unfrozen static import heap. That matches TASK-31966's observed 79 ms Console-activation gen-2 pause.

**Severity.** Each pause is below the 100 ms P0 bar. Amortised, it is about 20 ms per Console visit, so P1 on the per-visit hot path.

**Extra measured boot win.** During the boot import itself, GC ran 4 gen-2 collections totalling 140 ms (max 65.9) plus gen0/gen1 collections totalling 81 ms. So gc.disable() around the app_entry boot imports would save a further ~100-200 ms before first paint.

**Coverage.** Known as TASK-31966 (open; its AC#1 already names a frozen baseline and AC#2 requires an ADR). The new evidence is the attribution to the static heap and the session-wide scope.
fix:
1. Get the ADR TASK-31966 requires.
2. Call `gc.freeze()` once right after `self._ui_ready = True` (app.py:16160), and again when the background screen pre-import pass finishes (so the ~550 pre-imported modules join the frozen set).
3. Optionally `gc.disable()` around the boot import block in app_entry and re-enable it before `run()`.
4. Verify with the existing console mount profile and the TASK-31966 activation matrix. Record the maximum gen-2 pause before and after.
fix_notes:
- **ADR first.** TASK-31966 AC#2 forbids implementing this without the ADR.
- **Freezing at _ui_ready also freezes the first-mounted Console DOM.** Since the Console re-mints its widgets on every visit (TASK-24452), cycles in the first visit's widget tree would never be collected: a bounded, one-time leak.
- **Prefer freezing right after construction.** Freeze in app_entry immediately after TldwCli() construction and before run(), when the heap is mostly modules, classes and long-lived services. Then freeze again when the pre-import thread finishes (gc.freeze is global and safe from any thread).
- **Do not gc.collect() on the loop first.** That costs the same ~65 ms.
- **Expected side effect.** After freezing, full collections become more frequent but cheap, because long_lived_total shrinks.
evidence:
app.py:16160  self._ui_ready = True     # no gc.freeze()/gc.disable() anywhere in tldw_chatbook
# grep -rn 'gc\.(freeze|disable|set_threshold)' tldw_chatbook -> 0 hits
reason:
The cited code is as described. app.py:16160 is `self._ui_ready = True`. A repo-wide grep over tldw_chatbook finds 0 hits for gc.freeze, gc.disable or gc.set_threshold (only explicit gc.collect calls in Embeddings/PDF).

I re-measured in isolation after app and chat_screen: 250,683 tracked objects; gc.collect(2) median 65.2 ms; 0.0 ms after gc.freeze(). That matches the finder's 62.3 ms.

TASK-31966 (open) owns the Console-activation gen-2 pause: 79 ms observed, ownership unknown. Its AC#1 already asks for a comparison against a frozen baseline, and its AC#2 requires an ADR for any global GC policy.

The new evidence is the cause and the scope. About 62-65 ms of every full collection is the static import heap alone, independent of Console allocations. So every automatic gen-2 anywhere in the session pays it, not just Console activation. That is new scope, so this is confirmed rather than 'known'. With the Console re-minting about 559 widgets per visit (TASK-24452), gen-2 promotions accrue quickly.
