cost:
End-to-end benchmark at audit tree 840ed2ca58 in an isolated scratch profile. It drives the real ConsoleChatStore, ChatPersistenceService and a file-backed CharactersRAGDB, populated the way the app populates them: append_message(persist=True) writes the user and assistant trajectory rows; admit_library_activity then flush_library_activity writes library_activity rows from real minimize_library_activity events with 6 source refs, about 1 KB each; upsert_trajectory_rows writes tool_call and tool_result pairs. Each test calls store.library_activity_snapshot(session, selected) while cycling the selection, which is exactly what sync_projection does on a j/k token miss. Script: scratch/f1-second-lens/bench.py.

The host was loaded (loadavg 31-46 on 18 cores), so figures are process CPU time (min of 15 runs). Median wall time was 1.2-2.5x higher.

CPU per selection keypress (T turns, R trajectory rows, L library rows):
- No Library use (plain): 8.3 ms (T10/R20), 11 ms (T50/R100), 15 ms (T100/R200), 20 ms (T200/R400).
- 1 Library search per turn: 12 ms (T10), 17 ms (T25), 32 ms (T50), 54 ms (T100/L100).
- 2 Library searches per turn: 50 ms (T50/L100), 102 ms (T100/L200).
- Agentic, 2 Library searches and 4 tool calls per turn: 31 ms (T25/R300), 55 ms (T50/R600), 119 ms (T100/R1200/L200).
- Agentic, 4 tool calls and no Library use: 69 ms (T200/R2000).

Where the time goes:
- The strict per-row decode dominates whenever Library is used: decode_library_activity_event costs 374-387 us per row, so 75-78 ms is spent re-decoding all 200 Library rows on every keypress at T100. Pending events are re-encoded at 346-358 us each, but only while they are unflushed.
- The T x R scan (project_library_activity once per active turn, plus the dict comprehension at console_chat_store.py:4764) is really quadratic but secondary: 0.7 ms at R100, 11 ms at R400, 54 ms at T200/R2000.
- The synchronous fetch db.get_trajectory_rows (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:15823) costs a flat 8-10 ms CPU at any R (100 to 2000). The raw SQLite query is only 0.54 ms. The empty db.transaction() enter alone costs 5.3 ms: about 245 posix.open calls per transaction from Backup_Recovery _core_operation / acquire_storage (storage_admission.py:835). That is the known per-call storage admission cost (PERF-06), not new. It means even a 10-turn chat with no Library use pays about 8 ms per j/k.

Trigger, rechecked with untruncated grep. library_activity_snapshot has exactly one caller: UI/Console_Modules/library_activity.py:162 (sync_projection). sync_projection is reached from:
- chat_screen.py:21804 (_sync_console_control_bar_under_config). That runs from _sync_console_control_bar, which has 30 call sites, including ConsoleTranscript._notify_selection_changed. The transcript binds "down,j"/"up,k" (console_transcript.py:2992-2993) through select_message to call_later (:5339); action_clear_selection goes through :5460.
- _sync_console_rail_and_controls (chat_screen.py:18751), inside _sync_native_console_chat_ui, which the 0.2 s _poll_transcript interval (:18947) runs throughout streaming.
- sync_transcript (:18339), open_selected, and retry.

The only guard is the token (session, revision, active_path, selected, citation_count), and selected is part of it, so every j/k or arrow keypress (about 30 Hz on key-repeat) misses the guard. Every active-path growth during a send (user row, assistant placeholder, each TOOL marker) and every Library capture also misses it, via 6 _bump_library_activity_revision sites. Nothing upstream moves this work off the loop or caches it: no worker, no to_thread.

Correction to the first pass, confirmed: only the selected turn's rows are decoded twice. Every other Library row is decoded once per snapshot.

Why not P0: the cost reaches 100 ms or more only for long conversations with heavy Library use (T100 with 2 searches per turn, or agentic runs). Typical sizes cost 8-55 ms per keypress. That is squarely P1 (per-keystroke cost of 10-20 ms or more that scales with user data).

Fix priority based on these numbers:
1. Memoize decoded events by payload string, so the O(L) decode cost disappears.
2. Cache per-turn counts per (session, revision, active_path), so selection changes stop re-running the count loop.
3. Group rows by turn once, O(R).
4. The fetch cost falls with the PERF-06 admission fix.

Dedup note: the same finding is already in this audit's earlier compile, qa/perf-structural-audit-2026-09-27/data/items.md:2668 and report.md:393 (PERF-12, "library_activity_snapshot becomes linear"). It has no open backlog task in the audit tree: grep for library_activity_snapshot and project_library_activity in backlog/ returns 0 hits.
fix: (1) Build the selected view and the per-turn counts in one pass: group rows by turn_id once, O(R). (2) Split counts, which depend only on revision and active_path, from the selected-turn view, so a selection keypress reuses cached counts and decodes only the selected turn's rows. (3) Memoize decoded events in a small bounded dict keyed by (message_id, seq) or by the payload string; durable payloads are immutable. Pending events can carry their already-validated event objects instead of being re-encoded. (4) Query only event_kind='library_activity' rows (capture the index plan per CLAUDE.md), and run the fetch off-loop or cache it per library_activity_revision.

Caching them per (session, revision, active_path) and projecting only the selected turn on a selection change removes the T x R loop without restructuring anything. It is safer than moving the fetch off-loop, because sync_projection is called synchronously inside _sync_console_control_bar_under_config and pushes to the rail immediately; making it async needs a coalesced worker plus a stale-token check. A single O(R) group-by-turn pass is a straightforward replacement for the dict comprehension. If you memoize decoded events, key them by the payload string, not by (message_id, seq): pending rows get a synthetic seq that shifts between snapshots. Filtering event_kind='library_activity' in SQL needs a captured query plan with sqlite_stat1 absent, per CLAUDE.md, if an index is added. Separately, review_selection.py:143 also calls get_trajectory_rows on the sync path and is worth checking under the same fix.

title: Hands-free TTS PCM producer busy-polls at 1 kHz on the Textual event loop for the whole duration of spoken playback
trigger: Only reachable when speculative_voice_qualified() is True, which is false on all platforms in the shipped manifest, or through the dev-only scripts/run_speculative_voice_dev.py. In that state, the producer tasks run on the app loop and poll at 1 kHz while PCM drains and until tts_closed is acked.
cost: asyncio.sleep(0.001) loops cost ~800-1000 wakeups/s per poller, which is the known asyncio behaviour and consistent with the finder's measurement. The cost is real while speech is playing, but zero for shipped users today.
fix: CreditWindow already has an event-driven waiter: _waiter plus _wake() via call_soon_threadsafe, fired from acknowledge. Add an `async def drained()` that uses the same waiter and is woken when outstanding reaches (0, 0) or the window closes. Await it in both places instead of sleeping. The test-only _PhraseState.put/next_block 1 kHz loops should become an asyncio.Queue or be deleted (F10).
fix_notes: CreditWindow has exactly ONE _waiter slot, and reserve() raises ProtocolError('voice_capacity_exceeded') if a waiter is already present. A drained() that reuses that slot can collide with a concurrent reserve() on the same window. Use a separate drain waiter/Event, or make sure the drain waits only on windows no producer is still reserving from; the predecessor's PCM window is finished by then, and the cleanup window is serialized through previous_retirement. _wake() fires on every settled ack, not only at empty, so drained() must re-check outstanding in a loop. acknowledge() arrives from the IPC reader thread, so the wake must stay call_soon_threadsafe. The first poll reads self.outstanding, which follows whichever self._window is current, so the waiter must bind to the window it observed. Fix it before any platform is qualified.

...
while self.outstanding != (0, 0):          # wait for previous phrase's PCM to be acked (played) by the child
    await asyncio.sleep(_POLL_SECONDS)
...
while (self._cleanup_window.outstanding != (0, 0) and self._transport_failure is None):
    await asyncio.sleep(_POLL_SECONDS)

title: Provider-continuation checkpoint is fully re-parsed ~7x and rewritten whole on every tool-call transition (quadratic over an agent run)
trigger: For continuation-protocol providers, each ToolBatchReady, ToolCallExecuting and ToolCallFinished event goes to ConsoleChatStore.persist_provider_continuation_event on the agent worker thread, and AgentRuntime.transition_call also transitions locally. Each tool call produces 2 events.
cost: Re-measured in an isolated env on a heavily loaded host (loadavg ~55), so the figures are pessimistic. transition_provider_call: 0.4 ms at 8 calls/17 KB, 3.9 ms at 64 calls with 2 KB results (151 KB), 4.5 ms at 128 calls (303 KB), 22.6 ms at 64 calls with 12 KB results (766 KB) and 26.4 ms at 128 calls (1.5 MB). parse(str) takes 17 ms at 1.5 MB. With ~7 passes per event, that is ~3-30 ms of GIL-held CPU per event at typical sizes and ~100+ ms at the 128-call/large-result cap. The per-event full-checkpoint UPDATE amplifies WAL writes, up to about 128 x ~1.5 MB in the worst case (estimated).
fix: Trust instances the parser itself produced. title: Chunk_Lib offset synthesis is O(N*S) and cubic on its fallback path; it dominates every improved_chunking_process call
trigger: Every improved_chunking_process call: Library text/document/PDF/OCR/ebook ingest, Library re-chunk (per media item, including bulk), and summarization chunking. These run in the parse pool or a worker thread. Media defaults: document=sentences 1500/100, plaintext/web_article=paragraphs 500/200, audio/video=sentences 500/200.
cost:
The cost is real and large, but on the default paths it is linear and off the event loop, so P2 fits the rubric (import and re-chunk path, and it only blows up on opt-in methods). Known task: TASK-33288 (PERF-29, medium), whose AC#3 already names 'chunking offset synthesis'.

METHOD. Micro-benchmark in an isolated env: scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, TLDW_TEST_MODE=1, audit tree 840ed2ca58, scripts in scratch/slice15-lens2/{bench,bench2,diag,fixcheck,gil}.py. It runs improved_chunking_process on real repo Markdown (Docs/**/*.md) and on clean synthetic prose, and times the part inside _synthesize_flat_offsets by monkeypatching it. Each figure below is synth time / total time, taken from one run (not best-of-N). The box was shared with other agents, so expect noise of about ±30%.

TRIGGERS (untruncated grep, 51 references). Four callers pass defaults:
- Library import: the form defaults are chunk on, words 1000/100, and app.py forces method=words for text, pdf, audio/video and image. It runs in a spawn-context multiprocessing.Pool, a separate process, so it takes no GIL from the UI.
- Library re-chunk: PLAIN_RECHUNK_OPTIONS is words 500/100, and it runs in a run_worker(thread=True) thread in the app process.
- RAG index: config words 400/100, run through loop.run_in_executor in a thread in the app process.
- Ebook import: ebook_chapters.
The summarization default (sentences 500/200) is unreachable in production. No analyze() call site passes recursive_summarization or chunked_summarization as True; I checked all 24 references.
Sentences and paragraphs are reached only by opt-in routes: the Auto picker (plan_auto_chunking gives sentences 900/120 for plaintext, audio, video and image), the ebook panel's sentences/paragraphs choice, templates, and the agent library_rechunk_media spec. [chunking] default_template is "", so re-chunk defaults to the plain tier.

DEFAULT WORDS PATHS. diag.py shows every chunk matches as a word run (28/28, 167/167), so the scan is about N slice positions in total and the cost is O(N*S), not quadratic.

| Config | 50 KB | 200 KB | 488 KB | 977 KB | 1.95 MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Library import, words 1000/100 | 16.5/24.6 ms | 52.7/81.4 ms | 162/225 ms | 276/380 ms | 974/1720 ms |
| Re-chunk, words 500/100 | 8/19 ms | 27/46 ms | 99/290 ms | 119/213 ms | 526/1069 ms |
| RAG index, words 400/100 | 7/17 ms | 55/96 ms | 56/106 ms | 243/342 ms | 394/799 ms |
| Ebook chapters | — | 36/87 ms | 114/193 ms | 571/685 ms | 927/1165 ms |

That is 35-83% of chunking time, but tens to hundreds of ms per document on a background path.

OPT-IN SENTENCES PATH. On real Markdown every sentence chunk fails the word-run match: the engine re-splits tokens such as '3.13'. diag.py shows 0 of 8 chunks matched and 198,536 slice positions for 24,817 words, so each chunk scans the whole word list and the cost is O(C*N*S). Auto sentences 900/120 cost 1156/1179 ms at 195 KB and 11,502/11,535 ms at 488 KB (99.7%). Clean prose does match but S is about 15k words: 826/836 ms at 195 KB and 2648/2673 ms at 488 KB.

GIL. In-process threads (re-chunk and RAG index) slow the event loop. An asyncio 10 ms ticker lags 13.4 ms at p50 (1.07 ms idle) while the synthesis runs in to_thread. That is jank, not a freeze.

FIX, MEASURED. A one-line first-word pre-check before the slice (`if words[wi] == chunk_words[0] and words[wi:wi+run_len] == chunk_words:`) gives byte-identical spans (identical=True in all 4 cases). Speedups: Markdown sentences at 488 KB, 12,181 to 85 ms; clean prose, 2867 to 24 ms; words at 976 KB, 221 to 43 ms; ebook_chapters, 225 to 39 ms. It is lower risk than switching to the engine's offsets, which changes the offset contract. Location: tldw_chatbook/Chunking/Chunk_Lib.py:650. The unconditional call is at :1668. The template_runtime.py:556 caller is used only in tests.
fix: (1) Use the offsets the engine already computes. title: Semantic chunking calls sklearn cosine_similarity and slices sparse rows once per adjacent sentence pair
trigger: Any engine chunk with method='semantic' (pdf ingest default when no method is injected, auto planner, templates). Once per document, off the loop.

Keep the existing error fallback (similarity=1.0) for the degenerate case.

title: structure_aware _in_processed_range linearly scans a growing range list for every element: O(E^2)
trigger: chunk with method='structure_aware' via templates or the auto planner, once per document, in a background worker or Lab child.

A bisect that checks only the predecessor by start is therefore exact only if ranges are merged on insert, or if you keep a running max-end. trigger: Every engine chunking call (ingest, re-chunk, RAG parent/child, Lab admission and execution). Off the loop.

title: AgentRuns orphan reconcile still parses every step of every terminal run on each process launch, holding the write lock and spiking memory
trigger: First AgentRunsDB construction with reconcile_on_init=True per process, from Console runtime's to_thread receipt service init or other worker constructions, plus the Settings panel's on_mount thread worker. All off-loop, once per app launch.

1. Persist a sweep watermark (max created_at or rowid already checked) and scan only newer terminal runs.
2. Do the lifecycle check in SQL instead of hydrating everything in Python: `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM agent_run_steps s WHERE s.run_id = r.id AND json_extract(s.payload, '$.kind') = ?)`, which avoids loading every payload.

The file's own comments warn that a DEFERRED read-then-write hits SQLite's non-retryable snapshot/upgrade deadlock. Instead, run the scan in a separate read transaction, then open a fresh IMMEDIATE transaction that re-verifies each candidate before inserting the repair diagnostic. A json_extract(payload,'$.kind') EXISTS in SQL avoids hydrating payloads. A persisted watermark needs an agent_runs schema bump.

title: Storage admission serializes every DB operation process-wide through one per-root 'initializing' section (~200 ops/s cap)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/storage_admission.py:216 (initializing), tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/storage_admission.py:244 (follower wait), tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/storage_admission.py:914 and :938 (file I/O under the global _lock), tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/participants.py:420
trigger: Any concurrent DB activity on worker threads while a loop or UI-thread DB op runs. Examples: Library ingest workers writing MediaDatabase while the UI thread upserts ingest jobs, and parallel Console sessions persisting while another session sends.
cost: b2.py (isolated, loadavg 48-57) instruments _Acquisition.initializing. The main thread really does wait for the leader: median 13-14 ms with 1 background MediaDatabase.transaction thread and 27-53 ms with 3. However, a control that replaces `initializing` with a no-op (all file I/O kept) did NOT help. Main-op median with 3 background threads went 77 -> 95 ms and 45.5 -> 82 ms across two runs; p95 went 284 -> 163 and 152 -> 169, which is noise. Aggregate background throughput was 40-62 ops/s normally and 30-44 ops/s with the section bypassed, and it stayed flat from 1 to 4 threads in BOTH modes. A GIL-only control (background threads running a pure-Python loop, no DB at all) inflated the same main op to 155 ms (1 thread) and 502 ms (3 threads). So the latency under contention comes from F1's per-op GIL-bound CPU plus a GIL convoy (about 800 GIL-releasing syscalls per op), not from the per-root leader section. The '~200 ops/s cap' is simply 1/(per-op CPU). The finding's alternative fix (let followers skip initializing) would buy nothing measurable; only F1's fast path removes the cost. The effect is real but is not an independent root cause, so fold it into F1 as one fix. Caveat: the box was saturated, so a possible gain of up to 2x from overlapping syscalls in parallel on an idle multi-core machine could not be measured.
fix: Mostly solved by F1's fast path, which never enters `initializing`. Otherwise, take the leader section only for the first acquisition that creates the hold for a root, and let followers with a live hold skip it.
fix_notes: The alternative fix (skip initializing only for followers that have a live hold) is NOT sufficient. The post-hold startup_permission and _scope re-check does file I/O under the global _lock and would still serialize every op. Only F1's fast path, which skips both sections when the token matches, removes the cap. Treat this as one fix with F1, not a separate change.

    allowed, reason = bootstrap.startup_permission(selector, root)
    ... qualified_for('admission', existing) ...
    authority = admission_authority(root)
# followers: while leader exists: _changed.wait(0.01)  (line 244)
# every store shares ONE bootstrap root -> all DB ops queue here
reason: _Acquisition.initializing (storage_admission.py:215-249) allows one leader per (root, pid). Every store shares bootstrap.default_bootstrap_root(), so the file-I/O body at 883-912 (startup_permission, qualified_for, admission_authority) is serialized process-wide. Followers loop on _changed.wait(0.01) and are woken by notify_all on leader exit. Also parse the head only (`statement[:32].lstrip()`) to avoid copying the full string. Keep the existing semantic-guard escape tests.
fix_notes: Prefer installing the trace callback on scope entry in _authorize and _authorize_trace_gc_deletion and calling set_trace_callback(None) in the finally. Generation comparisons are relative to the value captured at scope entry, so a boundary inside the scope is still detected. Connections are thread-local, so toggling is safe. Do NOT rely on bumping the generation only in TransactionContextManager, because that misses a raw conn.execute('COMMIT'/'BEGIN') from non-manager code, and the trace hook exists to catch exactly that. title: Every file-backed private SQLite open spawns, drives and reaps a fresh Python helper process (~43 ms per open, GIL-holding fork)
known_task: TASK-24457 (related: Library per-visit opens; predates the helper, so this finding multiplies its cost). No task covers the per-open helper cost.
trigger: Every connect_private_sqlite / BaseDB / CharactersRAGDB._get_thread_connection open of a file target on POSIX (94 call lines in 51 modules). Verified sites: boot constructors in App.__init__ (app.py:8118-8121, plus the :8020 parallel phase), the launch-wake open on the loop (console_launch_wake.py:69), a RAG keyword-leg open per search, Personal Context per operation, and owned-call reopens (F2).
cost: Measured in an isolated scratch env on this box. HelperLease.start median 54.3 ms plus close 10.8 ms, about 65 ms per open, vs raw sqlite3.connect+close at 0.11 ms. A bare 'python -I -S -c pass' spawn+exit is 25 ms. GIL probe with a 600 MB touched heap and a thread looping Popen: the main-thread 1 ms sleep loop's max gap went from 16 to 37 ms and p99 from 5.7 to 16 ms (50 MB: no measurable change). This matches the finder's claim of a stall on macOS, where fork() runs under the GIL. The design plan's own benchmark (plans/2026-09-07-...implementation.md:773) records 142.452 ms vs 6.428 ms for a repository open.
fix: Three options, lowest risk first. (1) Cut the number of opens: F2, plus TASK-24457 reuse. This leaves the security seam untouched. (2) Launch the helper with posix_spawn on macOS (close_fds=False, allowed because PEP 446 fds are non-inheritable). First verify that no inheritable fd, SQLite's included, can reach the child. Measured stall at 600 MB drops from max 22 ms to 7 ms. (3) Needs an owner decision, because the 2026-09-07 spec's 'Rejected alternatives' covers it: a stat-only already-private fast path. Use os.stat(follow_symlinks=False) on main/-wal/-shm/-journal: regular file, uid == euid, mode 0600, nlink 1. That opens no fd, so POSIX locks are safe. Fall back to the helper only when the file must be created or hardened, or a check fails. The pathname race is the same one verify_expected_named_identity already accepts. Keep the helper for TTS proof leases.
fix_notes: Option 3 (stat-only fast path) and any persistent helper pool are both explicitly rejected in ADR-125 'Alternatives' and in the 2026-09-07 design spec 'Rejected alternatives' ('A metadata-only fast path does not handle wrong-mode hardening or live proof closes'). Either needs an owner decision and an ADR amendment, not a perf PR. Option 2 (posix_spawn): CPython 3.12 on macOS takes the posix_spawn path only when close_fds=False, because there is no closefrom file action. That puts the burden on proving no inheritable fd leaks; PEP 446 and SQLite's O_CLOEXEC make that likely but not guaranteed across native extensions. A child inheriting an fd does not cancel the parent's POSIX locks. Lowest-risk levers: batch or share boot opens (one helper prepare per database, not per constructor-internal reopen), move the boot constructors at app.py:8118-8121 into the existing parallel phase, and cut per-call reopens (F2). Measure boot before and after with the ADR-125-required startup qualification.

title: Owned DB calls close their thread handle after every call, and ChaChaNotes close runs a blocking wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE), so hot async paths can pay F1 on each call
known_task: TASK-31501 (partial: the 1 Hz loop exists, but that task predates the owned-call reopen/TRUNCATE-per-tick cost)
trigger: There are 47 non-import run_owned_db_call/operation_owned_connection lines (console_fleet_wake 15, character_context 8, app.py 7, trace service/runtime 9, and others). Two hot paths verified: the 1 Hz maintenance loop (console_runtime.py:3290) and the 5 Hz run-time poll -> refresh_if_scope_changed -> _capture_scope (2 owned calls per tick). A reopen happens only when the executor thread chosen has no registered handle.
cost:
This raises the first verifier's P1 to P0, because the reopen frequency is now measured, not estimated.

Live app, isolated boot probe, second launch, 30 s idle A/B windows:
- **Maintenance on:** 26 owned calls, 25 reopened (96%, no registered handle on the chosen executor thread), 25 helper spawns (all ChaChaNotes, med 73.7 ms each). Child CPU 3.84% vs 0.16% with the 1 Hz task cancelled. Self CPU 18.11% vs 16.72%.
- **Loop:** gaps >50 ms were 46 vs 13; p99 was 69.9 vs 42.0 ms (loaded box).
- **Net:** about 5% of a core, always on while idle, of which the child 3.7% is unambiguous helper CPU. A peer's independent earlier run matched: 25/26 ticks without a handle, child 4.02%/4.08% vs 0.16%.
- **Executor:** the default executor had 22 threads, almost none holding a ChaChaNotes handle.

5 Hz sync probe (boot_poll.log): await ChatScreen._sync_native_console_chat_ui() every 0.2 s for 10 s with maintenance cancelled.
- 8 syncs, 20 owned calls (16 CharactersRAGDB, including character_context._capture_scope, and 4 WorkspaceDB). 20 of 20 reopened, 21 helper spawns, about 2.5 spawns per sync.

Standalone, the same owned call costs med 128-167 ms cold (reopen) vs 31-45 ms with a registered handle.

The 1 Hz loop itself is known (TASK-31501), but its per-tick reopen/helper cost came with TASK-32628 (b5251e9a6e) after that task was filed. Fixing 31501 removes the idle tax only. Retaining handles (quiescence-retirable, or a dedicated executor) also removes the per-sync and per-keystroke spawns. Keep TRUNCATE for shutdown and backup, and skip it only on owned-call retirement.
fix: The ideal fix is for owned calls to keep healthy handles: retire them lazily and let the quiescence registry close them for maintenance, rather than closing per call. Alternatively run owned calls on one small dedicated executor whose threads keep a registered handle. Give the 1 Hz maintenance loop a single long-lived connection (TASK-31501 removes the poll; this removes the per-tick reopen). Drop wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) from close_connection: use PASSIVE or rely on wal_autocheckpoint, and keep TRUNCATE for explicit shutdown and backup.
fix_notes: TASK-32628 added the per-call close deliberately so executor threads do not hold handles that block backup/recovery quiescence. Any keep-alive scheme must still let the quiescence registry retire idle handles on demand. A small dedicated executor with long-lived registered handles is the cleaner option. Do not remove TRUNCATE from close_connection globally, because explicit shutdown and backup rely on it to bound WAL size. Instead skip the checkpoint, or use PASSIVE, only on the owned-call retirement path. Add a connect counter test (idle 60 s plus one streamed turn) to pin the reopen rate.

title: Console Character search runs a full DB pipeline on every keystroke, with no debounce and no cancellation, including a BEGIN IMMEDIATE write
trigger: Every keystroke in the Console Character section search input. The cost is off-loop on default-executor threads, but it contends for the ChaChaNotes write lock and can trigger F2 reopens that stall the loop.
cost:
Standalone controller benchmark (bench_f3.py): the real ConsoleCharacterContextController against a scratch ChaChaNotes, typing 'lantern' as one uncancelled task per key at 120 ms, which is the shipped widget shape.

| Scenario | 1.2k messages | 10k messages (100x100) |
|---|---|---|
| Shipped, cold threads (live-app shape) | 1.58-1.63 s after last key; 10.4-10.7 s summed worker wall | 2.03-2.25 s; 13.6-14.2 s worker |
| Debounced single search, cold | 5 owned, 5 spawns, 1 IMMEDIATE; 0.68-0.77 s | 0.83-0.89 s |
| Shipped, warm handles | 0.30-0.68 s | 0.77-0.81 s |
| Debounced, warm | 0.23-0.26 s | 0.24-0.29 s |

In the shipped cold case, 7 keys made 23 owned calls, 23 helper spawns and 7 BEGIN IMMEDIATE + UPDATE search_state writes.

ensure_keyword_index takes 8-24 ms alone but 106-143 ms inside the burst, because overlapping pipelines serialize on the ChaChaNotes write lock. That confirms the write contention.

Correction: stale pipelines make 3 owned hops (scope capture x2 + _search_sync), not 5. Only the final one makes 5, so 7 keys cost 23 hops.

In the live app, the same 7-key burst made 29 owned calls, 28 reopened, 28 helper spawns and 8 ensure_keyword_index calls.

Loop lag in the standalone stays at max 16-27 ms. The cost is off-loop result latency plus lock contention, not a loop freeze, so it stays P1 (per-keystroke), not P0. The fix stands: debounce plus cancel, a generation check before _search_sync, and ensure_keyword_index off the keystroke path.
fix: Reuse the repo's debounce-with-cancellation-token pattern, which CONTEXT marks GOOD (browser search): about 250 ms debounce, and cancel self._task before starting a new one. Take ensure_keyword_index off the keystroke path: run it once on activation or first focus in a worker, and let keyword_search read the ready generation. Build the repository or service once per scope fingerprint instead of per call. Compare the fingerprint with one owned call, not two before and two after.
fix_notes: The low-risk fix holds: a debounce of about 200-250 ms plus cancel of the prior task, or reuse of the switcher modal's set_timer debounce. Cancelling an awaiting coroutine does not stop an in-flight to_thread callback, so also check the generation before issuing _search_sync. Move ensure_keyword_index to activation or first focus, or at least skip the state UPDATE when activated=1 and the policy/authority are unchanged. It must still run whenever the revision advances, otherwise results stay stale until maintenance runs.

title: Keyword-index maintenance does O(corpus) work inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE and rewrites every document's source_revision each pass
trigger: The first character search after any message or conversation write triggers a dirty pass: O(dirty projections) plus an O(all documents) UPDATE. The first search after importing or creating a character card with no chats triggers a full reconcile over every local character conversation, holding the write lock throughout. Both run off-loop in owned calls.
cost: Estimated. A full reconcile is about 1.25 ms per 500-message conversation (the finder's measurement, plausible given the json.dumps plus sha256 per projection), so 300 conversations is about 0.4-2 s holding the ChaChaNotes write lock. Streaming persistence and other writers block for that time, up to the 15 s busy timeout.
fix: Chunk maintenance the way the build path does: one short transaction per at most 128 conversations, with the fts_backfill_pacing INTER_CHUNK_PAUSE between chunks, fenced by _require_ready_ownership each chunk. Store the maintained source_revision on the generation row only, and have the search SQL compare against the generation instead of `d.source_revision = ?`, so a pass stops rewriting every document. Run maintenance in a background worker, not inline in the search (see F3).
fix_notes: Chunking into multiple transactions breaks the current atomic invariant that every document in the ready generation shares the generation's source_revision. The search SQL requires d.source_revision = generation.source_revision, so mid-maintenance chunks would fail closed and hide results unless the fence design changes as well. Moving the maintained revision onto the generation row only is the bigger win (O(changed) instead of O(documents)), but it must keep the dirty-ledger NOT EXISTS exclusion semantics. The medium risk rating is right.

trigger: Every outermost EvalsDB call. For Evals that means the per-cell writes (F3), the per-swap reads (F4/F5), and the Home run counts. Nested calls inside an admitted operation are free.

At depth 16, EvalsDB.get_task(missing) cost 9.1-9.8 ms CPU, list_tasks() with 20 rows 9.0-9.8 ms, and list_runs() 9.6 ms, each with 249 open() calls; the identical raw sqlite SELECT cost 0.003 ms with 0 opens. At depth 25, get_task and list_tasks cost 16.7-16.8 ms with 393 opens. The slope is 16 opens and about 0.77 ms per path component, and the intercept is about 0, so the cost is all path-walk. That predicts about 121 opens and about 3.6 ms per outermost call at the real depth-8 path. It also matches the first verifier (6.88 ms at depth 12, predicted 6.7) and the finder (7.84 ms at depth 14, predicted 8.3). Hot trigger: LibraryRail.compose (library_rail.py:465-606, 792-793) runs on the event loop and makes 7 separately admitted EvalsDB calls through EvalsViewModel: datasets, run_groups (list_runs plus run_group_cell_failure_counts), benches, classic_tasks, word_bench_datasets and probe_sets (each a fresh list_tasks or list_datasets). Measured for that exact read sequence: 47.5 ms CPU and 1743 opens at depth 16, 76 ms and 2751 opens at depth 25, which extrapolates to about 22 ms at the real depth. The same 7 reads inside one admitted _core_operation cost about 12 ms (249 opens). So about 15-20 ms of every rail compose is pure admission tax on the UI thread, for each Evals visit and each rail refresh(recompose=True) (section toggle, skills probe, selection). Nested calls are not free either: 10 nested get_task cost about 0.55 ms each (_core_access and metrics). The mechanism is shared by the 16 _core_transaction repositories, and post-pin TASK-33267 (PERF-08) covers it fully (it needs the ADR-126 amendment, D1). P1 stands; the Evals-local mitigation (one admitted operation per compose, or memoized list_tasks and list_datasets per compose) cuts about 6 of the 7 admissions safely now.
fix: Owner is the Backup_Recovery/DB slice, so confirm the cross-repository impact there. Direction: admit once per (repository, thread, storage generation) and re-validate only when the storage generation or pause state changes, e.g. a cheap in-memory epoch check on the uncontended path, as TASK-31502 proposes for the quiescence lock. Do not re-walk and re-verify the whole directory chain on every `with connection()`. Evals-local mitigation: batch writes (F3) and cache reads per compose (F4) to cut the call count.
fix_notes: High risk as stated: amortizing admission needs the ADR-126 amendment that TASK-33267 tracks (owner decision D1), and it must still refuse a moved, replaced or re-permissioned admitted directory or ancestor before dependent I/O. Keep it out of any Evals-local PR. The Evals-local mitigations (batching writes, memoizing per swap) are safe and cut the call count now.
reason: EvalsDB.connection (Evals_DB.py:236-239) is decorated with _core_transaction (participants.py:429-436). That wraps every outermost use in _core_operation, then participant.operation(), then storage admission (acquire_storage, storage_admission.py:835). EvalsDB is registered as a repository type ('db.evals', participants.py:313), and 38 EvalsDB methods open `with self.connection()` or `with self.transaction()`. The same decorator is used by 16 repositories (AgentRuns, Client_Media_DB_v2, Library_Collections, Library_Ingest_Jobs, Prompts, RAG_Indexing, Subscriptions, Workspace, local_kanban_service, notes_device_state_store, both Notifications DBs, local_research_service, scheduled_tasks_db, local_writing_service, Evals). At the pin, no open task covers DB-repository admission cost: TASK-32804.1 amortizes admission only for cached config reads, and TASK-31502 is the separate quiescence lock. Post-pin TASK-33267 (PERF-08, filed 2026-09-28) covers the mechanism fully ('about 245 opens and 4-15 ms per DB transaction on about 12 DB owners'), so this row adds Evals as one more owner rather than new mechanism.

title: Run-log append takes storage admission twice and reopens the segment file for every record (~12 ms per record)
known_task: TASK-32804.1 (related: the same per-call admission handshake, fixed only for config reads; the run-log site is not covered)
trigger: Every agent run with a Console scratch space (default path): at least one model record per step, plus a tool_call and tool_result record per tool call, through RunLogWriter.append -> _append_under_scope. Runs on the agent worker thread; sub-agents serialize on writer._lock for the inner acquire and write.
cost:
Isolated micro-benchmark (scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, TMPDIR in scratch, admit_startup() held via config import, bootstrap root asserted inside scratch). Script: scratch/second-lens-agents2/bench_runlog.py and bench_runlog_depth.py. The run is UNBOUND, which is the default: profile records are only written by restore/activation (replacement.py:1248, activation.py:45).

RunLogWriter.append of a 2 KB record at scratch depth (bootstrap root 14 parts, log dir 14 parts): median 29.3 ms, p90 77 ms. acquire_storage(log_dir) alone: median 14.6 ms. Raw open+write+flush: 0.047 ms.

The fix is proven by measurement. One outer acquire plus a raw write (the nested acquire in _write_bytes dropped) gave median 13.6 ms, about half the current cost.

cProfile of 100 appends: 200 acquire_storage calls, 49,000 posix.open calls (about 245 fd-verified opens per acquire through bootstrap.pinned_directory/_open_verified_parent), 400 startup_permission, 400 _scope and 1,000 _registry reads. posix.open alone was 1.9 s of 3.44 s.

Depth series:
- 16 parts: 554 opens per append, 20.6 ms median
- 20 parts: 682 opens, 27.8 ms
- 26 parts: 874 opens, 38.2 ms
That is exactly +32 opens per path component, so opens ≈ 42 + 32×depth. A real macOS install has a bootstrap root of about 6 parts (~/.config/tldw_cli/recovery-bootstrap) and a mkdtemp log dir of about 9 parts, so about 280 opens per append. A directory openat measured 30 µs on this machine, which puts a realistic cost at about 6-10 ms per record on macOS. Linux is estimated at about 1.5-3 ms (cheaper openat). This is lower than the 12-25 ms that the finder and first verifier measured under deep scratch paths, but the order of magnitude is the same.

Trigger, checked in code:
- on_record (agent_service.py:7639) calls writer.append for every _emit_record, which has 10 sites in agent_runtime.py: model, tool_call, tool_result and error.
- It runs on the agent worker thread. The UI loop is not blocked.
- A step with 3 tool calls writes 7 records, about 40-70 ms on macOS. A run with about 100 records is about 0.6-1 s.
- The inner acquire and the write run under writer._lock, which sub-agents share, so they serialize there.
- _scope/_records/_registry file reads also run under storage_admission's process-global _lock.

Nothing upstream caches this: the scratch_lease access_scope is only an in-memory identity check. raw_cli.py:417 runs on a thread=True worker and pays bind + 2 appends + manifest per command.

Severity stands: P1, a per-agent-step cost well above 10 ms on macOS. The first verifier's caveat holds: a lease held for the whole run would block backup drains. The safe first step is to drop the nested acquire, which the measurement shows halves the cost.
fix: Acquire one StorageLease in bind() (or per segment) and hold it until close() or segment roll. Keep the segment file handle open and do write+flush per record. Drop the nested acquire_storage in _write_bytes when the caller already holds the writer's lease. If maintenance needs to drain holders, have the lease expose a cheap revoked/generation flag and re-acquire only when it flips. Also worth filing for Backup_Recovery separately: acquire_storage re-reads control records and re-walks ~145 path components on every call and has 88 call sites.
fix_notes: Holding one StorageLease from bind() until close() is risky. Leases are deliberately per-operation so that maintenance (_LocalPause.drain / backup capture) can drain holders. A lease held for the whole run would make any backup or restore started during a long agent run time out on drain. The safe first step, with no semantic change, is to drop the nested acquire_storage in _write_bytes when it is called from _append_under_scope, _close_under_scope or _write_manifest_under_scope: the outer lease on log_dir already covers the segment file under it. That halves the cost. Keeping the segment fd open across records is fine only if it is closed or reopened whenever admission is lost. The larger lever belongs in storage_admission itself: amortise the admission handshake per generation, as TASK-32804.1 did for config reads. That benefits all 86 call sites, so file it against Backup_Recovery rather than only run_log.
evidence:
from ...storage_admission import acquire_storage
with acquire_storage(self.log_dir):      # outer, per record
    with self._lock:
        ...
        self._write_bytes(self._segment_path(), payload)
# _write_bytes:
with acquire_storage(path):               # inner, per record again
    with open(path, "ab") as handle: handle.write(payload); handle.flush()
reason: Code matches on 840ed2ca58. _append_under_scope (run_log.py:856) wraps every record in acquire_storage(self.log_dir), then calls _write_bytes (run_log.py:896), which runs acquire_storage(path) again at :767 and reopens the segment with open('ab') for each record. So there are two full admission handshakes per record. acquire_storage (storage_admission.py:835-963) is not reentrant-cheap. Each call runs bootstrap.startup_permission twice, _scope twice (bootstrap._records control-record reads plus _registry, which opens admission/registry.json under flock), qualified_for and _execution_selection_for, all under the module-global _lock RLock. Callers: agent_service.py on_record closure -> writer.append at 7680, reached from agent_runtime._emit_record at 9 sites (model, tool_call, tool_result, error). The Console bridge builds the writer at console_agent_bridge.py:7126 whenever a scratch space exists. run_log_enabled defaults to True. Child runs share the parent writer, since bind() ignores later calls. raw_cli.py:417 is a second constructor. It runs on the agent worker thread, not the event loop, but it adds wall time before every step's next model request, so per-send and per-step. The existing task TASK-32804.1 amortised the same per-call admission handshake only for get_cli_setting, and 86 other acquire_storage call sites remain. This finding is a new site with new evidence.

title: Nested AGENTS.md resolution re-walks and re-reads the whole target directory chain on every tool batch, under the shared ledger lock. Over SSH that means 4×depth remote ops per batch plus 4 per send
trigger: Every tool batch that touches a path-aware local fs tool (read/grep/ls/edit) in a Console run with a project-instruction binding, via AgentRuntime prepare_tool_calls -> ledger.prepare. P1 applies to SSH remote bindings (shipped in PR #2838): 1 stat per path component plus 3 fs_read per absent directory, every batch, plus ping + 3 reads per send. On local bindings the same re-walk costs only a few ms on a worker thread, which would be P3.
cost:
Op counts measured with the real ProjectInstructionResolver + RemoteInstructionIO and a counting fake executor (scratch/second-lens-agents2/bench_instr.py). A target with no AGENTS.md costs 4 executor ops per path component per batch, identical on every batch:
- depth 1: 4 ops
- depth 3: 12 ops (3 stat_path + 9 fs_read)
- depth 5: 20 ops (5 stat_path + 15 fs_read)
The first batch adds 1 ping. resolve_startup on a fresh IO costs 1 ping + 3 fs_read per send.

The code path confirms why. _resolve_nested_directory returns only a fallback_condition for absent candidates. resolve_targets adds nothing to sources or outcomes for them, so the ledger's _terminal_scopes never records them, and InstructionActivationLedger.prepare (project_instruction_runtime.py:500-515) re-resolves them under self._lock on every batch.

Per-op latency comes from the user's recorded live LAN UAT; I did not re-measure it here:
- Audit pin 840ed2ca58: one-shot ssh exchange at about 0.7 s per warm call. A depth-3 batch then costs about 8.4 s, much worse than the finder's 0.6-1.8 s estimate.
- Current origin/dev: the SSH session worker (#2879, ad228213cd, merged after the pin) is on by default. The send path passes session_key into _default_remote_instruction_executor, and ops ride the run's session: 12-15 ms median warm, 3.3-5.1 ms with coalescing. A depth-3 batch is then about 40-180 ms on a LAN and scales with RTT on a WAN. Startup is ping (plus a local ssh -G) + 3 reads per send.

The context-snapshot preview (build_context_snapshot, dev line 21487) still passes session_key=None. It stays on the one-shot path at about 0.7 s per op, off-loop.

The fix should target dev, where it is still P1 for remote bindings (every fs-tool batch, multiplied by target depth).

Local bindings measured 4.6 ms and 546 lstat per depth-5 batch at scratch root depth 11, less at real depth. That is P3, as the first verifier said. Fleet chains share the ledger RLock and serialize behind the remote round trips (confirmed in code).
fix: (1) Memoize per ledger for the dispatch lifetime: record directories already walked, and directories resolved as 'absent' for both candidates, alongside _terminal_scopes. Resolution is already pinned to dispatch_started_wall_ns, since a later-created file would only yield a content-free 'stale' outcome. Only resolve directories not seen before. (2) For remote bindings, reuse the status cache's identity chain (cfg.cache.identity_for) instead of RemoteInstructionIO.ping() per send, or cache the IO per binding. Add one batched worker op that stats a chain and reads both candidates in one round trip. (3) Resolve outside the ledger lock and merge results under the lock with an activation-revision check.
fix_notes: Memoising 'absent' directories for the dispatch changes semantics slightly. Today, a file created mid-dispatch surfaces a content-free 'stale' outcome and warning. With a memo it would silently stay absent. That is probably acceptable, but this is a trust boundary (ADR-068/069), so it needs a security review and a pinning test. Key memo entries by canonical path, and invalidate them on any resolution_failed. Caching RemoteInstructionIO per binding across sends must still honour the status cache's identity re-capture: a stale or retargeted root must re-ping. A batched worker op (stat the chain and read both candidates in one round trip) is the highest-value lever, but it needs a worker bundle and protocol change. Resolving outside the ledger lock requires a revision check on merge. The lowest-risk first step is to memoise absent scopes plus walked directories for the ledger lifetime.
evidence:
with self._lock:                      # ledger lock shared by all chains
    ...
    if targets:
        batch = self._resolver.resolve_targets(... terminal_scopes=frozenset(self._terminal_scopes) ...)
# absent scopes never become terminal/pinned, so each batch re-does:
failure = self._remote_io.walk_component_chain(root, lexical, ...)  # 1 stat_path per component
result, was_pinned = _resolve_nested_directory(...)  # override + AGENTS.md + override recheck
reason: The code matches. InstructionActivationLedger.prepare (project_instruction_runtime.py:500-515) calls resolver.resolve_targets inside `with self._lock` (an RLock shared by every model chain of the dispatch). resolve_targets (resolver.py:486-557) re-walks every target chain on every batch: in the remote branch, one stat_path executor op per component through walk_component_chain (1589-1628), and in the local branch, lstat per component. Only scopes in terminal_scopes are skipped. An absent AGENTS.md produces neither a source nor an outcome (_resolve_nested_directory returns a fallback_condition), so absent scopes are never recorded and are re-resolved on every batch: override read, standard read and override recheck, i.e. 3 fs_read ops per directory remotely (read_candidate -> _fs_read_all -> executor.execute). Pinned sources are also re-validated. For remote roots, LocalToolProvider.path_targets -> _remote_path_targets maps targets lexically, so the ledger receives real remote scopes before each remote op. Per send, _resolve_remote_project_instruction_startup (console_chat_controller.py:21767, called at 21888 for the preview and 27901 for the send) builds a new RemoteInstructionIO through _remote_instruction_io_for_selection (line 2024). ping_payload is cached only per IO instance, so every send pays a ping plus 3 or 4 fs_read/stat ops. Each executor op is an ssh ControlMaster client spawn plus a remote python bootstrap (remote_workspace_transport.py). It runs on the agent worker thread and in asyncio.to_thread for startup, not on the event loop. No open task covers it: grep of backlog/tasks for RemoteInstructionIO, walk_component_chain and terminal_scopes finds only Done tasks (TASK-19635) and TASK-32562 (backup).

trigger: Every Console agent send (run_reply -> build_console_first_request_plan -> build_first_request_schema_plan -> probe_initial_catalog), plus every sub-agent spawn without a precomputed plan, plus the inspector's Next-Send previews. Runs on a to_thread worker before the first provider request.
cost:
Measured with REAL tool schemas (21 LIBRARY_TOOL_DESCRIPTORS + 29 local specs from _default_specs = 50) and the real catalog_schema_tokens (gpt-4o/openai, tiktoken available); script scratch/second-lens-agents2/bench_probe.py. The full rendered set is 40,356 chars (native) and 53,010 (fence).

| Tools | Mode | Cold memo | Warm memo | Single measure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | native | 51.5 ms | 5.5 ms | 1.7 ms (warm 0.21 ms) |
| 50 | fence | 111 ms | 27.3 ms | 3.9 ms (warm 0.99 ms) |
| 70 | native | 90 ms | 13.1 ms | 2.2 ms |
| 70 | fence | 198 ms | 54.8 ms | 5.1 ms |
| 100 (MCP-sized) | native | 192 ms | 24.4 ms | 3.4 ms |
| 100 (MCP-sized) | fence | 450 ms | 146 ms | 7.2 ms |

The probe costs 25-60x a single measurement and grows quadratically with catalog size. Even with a warm memo, each prefix must be rendered and hashed, so the O(N²) character work remains.

Callers, exhaustive: build_first_request_schema_plan is called from console_agent_bridge.py:4926 (build_console_first_request_plan) and agent_service.py:5004 (sub-agent _run_one when no plan is passed). build_console_first_request_plan is called per send at bridge 6076 (run_reply, to_thread) and by the previews at 5559 and 5680. There is no early exit before the probe apart from an unknown context limit, and no plan memo.

One correction to the finder: the 4096-entry memo churn happens only when the catalog or model changes. Steady-state sends hit the same prefix keys and insert nothing new.

Severity stays P1. It is per send and quadratic in catalog size, which grows with connected MCP servers. The first send after boot costs 51-200 ms, and steady state is 27-146 ms in fence mode. Caveat: the most common configuration (native-tools cloud provider, about 50 tools, warm memo) is only about 5-13 ms per send, all on a worker thread. The fix is trivial and low-risk: measure the full set once.
fix: The function is all-or-nothing, so measure the complete allowed set once and return None if it exceeds the limit. A concatenated schema list's token count bounds every prefix. If a prefix proof is truly required, add schemas cumulatively but measure only at geometric checkpoints or the end, and keep the positive-int validation. Optionally skip memoizing schema-set estimates to avoid churning the shared estimate cache.
fix_notes: A single full-set measurement is safe. The function is all-or-nothing, and the full rendering is a superstring of every prefix's rendering apart from the closing delimiters, so its token count is at least every prefix's count in practice (BPE is near-monotonic, and the check only needs `> limit`). Keep the positive-int validation on the single result. Skipping memoisation of schema-set strings is optional: after the fix only one entry is inserted per plan, so the cache churn goes away on its own.
reason: The code matches at tool_catalog.py:2349-2358. Each loop iteration calls measure_schema_set(tuple(schemas)) on the whole growing prefix, so the cost is O(N^2) in rendering, json.dumps/render_tool_protocol and tiktoken. The only caller is agent_service.build_first_request_schema_plan:980, using catalog_schema_tokens (agent_service.py:1009-1047). The plan is built per send in ConsoleAgentBridge.run_reply (console_agent_bridge.py:6076, run through _run_maintenance_agent_call -> asyncio.to_thread), per sub-agent _run_one at agent_service.py:5004 when no plan is passed, and in the two inspector previews (5559 and 5680, both run through asyncio.to_thread). So it runs on worker threads, not the loop, but directly on the pre-provider span of every send. The estimate memo (token_counter.py _ESTIMATE_CACHE, 4096 entries, cleared wholesale) makes repeated prefixes a hit on later sends, but every prefix still has to be rendered, json-dumped and hashed. No open task covers it: TASK-31212 is about graceful degradation, not cost.

title: PreToolUse hooks run serially per tool call in wrap_review
trigger: Opt-in: only when [hooks] has PreToolUse entries. Then every tool batch with N calls fires N hook subprocess rounds serially on the agent worker thread before review and dispatch.
cost: Not re-measured. The finder's 4.7 ms per fire with /usr/bin/true is plausible (process spawn plus asyncio.run plus a JSON round trip). A real Python hook of 50-80 ms scales linearly with batch size. The cost is real, but gated behind opt-in config, so P2.
fix: Submit every call's matching hooks to self._pool up front, keyed by call. Then reduce per call, keeping the first-deny-wins semantics per call and the same refusal mapping. Admission and closed checks stay under _admission_lock.
fix_notes: Firing all calls' hooks at once changes externally observable ordering. User hooks that append to a log, rate-limit or keep state may assume serial per-call invocation, so document the change or make it opt-in. With N calls x M specs and a 4-worker pool shared across concurrent fleet chains, one chain's batch can queue behind another's, so keep the per-call first-deny-wins reduce and the fail-closed mapping when a future is cancelled at close(). Keep admission under _admission_lock as proposed.
evidence:
for call in calls:
    outcome = self.fire("PreToolUse", session_id=session_id, run_id=run_id,
                        data={"tool_name": call.name, "tool_args": call.args})
    # fire() blocks until every matching hook process for THIS call exits
reason: The code matches at run_hooks.py:839-849. wrap_review loops over calls and calls self.fire('PreToolUse') for each one. _fire (676-705) submits the matching specs to self._pool (4 workers) and blocks in _results_from_futures until they finish, so calls are strictly serial even though the pool could run several at once. It is installed at console_agent_bridge.py:7054-7056 only when _ensure_run_hooks() returns an engine, i.e. [hooks] is configured (opt-in), and _fire returns immediately when _matching() finds no PreToolUse spec. It runs on the agent worker thread. The serial loop does not short-circuit on a deny (every call fires regardless), so parallel firing would not do extra work. No open task covers it.

title: InstructionChainPayloadState.capture deep-copies the whole history and schemas on every tool batch, even when prepare returns 'proceed'
trigger: Every tool batch in a Console run with a project-instruction binding, on the agent worker thread.
cost: Not re-measured. 0.8-2.2 ms per batch for 60-600 messages is plausible for deepcopy of the history, on a worker thread. That is minor.
fix: Capture references (tuple(messages), active_schemas, calls) and deep-copy lazily inside safe_input_tokens/count_input_tokens, which already copy again. Those only run when _issue_delivery has unseen sources or outcomes.

The runtime appends to the list, so tuple(messages) protects membership, but in-place edits of the dicts (e.g. restore or pruning paths) would leak into a later safe_input_tokens. Keep a shallow tuple snapshot and deep-copy inside safe_input_tokens, which already copies, so there is exactly one copy. Verify that nothing mutates the message dicts after capture before relying on it.

self._messages = tuple(deepcopy(dict(message)) for message in messages)
self._active_schemas = tuple(deepcopy(tuple(active_schemas)))
self._calls = tuple(ToolCall(call.name, deepcopy(dict(call.args)), call.call_id) for call in calls)

It is called from agent_runtime.py:2237 before every prepare_tool_calls when project_instruction_payload_state is set, and once per chain from agent_service.py:2938. _issue_delivery returns 'proceed' at line ~629-630 when there are no unseen sources or outcomes, which is the common case after the first delivery, so the copies are then discarded. safe_input_tokens deep-copies self._messages again when it is actually used. title: Tool-result post-processing does per-character and per-leaf Python work: virtual CLI sanitization before truncation, and locator recomputation per leaf
trigger: Every virtual CLI call (sanitize) and every builtin/virtual-CLI result (redact) on a tool thread. The cost only matters for large outputs, such as a git_diff near the 1 MB cap or results with thousands of leaves.
cost: Not re-measured. About 50 ms per 1 MB through the char-by-char generator, and single-digit ms for a 5000-leaf redact, are plausible. Both are on tool threads and scale only with large outputs, so P3.
fix: Byte-truncate to _MAX_RESULT_BYTES plus a small margin before the character filter, and replace the generator with str.translate using a precomputed deletion table for C0/C1 controls. In redact_root_locator, compute the sorted locator tuple once and recurse through an inner closure.
fix_notes: Pre-truncating before the filter changes what survives when the output is dense with ANSI or control bytes: less content may fit than today. Use a generous margin (e.g. 2-4x _MAX_RESULT_BYTES). Also, a byte cut can split an ANSI escape: the ESC byte is dropped by the control filter, but the '[31m' residue remains as text, so strip ANSI before cutting, or cut and then drop a trailing partial escape. str.translate with a precomputed deletion table for C0 (minus \n and \t), DEL and C1 is behaviour-identical. Hoisting the sorted locator tuple for redact_root_locator into an inner closure is safe.
evidence:
text = _ANSI_ESCAPE.sub("", text)
text = "".join(char for char in text if char in "\n\t" or (ord(char) >= 32 and not 127 <= ord(char) <= 159))
... then truncated to 32 KB
# redact_root_locator, per string leaf:
locators = {str(root), root.as_posix()}

title: ChatImageHandler exposes async-but-fully-sync image processing, so callers spin up a new event loop in a thread for every attachment
known_task: qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/report.md:2724 (P3 D3 UI-chat); no backlog task filed
trigger: Yes, but the trigger is user-initiated and infrequent: Console file-picker attach, drag-drop path-paste, and Alt+V clipboard image, through chat_screen._process_console_attachment and the clipboard-grab handler. Both paths are already offloaded with asyncio.to_thread, so the event loop never runs the PIL work.
cost: Measured, not the event loop: about 0.5 ms extra per image or text attachment (nested loop setup and teardown), and about 1.2 ms per PDF, doc or ebook attachment (nested loop plus throwaway executor thread). Everything runs on a worker thread. Zero UI stall.

Five test modules call these via asyncio.run: Tests/Chat/test_attachment_core.py, test_image_payload.py, test_chat_image_pixel_bomb.py, and Tests/Event_Handlers/Chat_Events/test_chat_image_events.py and test_chat_image_properties.py. Do NOT 'fix' this by awaiting process_attachment_path directly on the loop: that would move the PIL decode, resize and optimize work and the text-handler file reads onto the UI thread, which is the real hazard. Given the roughly 1 ms off-loop cost, the best disposition is to leave it or fold it into a hygiene task. If it is changed, sync variants plus to_thread is correct.
evidence:
chat_image_events.py:42 async def process_image_file(file_path) -> ...: path.read_bytes(); PILImage.open(...)
199 async def prepare_image_payload(...): pil_image.load(); thumbnail(LANCZOS); save(optimize=True)
chat_screen.py:20511 attachment = await asyncio.to_thread(
    lambda: asyncio.run(process_attachment_path(file_path)))
reason: The code is present on pin 840ed2ca58. chat_image_events.py:42 `async def process_image_file` and :208 `async def prepare_image_payload` contain no awaits of real async I/O; they do PIL open/load/thumbnail/save synchronously. chat_screen.py:20476-20480 (clipboard bytes) and :20511-20513 (file path) wrap the chain in `asyncio.to_thread(lambda: asyncio.run(...))`. Both are already off the loop, so nothing blocks the loop and the 'latent risk' is hypothetical, not a present cost. I measured the overhead with a stdlib-only micro-benchmark on the same interpreter, off the loop. `to_thread(asyncio.run(noop))` has a median of 0.69 ms against 0.20 ms for a bare to_thread, about 0.5 ms extra. cost: The finding is real: on 840ed2ca58, recovery_review.py:513 runs `with _using(self.operation)`, and so op.check() and _history, on every next(). But both earlier measurements were inflated about 2x by the scratch profile's path depth, and the cost never touches the event loop. Probe: scratch/second-lens-slice21/bench_f1.py and bench_depth.py. It is an isolated HOME with admit_startup, and the bootstrap has the same shape as the real one: admission/ with gate, lease, incompatible and registry.json holding 1 entry, plus unbound-owner. (1) Cost depends on path depth. _open_verified_parent opens, fstats and closes every path component. Real syscalls per check() measured 280 (76 open) with the bootstrap root at depth 13 (the scratch path both earlier passes used), 433 at depth 22 and 586 at depth 31. That is exactly 17 syscalls per component. A real ~/.config/tldw_cli/recovery-bootstrap is at depth 5, so about 144 syscalls per check. (2) CPU per check() at depth 13 with host load 36-50: thread-CPU median 2.4-3.2 ms (min 1.3-1.6 ms), split about 0.62 ms user and 2.3 ms system. Linear extrapolation to depth 5 gives about 0.39 ms user plus 0.91 ms system, about 1.3 ms under load. Scaling the finder's lower-load 1.29 ms by the same syscall ratio (0.51) gives about 0.6 ms. So the real-profile cost is about 0.5-1.3 ms per streamed chunk. The earlier passes reported 1.3-5 ms. (3) Iterating a 1000-item @unqualified iterator at depth 13 cost 3.73 ms wall and 3.35 ms CPU per item; the raw generator cost 0.02 us per item. So the guard is still 25-60x the real per-chunk work (SSE decode is about 20 us). (4) Where it runs: the Console consumes the stream in asyncio.to_thread(worker) at console_provider_gateway.py:6587. await_delivery (:6219) only lock-steps with the loop when voice_bounded, so on normal sends the guard overlaps network waits. There is no loop time. (5) Effect on the loop's CPU share: a main-thread pure-Python spin ran 24.2M/s idle, 22.9M/s with checks paced at 200 chunks/s (-5%, within noise at this load) and 21.9M/s with checks back-to-back (-9%). The check releases the GIL at each of its ~144 syscalls. Net effect: 0.25-0.65 s of worker CPU per 500-chunk reply, about 5-13% of a core while streaming at 100 chunks/s. The throughput ceiling is about 770-1700 chunks/s, so only the fastest hosted providers (above about 800 tok/s) see longer streams. At typical 30-150 chunks/s it is invisible. Per chunk that is 0.5-1.3 ms of off-loop CPU, well under the rubric's 10-20 ms per event, so P2. It is the top P2, and it shares one sound fix with F2: memoise _history on stat identity, or skip the redundant borrowed check. The openai_call second lazy _Operation is about 4 ms extra TTFT at real depth, also worker-thread.
fix: Check once per stream, not per chunk. The stream's _Operation holds its admission lease until close(), so witness history should not change underneath it. In _OpenAIStream.__next__, run _using/check only on the first next() (or at a coarse interval, such as every 5 s or 256 records). After that, only set the contextvar. Also skip the second check() that _ordinary_operation (:82) followed by _using (:477) does on borrowed nested calls. Optionally memoise _history() on the bootstrap and registry file identity (st_ino, st_mtime_ns). Add a probe pinning at most one _history call per stream.
fix_notes: The per-iteration check looks deliberate. TASK-32003's notes say 'Guard actual effect/iteration, including iterator created before restored generation', so relaxing it needs an owner review of the recovery design, not just a perf patch. Before switching to check-once-per-stream, confirm that a restore or activation cannot publish a new generation while this stream's StorageLease native hold is live. If it can, keep a check that is cheaper but still sound. One option: memoise _history on the stat identities (st_dev, st_ino, st_mtime_ns, st_ctime_ns) of the bootstrap dir, the registry.json and the witness generation dirs. Another: check on a time or record interval. Separately, dropping the redundant second check() on borrowed nested calls (_ordinary_operation:82 plus _using:477) is safe and cheap. Pin the cost with a probe that counts _history calls per stream.

title: Async provider-guard wrappers run the synchronous admission handshake on the Textual event loop (~21–27 ms per llama.cpp send, 75 ms per discovery)

Also complete_llamacpp_chat on the fallback and voice paths. discover_local_servers runs once per Console visit while the setup card is blocking, and in the first-run wizard. All of these are coroutines on the Textual loop.
cost: Measured on a real asyncio loop in the isolated profile (scratch/second-lens-slice21/bench_f2.py). The probe used the real rr.unqualified decorators with the production shapes and a 20 ms simulated network await. A heartbeat task (sleep(0)) measured the largest single loop stall. The unguarded baseline stall was 0.17-1.09 ms. Results at depth 13 (load 37) and depth 22 (load 50): (a) resolve_llamacpp shape (wait_for task, outer op, nested borrowed _is_reachable): 1 acquire_storage, 4 _history, 1960 syscalls. It is one contiguous stall of 31 ms median (min 26), because the nested call runs synchronously before the first real await. (b) stream_llamacpp_chat asyncgen entry: 1 acquire_storage, 2 _history, 1400 syscalls, 21 ms stall. (c) discover_local_servers with the 3 default candidates: 4 _Operations (each gather child is a new Task, so _identity differs and it builds its own op), 5600 syscalls, 69 ms stall. With 8 probes: 12600 syscalls, 153 ms. Syscalls scale 0.51x to the real depth-5 bootstrap root (1008, 720, 2880 and 6480). The real-profile estimates are therefore: (a) resolve about 16 ms under load and about 6.5 ms on a quiet host (the finder's 12.6 x 0.51); (b) stream entry about 11 and about 4.3 ms. That is about 11 ms (quiet) to 27 ms (loaded; this machine sits at load 40-50) of loop time per llama.cpp send, in two slices. Discovery is 20-35 ms contiguous with the default 3 probes and 40-78 ms with 8, once per Console visit while the setup card is blocking. Trigger path re-checked: send is a run_worker coroutine; _resolve_for_send_bounded wraps it in asyncio.wait_for on the same loop (console_chat_controller.py:4616-4631); then resolve_llamacpp (gateway:3737, called at :4226) and `async for` over stream_llamacpp_chat (:6013). chat_screen._maybe_start_console_local_discovery calls run_worker(coroutine) with no thread. None of this goes through to_thread. It is P1, at the bottom of the band. The finder's ~21 ms per send was also measured at the depth-13 scratch path, so on a quiet machine the real per-send figure is about half of that.
fix: Do the admission work off the loop. In the async and asyncgen wrappers, build the operation with `operation, owned = await asyncio.to_thread(_ordinary_operation)` and run the first check() the same way. Make borrowed nested calls skip re-checking. Make catalog_call and discovery_call borrow an active operation instead of always building a new one. The F1 memo alone would also shrink these costs to microseconds. Umbrella: TASK-32804 (sync work on the loop).
fix_notes: Watch the contextvar and task-identity semantics. _identity() includes the current task, and _current is a ContextVar. Building the operation in asyncio.to_thread is fine, because _Operation.__init__ does not use _current. But _using() must still set the contextvar in the calling task, and any to_thread check must not rely on the thread identity. Making gather children borrow the parent's operation would change the identity rule, which appears deliberate for leases held per task, so get an owner review first. The lowest-risk wins are dropping the redundant second check() on borrowed nested calls, and a sound _history memo (see F1).

    operation, owned = _ordinary_operation()  # sync: _Operation -> acquire_storage() + _history()
    with _using(operation):                   # sync check() again

# nested/borrowed: _ordinary_operation():82 check() + _using():477 check()

title: Every hosted request builds a new requests.Session, so each send and each agent step pays a fresh TCP+TLS handshake
corrected: tldw_chatbook/Utils/egress.py:1012-1040 (create_default_session, the shared factory; the natural single fix site)
trigger: Every hosted send via chat_api_call, and each agent-loop step, since AgentService re-calls chat_api_call once per step. Also each summarizer chunk and each retry attempt. Local http://localhost providers are unaffected.
cost: Full, untruncated trace. There are 14 create_default_session() call sites in tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls: hosted_chat.py:710; LLM_API_Calls.py:485, 855, 950, 1750, 2718, 3559 and 4386; LLM_API_Calls_Local.py:282 and 1093; qwencloud.py:1176; Summarization_General_Lib.py:1039; Local_Summarization_Lib.py:90. There is also one module-level requests.post at LLM_API_Calls.py:4299, which makes a Session per call. A grep for module-level or shared Session, PoolManager or cached-session patterns in LLM_Calls and Utils/egress.py found 0. create_default_session (egress.py:1012-1040) returns a new DefaultTimeoutSession every call. owned_json_post mounts a fresh HTTPAdapter per call. OwnedSSEStream.close() (hosted_chat_streaming.py:218-227) closes the response and its session at stream end, and non-stream paths close in finally. So no socket survives to the next request, even back-to-back ones. Frequency: every hosted send via chat_api_call and every agent step, since AgentService resolves chat_api_call (agent_service.py:1622) and re-calls it per step; also every summarizer chunk and every retry. Measured local part (no network), scratch/second-lens-slice21/bench_f4_ssl.py: the venv has requests 2.32.5 (no preloaded SSLContext) and urllib3 2.6.3. HTTPAdapter.cert_verify (adapters.py:300/311) sets conn.ca_certs to the certifi bundle, and urllib3 ssl_wrap_socket calls load_verify_locations on a fresh SSLContext for every new connection. That costs 11.55 ms median CPU (min 10.73) per new HTTPS connection on this host. Session plus adapter construction costs only 9 us. Estimated network part: TCP plus TLS 1.3 is 2 RTT, about 40-160 ms at 20-80 ms RTT, plus handshake crypto of about 1-2 ms. Every hosted request therefore pays about 12 ms of measured CPU plus 2 RTT of TTFT that a reused keep-alive socket would avoid. That is certain for back-to-back agent steps, summarizer chunks and retries (a 10-step agent turn is about 0.5-1.7 s) and depends on the server's idle timeout for human-paced sends. It is worker-thread time, not loop time, but it is user-visible TTFT well above the 10-20 ms per-send line, so P1 stands. The network share needs a live A/B test before a fix lands. Fix notes: a shared, thread-safe adapter or PoolManager per retry policy, where per-call close() must not close the shared pool. Even without reuse, passing one preloaded SSLContext would save about 11 ms per new connection.
fix: Keep a long-lived pooled requests.Session per (scheme, host), or one shared per provider module, with the retry adapter mounted once. The stream then owns only the response: closing an unfinished response discards its socket, so Stop and cancel semantics are kept. Keep a dedicated, trust_env=False session only for reviewed and recovered openai_post operations. This needs a one-line amendment to ADR-062's 'stream owns response/session' rule and a check against TASK-30015 (tearing down a wedged read).
fix_notes: Risks the finder did not name: (1) requests.Session is not guaranteed thread-safe, and parallel sub-agents and concurrent workers call handlers from several threads at once. Use a per-thread session, or share the thread-safe urllib3 PoolManager/HTTPAdapter across per-call Sessions: mount one module-level adapter per scheme on each new Session. Mounting a shared adapter keeps each call's own Session and close semantics while pooling sockets, which is the smallest diff. Session.close() closes its adapters, though, so a shared adapter must not be closed by per-call close() (subclass it or override close). (2) recovery_review.openai_post calls operation.own(session), and the operation closes it at the end. OwnedSSEStream also closes its session (the ADR-062 ownership rule). Both must close only the response, never a shared pool. (3) TASK-30015 (tearing down a wedged read) depends on closing the response or socket, and closing a response mid-stream discards its socket, which is fine. (4) Keep the TLS trust policy: the pooled adapter must use tls_trust.requests_verify() per request, which it does via session.verify. The adapter's max_retries differs per call site (Retry objects), which argues for one adapter per retry policy.
evidence:
session = create_default_session()        # hosted_chat.py:710, new pool per call
...
adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry_policy)
session.mount("https://", adapter)
...
stream = OwnedSSEStream(response=response, session=session)  # session closed at stream end
reason: create_default_session (Utils/egress.py:1012) builds a new DefaultTimeoutSession on every call; there is no shared session or pool. The cited sites each build a session per call: hosted_chat.py:710 (owned_json_post, with HTTPAdapter mounted per call), LLM_API_Calls.py:855, :1750, :2718 and :3559, qwencloud.py:1176, LLM_API_Calls_Local.py:282 and Summarization_General_Lib.py:1039. LLM_API_Calls.py:4299 uses the module-level requests.post, which also makes a Session per call. The session is closed at stream end (OwnedSSEStream owns it) or in a finally block, so no connection ever survives to the next request. The core review listed per-call Session construction as untimed and unverified (qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/report.md:3031), and no open backlog task covers pooling; I grepped for create_default_session, keep-alive and connection pool.

A file (st_mtime_ns, st_size) memo helps only for the file source, since on macOS the credential lives in the Keychain. Stopping the poll while the screen is suspended (TASK-32804.3) removes most triggers and is the bigger lever.

title: OwnedSSEStream reads with iter_content(chunk_size=8192), which batches tokens into ~8 KB bursts on non-chunked SSE responses
trigger: Every streamed hosted-engine/zai/hosted-summarization response flows through OwnedSSEStream, but the burst only happens when the server sends close-delimited SSE (no Transfer-Encoding: chunked, no Content-Length), which mainstream HTTP/1.1 servers do not do.
cost: When triggered, delivery is held until 8192 decoded bytes, about 30-50 OpenAI-shape delta events (150-300 B each), or until the connection closes. The legacy iter_lines default chunk is 512 B, 16x smaller. The cost is zero on chunked responses. It was not measured, and the finder's estimate is sound.
fix: Iterate with read1-style semantics, for example a loop on response.raw.read1(8192) guarded by decode_content, so each read returns whatever bytes are available. Alternatively use chunk_size=512 to match the legacy behaviour.
fix_notes: urllib3 HTTPResponse.read1(amt, decode_content=True) exists in the installed 2.6.3, but only from urllib3 2.3 onward. pyproject pins neither requests nor urllib3, and requests allows urllib3>=1.21.1, so a read1 loop needs a hasattr fallback. Do NOT switch to iter_content(chunk_size=None): for a response that is not chunked, raw.stream(None) calls read(None), which reads to EOF and is strictly worse. The minimal safe fix is chunk_size=512 at both sites (legacy parity), or a read1 loop with a fallback. Apply the same change to qwencloud_streaming.py:920.
evidence:
self._chunks: Iterable[bytes] = response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192)
# urllib3 2.6.3 HTTPResponse.stream(): "A call will block until amt bytes have been
# read from the connection or until the connection is closed" (non-chunked branch)
reason: The code is real on pin 840ed2ca58. hosted_chat_streaming.py:181 is `response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192)`. It is built at hosted_chat.py:752 inside owned_json_post, which uses requests with stream=True. owned_json_post is the shared transport for hosted_provider_engine.py:1982, zai.py:424, hosted_chat.py:603 and the Summarization_General_Lib hosted streaming paths. I checked the installed libraries (requests 2.32.5, urllib3 2.6.3). requests.iter_content calls raw.stream(8192, decode_content=True). For a response that is not chunked, urllib3 stream() calls read(amt), and read(amt) loops `while len(self._decoded_buffer) < amt and data` (response.py:1146-1156). It therefore blocks until 8 KiB of decoded data arrives or the connection closes, so the finder's reading of the semantics is correct. Chunked responses go through read_chunked and are delivered per chunk, so they are unaffected. The finder missed a sibling site: qwencloud_streaming.py:920 has the same `iter_content(chunk_size=8192)`. The trigger is real but rare. requests always sends HTTP/1.1, and the usual SSE servers answer an HTTP/1.1 client with chunked encoding: uvicorn/starlette, Go net/http, cpp-httplib (llama.cpp), and nginx, which re-chunks a close-delimited upstream by default. Only an unusual close-delimited proxy or server hits the batching. This is a token-delivery latency issue on a worker-side iterator, not loop-blocking. P3 stands.
