title: Proposal reads open write transactions, and commits decrypt every lifetime proposal (twice) while holding the write lock
trigger: Agent profile_propose/promote tool calls (agent worker thread), Settings My Profile load and reload (worker thread), and review-modal accept/reject/defer (worker thread). Each read takes an expire write transaction.
cost: Measured 31 us per proposal decrypt+validate, times 2 passes per commit under BEGIN IMMEDIATE: about 12 ms at P=200 and about 125 ms at P=2000. Plus one hardened connect (about 50 ms) per standalone expire transaction, even when nothing is due.
fix: Keep the content-free proposal state and expires_at in a plaintext side column (object_heads or a proposal_index table) so the pending count and due-expiry selection are SQL queries. Decrypt only the rows actually expiring. Run the expire write transaction only when that query finds due rows.
fix_notes: A plaintext side column for state/expires_at needs a schema migration and an ADR-102 review, because it adds plaintext metadata to an encrypted-at-rest store. That makes it medium-high risk. Lower-risk steps first: (1) count pending in the same loop as the expiry scan inside commit_proposal, which removes one full decrypt pass; (2) do the due-check as a read (inside the caller's read_operation) and open BEGIN IMMEDIATE only when a due row exists, re-checking inside the transaction; (3) optionally prune terminal receipts past a retention window, but check the sync/outbox receipt contracts first.
evidence:
with self._mutation(profile_id=proposal.profile_id) as connection:   # BEGIN IMMEDIATE
    if expire_before is not None: self._expire_due_proposals_in_connection(connection, expire_before)  # decrypt ALL heads
    rows = connection.execute("SELECT encrypted_objects.* ... WHERE object_type = 'proposal'").fetchall()
    for row in rows: current = ProfileProposal.model_validate_json(self._decrypt_row(row))  # decrypt ALL again
# _get/_list/_resolve_profile_proposal: self._repo().expire_due_proposals(...) = write txn on every read
reason: The code is as quoted. service.py:214-229: _get/_list/_resolve_profile_proposal each call repo.expire_due_proposals, which is a _mutation (BEGIN IMMEDIATE, own connect, commit, WAL truncate) even when nothing is due. repository.py:3146-3158: commit_proposal runs _expire_due_proposals_in_connection (decrypt all proposal heads), then a second full SELECT plus decrypt of every proposal head to count pending, all under the write lock. Resolved receipts stay as heads forever: _resolve_proposal_in_connection only deletes older versions, and no pruning exists. MAX_UNRESOLVED_PROPOSALS=200 bounds only pending proposals. Measured (P=40): decrypt+validate 31 us/proposal (finder: 37 us). expire_due_proposals with nothing due = 1 connect + 40 decrypts = 54 ms, dominated by the connect. Callers are off-loop: the agent tool worker via proposal_service.py:147/305/414-445/476, the Settings panel @work(thread=True) load (personal_context_panel.py:197) via settings_snapshot -> _list_profile_proposals (service.py:1545), and the review modal run_worker(thread=True) at personal_context_review_modal.py:301. So this is lock-hold time and latency, not a freeze. P2 fits: a less frequent path whose cost scales with lifetime proposal count. Side observation: unwrapped _list_profile_proposals measured 43 connects, 2.5 s, because of per-row _is_quarantined connects. That is the N+1 the finder attributes to F1-F5, not this finding.

title: Personal_Context package __init__ eagerly imports every submodule; the Console imports it on the loop just to build an empty snapshot dataclass
trigger: First Inspector open or first build_context_snapshot in a process where no send has yet imported Personal_Context. Runs on the event loop, once per process.
cost: Measured incremental import with Console loaded: about 11 ms (13 modules). A dependency-free snapshot-models module would make it about 0 ms. The finder's 17.4 ms overstates this, because tldw_profile_core is already loaded in a Console session.
fix: Move ProfileContextSnapshot/ProfileContextRequest, which are plain dataclasses, into a dependency-free `context_models.py`. Turn `Personal_Context/__init__.py` into a PEP 562 lazy facade (the Local_Ingestion template).
fix_notes: Moving ProfileContextSnapshot/ProfileContextRequest into a leaf module with no tldw_profile_core or service import is enough on its own. The PEP 562 facade is optional polish. Check pickling, isinstance and test imports that use `tldw_chatbook.Personal_Context.context_service.ProfileContextSnapshot`, and re-export it from context_service.
reason: Personal_Context/__init__.py:3-49 eagerly imports crypto, context_service, interview_coordinator, interview_diff, interview_draft_repository, interview_provider, key_protector, repository, runtime_policy and service. The helpers at console_chat_controller.py:4419 and console_chat_models.py:1416 import context_service lazily, but that still executes the package __init__. They run on the loop from async build_context_snapshot (console_chat_controller.py:21271/21427) and from the Inspector's reactive default (console_conversation_inspector.py:240-242 builds ConsoleContextSnapshot, whose default_factory triggers the import). Measured with console_chat_controller and the inspector already imported: tldw_profile_core was already in sys.modules, so the finder's 17.4 ms for it does not apply incrementally. The incremental cost is 10.7-11.3 ms and 13 modules through the package __init__, versus 6.7-7.2 ms and 8 modules without it. It is one-time per process and often already paid off-loop by the first send's worker-thread bootstrap. No backlog task covers a lazy Personal_Context facade.

title: Unlinked profiles enqueue encrypted outbox bodies on every mutation; first link deletes them all, and the pending scan has no status index
trigger: Every record, scope or proposal mutation on a never-linked profile (agent or user action), and every dispatch pass for linked profiles. All run on worker threads.
cost: Estimated, not measured: about 0.1-0.3 ms per commit for two extra AES-GCM encryptions and inserts. Disk grows linearly with mutations until first link. The dispatch scan is O(dispatched rows), sub-millisecond to a few ms at realistic volumes.
fix: Skip outbox enqueue while no link state exists, since the reviewed link rebuilds the delta anyway (2186-2196). Add a partial index `encrypted_outbox(sequence) WHERE status='pending'`; this needs a plan pin per CLAUDE.md's sqlite_stat1-absent rule. Prune dispatched metadata after the receipt retention window.
fix_notes: Link state lives in the separate sync_state_repository, so skip-when-unlinked needs a durable in-DB marker (for example, a first-link completed flag) plus care around the freeze and rebaseline window. Coalescing pending manifest entries (retire the previous pending manifest body on each new manifest) is the smaller, lower-risk change. Any new partial index on encrypted_outbox needs a sqlite_stat1-absent plan pin and a census row (scripts/check_index_plan_pins.py) per CLAUDE.md. Personal Context is not chachanotes, but the pin check applies repo-wide.
evidence:
self._insert_outbox(connection, object_type="manifest", ...)   # every record commit
if outbox_body is not None and record.controls.sync_mode is SyncMode.SYNCABLE:
    self._insert_outbox(connection, object_type="record", ...)
# first link: connection.execute("DELETE FROM encrypted_outbox")  -- provisional journal discarded
# list_pending: WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY sequence LIMIT ?  (dispatched rows kept forever; no status index)
reason: Every record commit enqueues a manifest outbox body (repository.py:2617) plus a record body when SYNCABLE (:2652-2662). _insert_outbox (:4158) encrypts the body, writes an object_heads row and runs MAX(sequence), which is served by the UNIQUE index encrypted_outbox_sequence_idx (:663), so it is O(log n) and not a scan. Pending manifest entries are never coalesced; _retire_pending_outbox_content only covers scope, record and proposal (:3940/:3963/:4019), and records only on tombstone or relink. So an unlinked profile accumulates one encrypted manifest copy per mutation until first link. First link then remaps and immediately deletes the whole journal (:2174-2196), so the remap loop is wasted work too. Acknowledged rows keep content-free metadata forever (acknowledge_outbox sets status='dispatched'). list_pending_outbox/list_dispatchable_outbox (:4246/:4260) filter status='pending' while walking in sequence order, so they step over all historic dispatched rows. This is real but small: well under 1 ms of CPU per commit, next to the 50 ms connect (F14), and disk growth of about 1-2 KB per user mutation. It is not a session memory leak, so P3.

title: Root multiplier (outside slice): every connect_private_sqlite on POSIX spawns a fresh `python -I -S` helper process, about 45 ms per connect
trigger: Every hardened file-backed SQLite connect on POSIX, from any of 50 owner modules. Per send for Personal Context users, per Library visit (TASK-24457's 8 connections), and once on the loop at deferred startup via launch wake.
cost:
Measured in isolation on a scratch DB at load average about 52 on 18 cores:
- Plain sqlite3.connect+close: median 0.2 ms.
- Bare `python -I -S -c pass` spawn: median 20.1 ms (16.7-27.8).
- connect_private_sqlite('personal_context.repository', file)+close: median 78.7 ms (61.0-88.7, n=15), with exactly 1 prepare_in_helper per connect. Split: open 76.7 ms, sqlite close 0.05 ms.

That is about 390x the plain connect and about 175x the roughly 0.44 ms that TASK-31504 recorded before ADR-125.

cProfile of 10 connects took 0.872 s in total (87 ms each):
- HelperLease.start: 55 ms per connect. Nearly all of it is selectors.select waiting on the child interpreter's boot, import and reply; fork_exec itself is only 1.7 ms.
- Lease close: about 11 ms, of which subprocess.wait is 9 ms, plus 26 time.sleep calls totalling 88 ms across the 10 connects.
- Admission wrapper: about 10 ms.
So most of the cost is interpreter start-up and import in the child, spent on every connect. The first verifier measured 44+9 ≈ 53 ms under load 20, which is consistent.

Code: private_sqlite.py:1878 calls prepare_in_helper on every non-Windows, file-backed target. Only MEMORY targets skip it. prepare_in_helper (1377-1386) runs HelperLease.start, which calls subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-I', '-S', private_sqlite_helper_entry.py]) at private_sqlite_process.py:366. There is no reuse or cache.

Scope (untruncated grep): 93 call sites across 51 modules. BaseDB._get_connection (base_db.py:823) opens fresh unless a subclass holds per-thread connections. AgentRunsDB holds one per thread, but each new executor thread pays one spawn.

Hot consequences confirmed here:
- Personal Context DISABLED/READY sends: 2 spawns, about 160-210 ms per send (F9).
- Absent first send: 2 spawns (F8).
- Library visit: 8 opens (TASK-24457).
- One on-loop spawn at deferred startup: console_launch_wake.py:69 opens a read-only connect_private_sqlite when agent_runs.db exists.

Severity stays P1 as the root multiplier; per-path freezes belong to those paths' findings. The fix still needs an owner-approved ADR-125 amendment for a long-lived helper or cached prepare. Lower-risk levers inside the ADR: operation- or thread-scoped reuse at callers, batch prepare, and trimming the close path's wait/sleep loop (about 11 ms per connect).
fix: Keep one long-lived, admission-owned helper per process (or per owner) and send prepare requests over its pipe, instead of exec'ing an interpreter per connect. Or cache the prepare result per (path, identity) for the process lifetime and re-validate only with a cheap lstat or identity compare. Owned by the DB and private-paths slice; noted here because it turns Personal Context's per-call connects into seconds.
fix_notes: Both proposed fixes conflict with ADR-125 as accepted. A long-lived per-process helper contradicts 'No listener, daemon ... is introduced'. Caching prepare results behind a cheap lstat contradicts its rejection of 'metadata-only checks alone', which miss wrong-mode hardening. Either needs an owner-approved ADR-125 amendment; do not implement without one. Lower-risk levers inside the current ADR: (1) cut connect counts at the callers with operation- or thread-scoped reuse. Personal Context's read_operation proved 64 -> 1 in F10, and ChaChaNotes and notifications already hold per-thread connections. Apply this to Workspace_DB and AgentRuns_DB per-call connects (TASK-3011/3012) and to Library's 8 per-visit opens (TASK-24457). title: Every PromptsDatabase.transaction() pays the storage-admission handshake (~4 ms, ~245 open() syscalls), dwarfing the 0.1 ms of SQL
trigger:
Yes: every `PromptsDatabase.transaction()`, including `list_prompts`, `browse`, drafts, collections, `add_prompt`/`update`/`delete` and usage recording.
- It is on the loop through F1's paths (the Console modal and the Draft Shelf).
- It is on worker threads for the Library prompts pages and imports.
- `add_prompt` opens one transaction per prompt, so an import of N prompts pays N admissions.
cost:
MEASURED (isolated scratch profile, audit tree 840ed2ca58, loguru removed; machine load avg 65-74 on 18 cores so absolute ms are inflated; opens are counted by an audit hook and do not depend on load). Admission takes the qualified native path (qualified_for('admission') = True, 'qualified_native_evidence') and runs no TLDW_TEST_MODE branch, so the path is the same as production. Bench: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-macbook-dev-Documents-GitHub-tldw-chatbook/15c5e43c-3dea-41a4-87ab-3b132387df58/scratchpad/audit/scratch/sl31-f2-lens2/bench_min.py (400 iterations each; 3000 prompts; 40 drafts). Per-call cost in ms as min/median, with opens per call:
- Depth 14-15: empty `db.transaction(); SELECT 1` = 6.9/19.7 ms, 265 opens. The same inside one outer `_core_operation(db)` = 0.22/0.40 ms, 0 opens. `list_prompts(per_page=10)` = 6.6/18.8 ms vs 0.45/0.71 ms in scope. `list_prompt_drafts` = 7.4/19.8 ms vs 0.46/0.82 ms. `execute_query('SELECT 1')` = 0.03 ms, 0 opens. `search_prompts(limit=25)` = 0.24 ms, 0 opens (it opens no transaction).
- Depth 24-25: empty txn = 11.8/30.7 ms, 425 opens.
- Scaling: 16 opens and about 0.48 ms (loaded min) per extra path component. A real profile (~/.config/tldw_cli, ~/.local/share/tldw_cli) is about 8 components shallower, so it pays about 120-140 opens and about 3 ms per transaction on this loaded machine. That is consistent with the finder's 1.5-3 ms unloaded estimate.
- `add_prompt`: 19.0 ms standalone vs 7.9 ms inside one scope (265 vs 2.65 opens), so admission is about 58% of per-prompt import cost.
- The handshake is real and dominates the SQL by 10-40x, and nesting inside one scope removes it. That confirms the first verifier's low-risk fix.

TRACE (why not P1):
- Loop callers found by grep:
  - `PromptScopeService` wraps `LocalPromptService` → `PromptsDatabase` directly (`app.py:8195`, `prompt_scope_service.py:2650`); `_maybe_await` calls the sync method on the loop.
  - `ConsolePromptsModal.reload_browse` is a coroutine worker (on the loop). Per modal open, page change or source switch it does 1 `list_prompts` or `list_prompt_drafts` transaction (`console_prompts_modal.py:368/793/805`).
  - A query on the Draft Shelf source costs 1 transaction per 200 ms-debounced query (`:1835`). A query on the local source uses `search_prompts`, which opens no transaction.
  - Draft save (`prompts.py:1322`) and draft update/delete each cost 1 transaction.
  - The per-keystroke Console prompt picker (`console_prompt_picker_modal.py:233`) and `/prompt` resolution use `search_prompts` / `fetch_prompt_details`, which open no transaction.
  - `record_prompt_usage` opens no transaction: `PromptsDatabase` has no such method, so it falls back to `get_prompt` (`prompt_scope_service.py:1035`). The finding's trigger list is wrong on this point.
- Every Library prompts call site found passes `isolate_in_worker=True` (`library_prompts_controller.py:918/1961/3186/3223/3266/4197/4545/4683/4764/4822/4937`). Local user-content evidence uses `count_prompts` via `asyncio.to_thread` (`:1781`). So the Library paths and the import `add_prompt` loop are off-loop, where they add latency but do not freeze the UI.
- ChaChaNotes, the per-send store, is NOT wrapped: none of the 26 `@_core_transaction` sites is in `ChaChaNotes_DB` (it only uses `_core_operation` for maintenance at :24222). A spot-check of notifications found no UI poller of local `unread_count`/`observe_feed`.
- Net: the Prompts impact on the loop is about 2-3 ms (real profile) per user modal action. That is below the rubric's ≳10-20 ms P1 bar and on a modal path, which the rubric lists as P2.
- Imports pay N admissions off-loop, about +2-3 s per 1000 prompts: data-scaled on a rare path, also P2.

The cross-store multiplier (26 wrapped `connection`/`transaction` methods in 16 stores) is a real structural tax. But no hot trigger (per-send, per-tick or per-keystroke) is evidenced in this finding, so any P1 for another store must come from that store's own trigger trace.

No open task covers it: TASK-32804.1 AC#2 is scoped to config reads only. Recommended fix unchanged: hold one `_core_operation` scope across multi-transaction logical operations (import loop, modal load, `_call_local` worker body), plus a per-transaction open-count pin.
fix:
Amortise admission per scope rather than per transaction, as TASK-32804.1 did for warm config reads with `_warm_config_cache_hit`. Two options:
- Cache a positive admission per (participant, thread) keyed on a cheap storage-generation counter that pause, restore and backup bump. The existing `storage._lock` checks (`_core_access`) stay per operation, but the filesystem re-verification only reruns on a generation change.
- Hold a per-thread lease across consecutive operations.

Pair this with a benchmark pin on the per-transaction cost.
fix_notes:
The proposed generation-counter cache is high risk. Admission re-reads on-disk bootstrap records and the registry, which OTHER processes can change (pause, restore, enrollment, pending recovery). A per-process counter bumped only by in-process pause/restore would miss cross-process changes. The TASK-32562 notes also record a deliberate "no validation cache" stance, and ADR-126 governs admission. Any cache needs a cheap cross-process invalidation token (for example, `stat` of the records and registry dirs) and sign-off from the backup/recovery owner.

A lower-risk first step uses the mechanism that already exists. Hold one `participant.operation()` / `_core_operation(db)` scope across multi-transaction logical operations, such as the bulk import loop, a modal page load, or an off-loop `_call_local` worker body. Nested transactions then reuse it: measured 6.0 to 0.34 ms per transaction. Add a benchmark pin on per-transaction `os.open` count.
reason:
The admission chain is verified:
- `Prompts_DB.py:658` `@_core_transaction` calls `participants.py:431 counted`.
- That calls `_core_operation`, then `_RepositoryParticipant.operation()`, then `storage_admission._repository_operation` (:109).
- On each new (non-reused) operation, that calls `acquire_storage` (:835), then `_acquire_storage` (:854).
- `_acquire_storage` runs `startup_permission` twice, `admission_authority`, `_scope` twice (each reads the bootstrap records and registry), plus `stat`.

There are 26 `@_core_transaction` sites in 16 files, as the finding says. They include read-only `connection()` contexts in `client_notifications_db` and `event_state_repository`, so reads pay the tax too.

No open task covers the DB-transaction admission tax. TASK-32804.1 (high priority) covers only the config-read instance of the same handshake, with AC #2 scoped to config, and every prior review attributed the handshake cost only to config reads. TASK-32260 (Done) did not trace it.

P1 is kept: this is a systemic 20-600x multiplier on every managed-store transaction across 16 stores. In this slice, the loop-visible impact is at modal frequency (the Console modal open/page and the Draft Shelf).

# controller.py:2481 (runs BEFORE the was_dirty check)
if self._library_prompt_text_fields_match_state(): return
# controller.py:2792
state = build_prompt_editor_state(detail)   # decode + decompose_legacy_lanes every keystroke
reason:
Verified:
- `_mark_library_prompt_dirty` (`library_prompts_controller.py:2456`) calls `_library_prompt_text_fields_match_state()` at :2481, before the `was_dirty` check.
- That function calls `build_prompt_editor_state(detail)` at :2792.

title: compile_prompt_variables lexes prompts one character at a time in Python
trigger: Yes, but once per user action: a prompt applied from the picker or modal, a variables dialog open or System-lane toggle, or a Library stage-to-Console.

- Use explicit `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`, never `\w`, which is Unicode. `_is_name_start`/`_is_name_continue` accept ASCII only.
- Keep the `\{\{` and `\}\}` alternatives BEFORE the variable alternative so escapes win.
- Pass `m.start()` as the position to `_register_variable`.
- Keep the `MAX_VARIABLE_NAME_LENGTH` issue path.
- An unterminated `{` stays literal, because the regex simply does not match it.

- Manifest loop, validate_path + stat: 32-46 ms. Lexical absolute/'..' check + os.path.join + stat: 1.2-1.6 ms.
- Walk with `Path(source).relative_to(package_root).as_posix()` per file (line 300): 103-113 ms. Stat-first, building the key only for a newer file: 28-33 ms.

- `python -m` -> `_run_module_main`:456
- textual serve -> `get_app`:660

The gate `_is_source_tree` (pyproject.toml beside the package) is true for the README's PRIMARY install path, `git clone` + `python -m pip install -e .` (README.md:74, 110). So this is the normal user boot, not dev-only.

Keep the `seen` check after the stat so a hash-matched moved-mtime manifest input is not regex-scanned into a false stale, and build the key with slicing plus `.replace(os.sep, '/')`.

Build the key only for the rare newer file, and with string slicing (source[len(root)+1:]) rather than Path.relative_to. The `seen` check must stay for newer files: a manifest input whose mtime moved but whose hash matched has an mtime above `newest_recorded`, and dropping `seen` would regex-scan it and report a false stale, which triggers a ~0.7 s rebuild. Build the key with `os.path.relpath` or slicing, then `.replace(os.sep, '/')`, or Windows keys won't match. Replacing validate_path with a lexical check (no absolute paths, no '..' parts) still blocks the hand-edited-manifest escape from the PR #1831 Qodo finding. title: General-mode ingest parse pool is never retired: spawn workers and a 20 Hz progress-drain poll live for the rest of the session after the first import
trigger: Yes. The first Library local import of any non-ebook type creates the general pool. After the queue drains, `_top_up_ingest_parse_pool` returns without retiring it.
cost: Estimated only, not measured. It is 3 resident spawn interpreters holding parser, transcriber and allocator high-water memory. Under `python -m tldw_chatbook.app`, spawn's init_main_from_name re-imports the app module in each child as __mp_main__. The drain thread adds 20 Hz wakeups, which is cheap per wake but never stops. Memory scale is plausible at tens to hundreds of MB. The 20 Hz poll alone would be P3.
fix: Arm an idle timer (e.g. 30-60 s after generation_jobs empties and next_queued() is None) that calls the existing _retire_idle_ingest_parse_pool; cancel it on the next submit. Have the drain thread block longer (get(timeout=0.5)) or wake on stop_event through a sentinel put.

Retirement sets `_ingest_parse_pool_retiring`, which gates new submissions until teardown completes, and the next import pays full spawn cost again (seconds, since each child re-imports the app under -m). So choose a generous idle delay. Drain thread: do not simply raise the timeout to 0.5 s. The coalescer flushes due batches every INGEST_PARSE_PROGRESS_FLUSH_SECONDS=0.25, so a longer blocking get delays progress. Block with no timeout while the coalescer has nothing pending, or use time-to-next-due as the timeout, and wake on stop through a sentinel put.

trigger: Every app boot for every user, gated only by execution_allowed on db.scheduled_tasks, which is normally true. It runs whether or not Schedules is used.
cost: Code confirmed: app.py:15027 calls reconcile_stale_automation_runs synchronously in the sync App.on_mount. app.py:15044 does asyncio.create_task(recover_inflight_transfers()), whose _recover_stuck_definitions (scheduling_service.py:2166) and awaited-but-never-yielding _recover_stuck_reminders (line 2215, returning early when nothing is stuck) run contiguously on the loop. Measured on a scratch DB, with the same contended-box caveat: reconcile 85-119 ms (1 open); recover_inflight_transfers with 0 stuck and no server 146-244 ms (2 opens, helper leg 105-158 ms); plus warm ScheduledTasksDB construction in App.__init__ (app.py:10469) 77-133 ms. So about 230-360 ms of on-loop boot time for every user. Root-cause split: with the helper stubbed, reconcile 27 ms + recover 61 ms. With a held connection, reconcile 9 ms + recover 16 ms (the Python filter over 12 definitions and 50 reminders is negligible; the residual is per-operation storage admission). About 90-95% of the cost is F1's per-open cost, and it runs once per session, so a P0 here would double-count F1. It stays P1 because the residual after either F1 fix shape (25-90 ms of boot loop time) is still above the 10-20 ms boot threshold. The F2-specific fix (move it into SchedulerLoop's _offload startup maintenance after _ui_ready) is low-risk and independent of F1. This agrees with the first verifier's downgrade.
fix: Move both calls out of on_mount into the post-_ui_ready scheduler start block (app.py:16260), or into SchedulerLoop.run's startup maintenance, which already offloads fail_interrupted_task_runs and prune_task_runs, and run them via asyncio.to_thread. Replace the Python filters with DB methods that query WHERE transfer_state = 'to_server_sent' (small tables, no JSON decode). Once F1 lands this drops to a few ms, but it should still come off the loop and out of the pre-paint window.
fix_notes: Moving reconcile into SchedulerLoop.run's startup maintenance (_reconcile_and_prune_run_ledger, which already _offloads) keeps the invariant that no live run of this process can be reconciled, because it still runs before the poll loop. It must stay inside the same execution_scope admission. recover_inflight_transfers has a genuinely async server half (list-and-match). Wrap only the two list reads and the per-row set_transfer_state CAS calls in to_thread. Replacing the Python filters with a WHERE transfer_state='to_server_sent' query is safe (small tables), but adding an index means the plan-pin census rule applies. If on_mount ordering is moved, re-check the Tests/Scheduling tests that reference recover_inflight_transfers and reconcile_stale_automation_runs.

self.scheduling_service.db.reconcile_stale_automation_runs(older_than_seconds=...)
self._recover_inflight_transfers_task = asyncio.create_task(self.scheduling_service.recover_inflight_transfers())
# recover: no await before both scans
stuck = [row for row in self.db.list_automation_definitions() if row.get("transfer_state") == "to_server_sent"]
stuck = [row for row in self.db.list_reminder_tasks() if row.get("transfer_state") == "to_server_sent"]
reason: Verified in app.py on_mount (a synchronous method). At 15015 it runs execution_allowed(...), a disk-reading admission check of about 6-8 ms. At 15027 it calls scheduling_service.db.reconcile_stale_automation_runs synchronously. At 15044 it runs asyncio.create_task(recover_inflight_transfers()). In recover_inflight_transfers (scheduling_service.py:2120-2160), _recover_stuck_definitions() is synchronous: list_automation_definitions() filtered in Python, at line 2166. It is followed by `await self._recover_stuck_reminders()`, a coroutine call that does not yield before db.list_reminder_tasks() at line 2215 and returns when nothing is stuck. So both full-table reads run contiguously on the loop in the first loop iterations. The scheduler loop itself is deliberately started only after _ui_ready (app.py:16248-16266, citing ADR-097). These two maintenance calls were not moved with it. This is not the verified-fine list, and no open task covers it. Downgraded from P0 to P1: this runs once per session in the boot window, and about 90% of the cost is F1's per-open helper spawn, not the scans themselves. Filtered in Python, the scans cost about 1 ms on a raw connection. Filing this as a second P0 would double-count F1's root cause. The fix specific to F2 (move off on_mount, into the post-_ui_ready block or _offload) is still worth doing independently.

title: SchedulingService reminder paths and all of SyncEngine run synchronous ScheduledTasksDB calls inside async def on the event loop (the definition paths already use to_thread)
trigger: Every Schedules visit (load_tasks calls list_tasks), every reminder save/toggle/delete/bulk action, 's' sync, each notification-triggered results pull, and each conflict resolution. All run on the app event loop.
cost: Measured the local-mode paths through SchedulingService on the scratch DB (contended box). list_tasks(None, include_projections=False) takes 77-100 ms (1 open) and runs on every visit plus after every mutation (_request_tasks_refresh). create_reminder takes 142-212 ms (2 opens), update_reminder (title only) 241-307 ms (3 opens), delete_reminder 181-209 ms (2 opens). All of them are sync self.db.* inside async def. Caller trace: the CRUD sites (workbench 2280/2342/2987/2990/4558/5150/5349) sit inside async closures (_delete_and_refresh 2274, _duplicate_and_refresh 2340, _save_and_refresh 2979, _update_and_refresh 4549, _bulk_delete 5141, _bulk_toggle 5341), each dispatched via run_worker(coro) at 2297/2357/2766/3005/4574/5168/5367. `grep -c thread=True` over UI/Screens/scheduling returns 0. In sync_engine.py there are 81 self.db call sites and exactly one to_thread match, a comment at line 795, so there is zero offload. _run_sync (5421) and _pull_results_worker (1083) are coroutine workers. ConflictsTab._resolve (conflicts_tab.py:307) calls sync_engine.resolve_conflict synchronously. NEW EVIDENCE that this is independent of F1: on ONE held connection the residual is still list_tasks 7-14 ms, create 16-20 ms, update 21-37 ms, delete 12-26 ms, from per-operation @_core_transaction storage admission plus pydantic. So even after F1 each reminder action keeps a 10-35 ms on-loop cost and the offload remains needed. The first verifier's claim that the cost falls to ~1 ms after F1 is not borne out. The sync, pull and resolve_conflict costs were traced, not run (they need a server). Reminder CRUD is not on the rubric's P0 common-path list, so P1 stands. It is new scope under the TASK-32804 umbrella.
fix: Give SyncEngine and SchedulingService one offload helper (the same shape as SchedulerLoop._offload) and route every self.db.* call through it. Or move each whole DB span into one to_thread closure, keeping transaction boundaries. Make ConflictsTab._resolve a worker calling an async resolve_conflict. Batch _server_id_for_local lookups for all mutations in one query. After F1 the per-call cost falls to ~1 ms, but the page upserts, JSON work and N+1 shape still belong off the loop.
fix_notes: Each ScheduledTasksDB method is already its own transaction, so wrapping individual calls in to_thread does not weaken atomicity. Where a sequence must be consistent (resolve_conflict's delete_reminder_task, delete_sync_mapping and delete_tombstone), prefer one to_thread closure over the whole span, or better, fold it into one DB transaction. SyncEngine mutates shared state (owner_id, set by SchedulingService at line 490); offloading only the DB calls, not the engine logic, avoids new races. If F1's held-connection fix lands at the same time, to_thread's pooled threads each get a thread-local connection that backup retirement must be able to close (see F7 and TASK-32628). ConflictsTab._resolve must become a worker, with the table mutations after the await guarded against the screen having been dismissed.

title: execution_scope (disk-reading admission check) is entered twice per 30 s scheduler tick on the event loop, plus once per dispatch
trigger: SchedulerLoop.run is a coroutine worker on the app loop (app.py:16261), so it fires every poll_interval (30 s) for the app's lifetime, plus once more per dispatched due task.
cost: Own probe: execution_scope median 8.2 ms (min 5.7 ms). About 14-16 ms contiguous per tick, of which about 7 ms is redundant, plus about 7 ms per dispatch.
fix: In _admitted_dispatch, skip re-acquiring when the current task already holds an admitted operation: _maintenance_tasks.get(asyncio.current_task(), 0) > 0 means the outer run() scope is live for the whole inner call. Or acquire the scope once around the poll iteration only. Admission semantics are unchanged because the outer scope spans the inner call.
fix_notes: execution_scope already accepts `retained=`. Passing the outer lease avoids acquire_storage but still re-runs activation_permission's disk reads, so the finder's skip-when-nested approach saves more. Key it on the current task's _maintenance_tasks depth (only this task's scope counts). Manual run_reminder_now arrives on a different task (a workbench worker) and must still acquire its own scope; the depth check handles that. Keep the `if not allowed: return False` semantics for the un-nested path.
evidence:
with (self._maintenance_operation(),
      execution_scope(("db.scheduled_tasks",), self.db.db_path) as allowed):   # run(), per iteration
    ...
    await self.tick()          # @_admitted_dispatch -> execution_scope(...) AGAIN
# dispatch_reminder is also @_admitted_dispatch -> a third scope per due task
reason: Verified. run() enters execution_scope(('db.scheduled_tasks',), db_path) per iteration (loop.py:460-464). tick() is decorated @_admitted_dispatch (loop.py:39-51, 502), which enters execution_scope again, and dispatch_reminder (732) and run_reminder_now (1074) do the same. execution_scope (activation.py:181-219) runs acquire_storage plus activation_permission, which reads control records and the registry from disk. With no reload pending there is no await between the outer and inner scope, so both costs are contiguous on the loop. The outer scope is held across the entire inner call, so the inner re-check is redundant for the same task. _maintenance_operation is entered only at the 3 loop.py sites, and each is paired with execution_scope, so the depth proxy is sound. Downgraded from P2 to P3: the removable part is about 7 ms once per 30 s poll, under one frame, a duty cycle of about 0.02%. The remaining outer scope (about 7 ms) stays.

title: automation_results has no retention and every listing sorts by an expression (full scan + temp B-tree); mark-all-read loads every unread row then does a per-row 2-connection review fan-out
trigger: Mark all read (the rail button or 'a', and per-definition mark-read at 3816) runs _unread_result_ids on the loop. Opening the results overlay runs 3 synchronous queries on the loop. The load_tasks inbox listing runs off-loop on every refresh.
cost: Own probe with 20k rows (about 13k unread): list_automation_results limit 200 median 94 ms, count_unread 65 ms, _unread_result_ids equivalent 377 ms on the loop. Even at zero rows mark-all-read costs about 120 ms on the loop (2 opens, per F1). The fan-out is about 120 ms per result serially (2 opens), so 100 unread takes about 12 s of background time.
fix: Add results retention, e.g. keep the newest N per definition in create_automation_result and upsert_automation_results_from_server, as runs already do. Normalize created_at at the write boundary, as definitions already do, so ORDER BY created_at can use idx_automation_results_owner_review; or add an expression index. Add list_unread_result_ids() selecting only id. Add a batch mark_results_read(ids) DB method: one transaction, UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...), with pending-mutation rows via executemany.
fix_notes: The strftime ordering is deliberate: its docstring explains that server-mirrored rows mix 'Z' and '+00:00' offsets, and raw text order inverts. Normalising created_at in upsert_automation_results_from_server, plus a one-off migration of existing rows, lets plain ORDER BY created_at use an index. Alternatively, an expression index on strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f', created_at) is allowed, since it has no 'now'. Either way, CLAUDE.md requires a plan pin in scripts/index_plan_pin_census.tsv, verified with sqlite_stat1 absent, and a schema bump to v8. A batch mark-read must keep review_automation_result's contract: the pending-mutation row for server mirrors goes in the SAME transaction as the UPDATE. Retention must not delete unread results or results referenced by a definition's resolved_result_id.
evidence:
f"SELECT * FROM automation_results {where_clause} "
"ORDER BY strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f', created_at) DESC, created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT ? OFFSET ?"
# EXPLAIN: SCAN automation_results / USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
# _unread_result_ids: list_automation_results(owner_id=None, review_state="unread", limit=unread_total)  -> ids only
# review_automation_result: to_thread(get_automation_result) + to_thread(update_result_review) per id
reason: Verified. list_automation_results (scheduled_tasks_db.py:2598-2606) orders by strftime(created_at) DESC, created_at DESC, id DESC. On my 20k-row DB, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN gives 'SCAN automation_results' + 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY', and for the unread filter 'SCAN ... USING INDEX idx_automation_results_owner_review' + temp B-tree. The only DELETE FROM automation_results is the one-time v6_to_v7 dedupe (migrations/v6_to_v7.py:50); runs have _RUNS_RETAINED_PER_DEFINITION=200 and results have nothing, so growth is unbounded. action_mark_all_results_read (workbench 4507-4538) calls _unread_result_ids synchronously on the loop, which is count_unread_results plus an uncapped list_automation_results. mark_results_read (results_tab.py:599-627) then loops serially over ids, awaiting review_automation_result, which does 2 to_thread calls, each opening its own connection. The _push_results_overlay _query() (workbench ~2468-2488) also runs list+count+definitions synchronously on the loop. The load_tasks inbox listing is correctly offloaded (_build_rows in to_thread). title: Every scheduler queue reload retires the SubscriptionsDB worker connection, forcing a reopen plus a WAL TRUNCATE checkpoint each time
trigger: Each reminder create/update/delete, run-now, automation schedule advance, and every 30 min periodic reload. It runs in the default to_thread pool.
cost: Estimated: about 60 ms for the SubscriptionsDB reopen (the same helper-spawn open measured in F1), plus a TRUNCATE checkpoint needing idle readers, plus 2 ScheduledTasksDB opens in queue.load. All of it is off-loop. I did not measure the checkpoint contention.
fix: Run scheduler DB work on a dedicated single-thread executor (loop.run_in_executor with one ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)). The thread-local connections can then stay held without leaking across pooled to_thread threads, and the per-load close/checkpoint can be dropped (checkpoint only at shutdown).
fix_notes: The retirement was added deliberately by TASK-32628 (commit b5251e9a6e, backup and selectable recovery): the scheduler must not leave cached SubscriptionsDB handles on pooled worker threads that live backup and recovery cannot retire. A dedicated single-thread executor that holds connections has to preserve that. Those handles must be retirable by the backup coordinator, for example closed in _maintenance_close_admission or _maintenance_drain. The per-load checkpoint could be dropped while keeping the close, but the close itself is what the recovery design requires.
reason: Verified. _load_queue (loop.py:249-273) registers retirement.callback(db.close) for each non-memory SubscriptionsDB behind the projections, then runs queue.load() in a to_thread worker. SubscriptionsDB.close (Subscriptions_DB.py:6751-6791) runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) and closes that thread's connection. queue.load() then reopens it lazily on the next reload through connect_private_sqlite, which spawns the helper. This happens on every _reload_queue: request_reload from each reminder mutation (on_queue_changed), run-now, and every 60 ticks. It is off the event loop, so it only contends with writers and delays the tick. Kept at P3.

title: Scheduler heartbeat forces a full durability barrier (fsync + F_FULLFSYNC + dir fsync) every 30 s for a liveness file
trigger: Every scheduler tick, every 30 s, for the app's lifetime, regardless of due tasks. It runs on a to_thread worker.
cost: Own probe: atomic_write_text(private=True) median 8.0 ms against 0.15 ms for a plain write + os.replace. That is 2,880 full barriers a day; the loop duty cycle is zero.
fix: Give atomic_write_text a durable=False mode (temp write + os.replace, no fsync barrier) and use it for the heartbeat. Optionally write only when tick_count/last_error changed or every Nth tick, since the reader's staleness window is at least 90 s.
fix_notes: The proposed durable=False mode reverses the task-32896 and tier-2 S08 decision. That review argued a truncated heartbeat after power loss reads as 'never_started'. The argument is weak, because the next process's first tick rewrites the file within 30 s. But any change has to rebut it explicitly, not just drop the barrier. A less contentious middle ground: keep fsync but skip F_FULLFSYNC and the directory fsync for this file only, or write every other tick. At the default poll, the 90 s staleness floor tolerates a 60 s gap, but a user-configured poll interval changes that arithmetic.
evidence:
atomic_write_text(path, payload, private=True)
# atomic_write_text: f.flush(); flush_file(fd) -> os.fsync + fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on Darwin; os.replace; fsync_parent_directory
reason: Verified. write_heartbeat (scheduler_heartbeat.py:93-119) calls atomic_write_text(path, payload, private=True), which does f.flush() + flush_file (fsync, plus F_FULLFSYNC on Darwin) + os.replace. The finder says this also fsyncs the parent directory; I did not re-verify that step. It runs every tick through tick()'s finally, via self._offload(self._record_heartbeat), so it is off the event loop. Durability was chosen deliberately: the tier-2 review (qa/tier2-code-review-2026-09-21/slices/S08-scheduling.md, P2 at L103) flagged the old hand-rolled non-fsync write, and task-32896 (commit 34c0316b01) adopted the hardened helper. The cost is real but minor and off-loop, so P3 hygiene is right.

title: Missed-occurrence counting walks croniter up to 100,000 iterations per late dispatch
trigger: Yes, but rare and off-loop. SchedulerLoop.dispatch_reminder -> await self._offload(self.db.mark_reminder_dispatched, ...) (loop.py:823/840) -> asyncio.to_thread -> _count_missed_occurrences, only for late recurring reminders. It runs once per overdue recurring reminder on the first tick after an absence.
cost: Measured in an isolated interpreter (Py3.12, installed croniter): get_next costs 10.7-14.5 us for a minutely cron, 14-20 us for hourly and 11-17 us for a minutely cron in America/New_York. A capped count (100,001 iterations) is 1.07-1.45 s of CPU holding the GIL in the worker thread. 7 days on '* * * * *' is about 0.1-0.15 s. The UI thread still gets the GIL at the 5 ms switch interval, so the user sees at most mild jank, not a freeze. The tick is delayed by the same amount.
fix: Lower the cap (e.g. 10,000); the _MISSED_COUNT_OVERFLOW 'more than N' sentinel is already rendered by the UI. Optionally add a closed-form count for fixed-interval crons.
fix_notes: Lowering the cap to 10,000 is UI-safe because task_detail.py:1657 renders the text from ScheduledTasksDB._MISSED_COUNT_CAP. But it breaks Tests/Scheduling/test_missed_fire.py:251-253, where 30 days of minutely expects the exact value 43_199 'under the 100,000 cap'. It also changes user-visible exactness: 'more than 10,000' where an exact count was shown before. Those semantics need an owner OK. A better fix that keeps exactness: a closed-form count for fixed-step crons (for example '*/N * * * *' or '0 * * * *' in UTC or a DST-free zone), keeping the iterator only as a fallback. Doing nothing is also defensible at P3. Side note: the overflow test at test_missed_fire.py:257-269 itself burns about 1 s per run.
reason: Code is exactly as quoted at scheduled_tasks_db.py:1254 (_MISSED_COUNT_CAP = 100_000) and 1288-1293 (the while/get_next loop). The only caller of _count_missed_occurrences is mark_reminder_dispatched (line 1206, recurring branch, only when late_by > grace). The only callers of mark_reminder_dispatched are Scheduling/scheduler/loop.py:823 and :840, both through SchedulerLoop._offload (loop.py:233-235 = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(...))). So it is off the event loop and the finder's framing is right. The real costs are GIL contention while the pure-Python croniter loop runs, and a delayed tick, because dispatch_reminder awaits the offload serially. It only triggers on a late dispatch of a recurring reminder, and the iteration count equals the occurrences skipped. An hourly or daily cron after a week away is a few hundred iterations or fewer (negligible). A minutely cron after 7 days is about 10k iterations. The cap is reached only by a minutely cron after about 69 days away, or a 6-field seconds cron after about 28 hours. It is rare, off-loop and bounded, so P3 is correct. No open task covers it. TASK-18937 (Done) introduced the cap and sentinel deliberately.

Besides scheduled_tasks_db.py:1230 (mark_reminder_dispatched), :1284 (_count_missed_occurrences), :1662 (create_local_copy_from_mirror) and scheduling_service.py:3109 (_compute_next_run_at), there is also scheduling_service.py:821 `croniter.is_valid(...)` in edit_reminder_fields. title: Unconditional ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE rewrites every unchanged re-fetched item; triggers cascade into two FTS re-indexes per row
trigger: yes, but off-loop. Every check re-delivers the feed's current items (compounded by F6), and mark-read/star/status updates also fire the any-column FTS trigger.
cost: Re-ran the finder's probe in scratch. Re-upserting 50 unchanged items: median 22.7 ms and exactly 1134 total_changes (about 22 per item). An existence-probe-only transaction: 10.2 ms. Both include the F2 admission tax, so the write amplification delta is about 12 ms per 50 items, consistent with the finder's 11.9 ms. This is background write-lock time plus FTS and WAL churn, not a loop freeze.
fix: The conflict key includes content_hash = sha256(title+content), so on conflict the text is unchanged. Restrict DO UPDATE to status/run_id with `WHERE subscription_items.status NOT IN ('reviewed','ignored','ingested') OR subscription_items.run_id IS NOT excluded.run_id`. Needs a schema migration: FTS trigger to `AFTER UPDATE OF title, content, author`, and the timestamp trigger given a `WHEN NEW.updated_at IS OLD.updated_at` guard.
fix_notes: The proposed fix has two errors. (1) `WHERE ... OR subscription_items.run_id IS NOT excluded.run_id` is always true on a new run, because run_id differs every run, so it filters nothing. (2) `AFTER UPDATE OF title, content, author` still fires whenever those columns appear in the SET list, whatever their values. cost: Measured on an isolated synthetic in-memory SQLite with the real indexes. One _effective_folder_links scan plus the set build costs 1.7 ms at 1k, 12.0 ms at 5k and 54 ms at 20k memberships. Per reconcile this adds roughly 24 ms at 5k and about 110 ms at 20k of extra write-lock hold on a worker thread. Any ChaChaNotes writer, including loop-side writes, waits behind it. It is not a loop freeze.
fix: Restrict both snapshots to the affected (folder_id, note_id) pairs: the owner's current memberships plus the `desired` set. A WHERE m.owner_id = ? OR (folder_id, note_id) IN (...) variant of the query is enough. Related but distinct: TASK-21132, the repository CTE anchoring on the whole closure.

The better approach is to compute the changed-pair set cheaply before mutating. Take the owner's active pairs (the idx_note_folder_memberships_managed_owner read that reconcile_managed already does) and diff them against `desired`, also counting owner_active flips; the result is usually 0-1 pairs per file event. Check only those pairs with the existing _folder_link_effective helper (notes_organization_sync_service.py:1711) before and after the mutation. Because effectiveness has union semantics, the 'before' check must run before the mutation, since another owner or a manual row can keep a pair effective. convert_owner_to_manual and remove_owner_memberships have no production callers, so the change could be limited to reconcile_managed. title: TTS core (38 modules) is imported at app import and TTSService is built in TldwCli.__init__ before first paint
trigger: Every launch: module-scope imports in app.py pre-paint, plus build_default_tts_service called synchronously in TldwCli.__init__.
cost: Isolated env, audit tree 840ed2ca58, load avg 36-52 on 18 cores, so the absolute numbers run high. (1) Imports: five `-X importtime` runs of `import tldw_chatbook.app`, with each tldw_chatbook.TTS* module's subtree charged to its first non-TTS importer. The TTS subtree cost 92, 72, 67, 79 and 130 ms, against a total app import of 1.82-2.22 s. That covers 36 TTS modules and is nearly all TTS self-time; the only third-party module under it is `wave`, at 2 ms. The biggest self-time costs are TTS_Generation 10.2 ms, audio_cpp_recipes 8.7, audio_cpp_supervisor 7.0, adapter_types 6.8 and effective_settings 5.7. (2) build_default_tts_service(load_settings()) after the app import took min 70 / median 110 ms over 10 calls. With get_user_data_dir stubbed out, the service's own work is only 3.0-3.2 ms: 7 `_legacy_config_snapshot` deepcopies at 0.4 ms each (count confirmed with a wrapper), plus the supervisor and registry setup. The rest is one warm get_user_data_dir call at min 75 / median 98 ms. That function is uncached, and cProfile shows 1,590 posix.open calls per call through the private_paths component walk and storage admission. The scratch data path is 14 components deep against about 6 for a real ~/.local/share/tldw_cli/<user>, so the real-profile cost of that call is probably around half. Pre-paint is confirmed: app.py:7907 sits in TldwCli.__init__, and binding happens only at on_mount (:14747). CAVEAT for the fix plan: the import saving is only real if ALL module-scope importers are deferred. Besides app.py's direct imports, tts_events.py:38-75 and stts_events.py:33-67 (both imported at module scope by app.py:403/412) import TTS_Generation, legacy_bridge, adapter_types and effective_settings. speech_tts_panel_types (app.py) pulls in settings_speech_tts, which imports AUDIO_CPP_RECIPE_REGISTRY. Deferring only app.py:303/304/385 saves about nothing, because TTS_Generation is merely attributed to app.py for being imported first. Separately, the get_user_data_dir cost is a cross-cutting lever much bigger than this finding: 25 call sites in app.py, 203 in 60 files, each uncached at about 75-140 ms per call in this environment. It should get its own finding. A lazy tts_service removes only one of those calls. Quiet-machine total for this finding is roughly 45-64 ms of imports plus about 3 ms plus one get_user_data_dir call, which is squarely P1 (boot ≥10-20 ms). It is not P0, because this is a first-paint delay, not a stall on an interactive path.
fix: (1) Make `tts_service` a lazy property and bind on first get_tts_service or the first TTS event (keep the build_default_tts_service call site so profile_source's exact-composition fence still holds; do not pass a pre-resolved data dir). (2) In app.py, make TTSProfileService, AudioCpp* and TTSPreferencesSnapshot TYPE_CHECKING-only and import them inside _ensure_tts_profile_service and the audio.cpp helpers, as TASK-21108 did for voice_bundle_service. (3) Move the TTS/STTS Message classes that app.py imports into a light tts_messages module so app.py stops pulling TTS_Generation via tts_events/stts_events. (4) Turn AUDIO_CPP_RECIPE_REGISTRY and AUDIO_CPP_RELEASE_ACCOUNTING into @functools.cache accessors. (5) In legacy_provider_config, project the needed sections first and deepcopy only those. This also buys ui_ready census headroom (TASK-23155/31816/32644).
fix_notes: (a) Most of the build cost is get_user_data_dir, which is uncached and cross-cutting: app.py calls it again at :7899 just before, and 28 times in total. A lazy tts_service saves only this one call; the real lever is the uncached secure-dir walk, which may belong to another slice. (b) Laziness has to keep _bind_tts_service/_close_tts_service semantics and the getattr(self,'tts_service',None) readers (:10337, the watchlists screen), and it must keep calling build_default_tts_service from its own frame, because profile_source.bind_default_materializer checks sys._getframe(1).f_code. Building it on a thread via the deferred-startup task is also viable. (c) Step (3), moving the Message classes, saves nothing unless adapter_bootstrap's module-scope TTSService import is also made lazy, because TTS_Generation is imported directly by app.py:385 and by adapter_bootstrap. title: First legacy TTS request imports all seven backends on the event loop, including higgs.py -> torch/torchaudio/librosa
trigger: Once per session: the first Speak, auto-speak or Playground generate with any legacy provider (OpenAI, Kokoro, ElevenLabs, Chatterbox, AllTalk, Higgs, OmniVoice), on the Textual loop.
cost: Micro-benchmark in the isolated env, after `import tldw_chatbook.app` to reproduce boot state. The first `TTSBackendManager(app_config={})` call, exactly what legacy_bridge's default_manager_factory does, took 884, 940, 1,025 and 1,169 ms across 4 runs and added 875 modules (torch 2.11 is installed in this venv; torchaudio is not). Per-backend breakdown over 2 runs: TTS_Backends module import 32-35 ms (+85 modules, numpy); higgs 764-774 ms (torch at module scope); kokoro 5-6 ms; omnivoice 2.7-3.0 ms; openai about 2 ms; chatterbox, elevenlabs and alltalk under 1 ms each. Registration after the imports takes 0.0 ms. With torch, torchaudio and librosa blocked through sys.modules, to simulate an install without torch, the first manager took 47-51 ms (+108 modules): still loop work, but small. Exhaustive caller trace (untruncated grep): ensure_builtins is called only at TTS_Backends.py:158, in TTSBackendManager.__init__. TTSBackendManager is built only in legacy_bridge.py:895-920 (default_manager_factory; the :36 import is type-only). That factory runs only from LegacyBackendHost._get_manager (async def, :577), which is reached from _run_operation. That path is driven by `async for chunk in response.byte_stream` in tts_events._generate_tts, an asyncio.create_task at :1118 on the app loop. There is no to_thread or run_in_executor in TTS_Generation, adapter_registry or legacy_bridge; the only one is _run_native_publication, for settings. The cost is paid once per process, because the class-level _builtins_loaded flag guards it. torch ships in the embeddings_rag, local_tts, chatterbox, higgs_tts, nemo, diarization, ocr_docext and all-tools extras, so the 0.9-1.2 s case (loaded machine; about 0.55 s quiet per the finder) is common among speech users. It shrinks to about 50 ms if torch was already imported earlier in the session, for example by embeddings. I did not raise this to P0: it is a once-per-session hit on a feature path (the first Speak, auto-speak or Playground generate), not a common per-action path. P1 stands.
fix: Make BackendRegistry lazy: store backend_id -> (module path, class name) and import only the requested backend in get_backend() (list_backends can still return the ids). Move torch/torchaudio/librosa/soundfile imports in higgs.py and higgs_voice_manager.py into the functions or properties that use them (the load path already runs in to_thread). Drop the module-scope numpy import in TTS_Backends.py (unused at module level) so TTS.backends.* voice managers stay light. Optionally create the manager via asyncio.to_thread and access kokoro_onnx_module inside _run_native_work.
fix_notes: A lazy per-backend import in BackendRegistry.get is the right root fix. get() prefix-matches over registered ids, so store (prefix -> module, class) and import on a match; keep list_backends returning ids, and check tests that assert list_backends or _registry contents. Moving torch, torchaudio and librosa into higgs's load path is also good. Running the factory via asyncio.to_thread alone is weaker: a torch import holds the GIL and import lock for hundreds of ms, so the UI would still jank, and the deepcopy'd config must not be shared across threads unsafely. Risk: low to medium.

title: AudioService.convert_audio is async def but runs pydub decode, ffmpeg encode and soundfile work synchronously on the loop, once per local-backend utterance
trigger: Once per spoken utterance with a local backend (Kokoro, Chatterbox, Higgs, OmniVoice) and the default mp3 format, plus ElevenLabs and AllTalk format conversions. Runs on the app loop through tts_events._generate_tts.
cost: This micro-benchmark replicates AudioService._convert_with_pydub for the Kokoro path, since pydub is not installed in the venv: float32 PCM at 24 kHz -> _numpy_to_bytes int16 -> temp WAV -> `ffmpeg -y -f wav -i tmp -b:a 192k -f mp3 out` via Popen.communicate -> read back, which is what pydub 0.25 AudioSegment.export does. It runs inside an `async def` with a synchronous body, awaited on an asyncio loop while a 5 ms heartbeat task records the longest loop gap. Results, 5 runs each: 5 s clip, convert 47-58 ms (median 56) and max loop stall 50-58 ms; 20 s, stall 86-119 ms; 60 s, stall 204-386 ms; 120 s, stall 322-361 ms. The stall equals the conversion time, so the loop is fully blocked, with no await inside. Load average was 36-52 on 18 cores; the finder's quiet-machine figures were 32, 60 and 131 ms. pydub's in-process WAV parse is excluded, so these numbers are a lower bound. Exhaustive callers (untruncated grep): the 8 convert_audio call sites are kokoro:1015 and :1463, higgs:625 and :766, omnivoice:933 (via _convert_format, awaited directly at :897 even though inference is offloaded), chatterbox:1285 (_encode_audio), alltalk:214 and elevenlabs:227. A numpy array input is converted to bytes first, which is fine to do inside the thread. Also apply it to create_m4b_with_chapters (subprocess.run at :503, with a 3,600 s timeout). Cancellation: to_thread cannot kill ffmpeg mid-encode, which is acceptable for encodes of a few hundred ms. Risk: low.

title: Briefing WAV stitch concatenates pydub segments pairwise (quadratic) and re-decodes the whole payload for duration, all on the event loop
trigger: Once per briefing audio synthesis, an occasional user action, on the app loop through a coroutine worker.
cost: Not re-run (pydub is absent from the audit venv). The quadratic copy volume is arithmetic: 60 turns x 10 s at 24 kHz mono, with gaps, is about 1.7 GB of copies, roughly 80-100 ms at memory bandwidth. That matches the finder's 83 ms for 60x10 s and 605 ms for 150 segments. Per-turn chunk stitching adds more.

title: acquire_storage re-derives ADR-126 authority from disk on every call, and every outermost DB transaction and private connect pays it

trigger: Yes. Every outermost ChaChaNotes transaction goes through __enter__ → _core_operation → participant.operation() → _repository_operation → acquire_storage; nested transactions on the same participant take the reuse branch. Other @_core_transaction repositories, private_sqlite._with_storage_admission (def at :1468), local_content_lifetime.operation (:73) and config guarded readers also call acquire_storage.
cost: Isolated probe (HOME in scratch, sandbox path 14 components deep): acquire_storage with a warm hold takes 7.0 ms median and 245 posix.open per call (4,900 opens / 20 calls). Components: admission_authority 2.57 ms, startup_permission 0.74 ms (×2), _scope 0.65 ms (×2), qualified_for 0.24 ms. An outermost ChaChaNotes transaction() with SELECT 1 takes 11.0 ms median. A real profile path is about 6 components deep, so the walk is roughly halved: estimated 3–5 ms per transaction.

Add a steady-state fast path to _acquire_storage. When _pause is None, `_holds[(pid, root)]` is ready with no error, the names match, and a cheap evidence fingerprint is unchanged since the last full derivation, mint `StorageLease(key)` and increment hold.count, skipping startup_permission, qualified_for, admission_authority and _scope. The fingerprint is os.stat (st_ino, st_size, st_mtime_ns, st_ctime_ns) of the bootstrap root dir, admission/registry.json, the unbound-owner marker and the selector config. Also:
- move admission_authority(root) below the `_holds.get(key)` check so it runs only when a new _Hold is needed
- memoize the native_qualification.json parse and native_identity (see F13)

fix_notes: The proposed fingerprint only stats leaf files (the bootstrap dir, registry.json, the marker and the selector), so it would miss an ancestor directory being swapped or re-permissioned. TASK-33267 AC#2 and PERF-07's D2 note both say a leaf-only re-check is insufficient, and the change needs the ADR-126 amendment (owner decision D1). Moving admission_authority below the `_holds.get(key)` check is the low-risk part: the post-hold startup_permission and _scope still re-validate records and the registry, and it saves about 37% of each call. Letting a transaction borrow the participant's connection lease changes what LocalPause.drain counts, since _operations drives quiescence, so the backup owner must review it.

cost: Isolated probe: _local_pause_requested takes 0.88 ms wall and 1.15 ms CPU per call, with 33 os.open per probe (posix.open is about half of the tottime). An asyncio loop reproducing monitor_app for 5 s used 1.90% of a core, against 0.08% for the same 10 Hz sleep loop without the probe.

- cache qualification and native identity (F13)

title: All acquire_storage calls in the process serialize through _Acquisition.initializing with a 10 ms poll-wait
known_task: TASK-33267 (PERF-08 AC#3; on origin/dev 857b3dd7d0, filed after the pin)
trigger: Yes. Concurrent acquisitions come from worker-thread DB transactions, provider-thread load_settings, the 1 Hz trace-maintenance transaction (TASK-31501), scheduler ticks and Skills/RAG admissions. All of them go through the same `with attempt.initializing(root, path)` gate.
cost: Isolated probe: 1 thread × 40 acquire_storage took 350 ms wall (p50 8.5 ms). 4 threads × 40 took 1,398 ms wall, 4.0× for 4× the work, i.e. fully serial, with per-call p50 24 ms, p95 86 ms and max 120 ms. A Console-turn transaction can therefore stall 50–120 ms behind background admissions.
fix:
F1's fast path skips the initializing section in the steady state, which is the main fix. Also:
- replace the `_changed.wait(0.01)` retry with an untimed or long-timeout wait, since close() already calls notify_all
- narrow the leader section to hold creation only (`_holds[key] is None`)
fix_notes: An untimed wait is unsafe. _begin_local_pause and resume do notify_all, but an operation-bound attempt's _check_operation can become invalid without any notify, so keep a bounded timeout (for example 0.05–0.1 s) rather than waiting forever; the 10 ms poll is not what causes the serialization anyway. Narrowing the leader section weakens the documented 'single same-process first-use interval' invariant (marker plus native registration). It is only safe when `_holds[key]` already exists and is ready without error, which is F1's fast path, so do it as part of the ADR-126 amendment, not separately.

...
_changed.wait(0.01)
reason: Confirmed on the pin. _Acquisition.initializing (storage_admission.py:216-244) picks one leader per (root, pid) and the others spin on `_changed.wait(0.01)`. _acquire_storage (:883-912) holds that section across startup_permission, qualified_for and admission_authority. known_task: TASK-33267 (PERF-08 appendix row, 'unverified'; on origin/dev, filed after the pin); umbrella TASK-32804 at the pin
trigger: Yes. Six boot sites run on the loop inside the first-paint/post-mount window. The scheduler tick (SCHEDULER_POLL_INTERVAL, about 30 s) and every admitted dispatch enter execution_scope synchronously in the loop coroutine.
cost:
Scratch: scratch/sl-br (bench_exec.py, bench_depth.py, bench_contend.py, boot_probe.py, boot_normal.json, boot_skipid.json). All runs used isolated env and admit_startup(). Host load average was 19-46 on 18 cores throughout, so absolute times are inflated; the minimums are the best proxy for a quiet machine.

(1) Microbenchmark, single thread, startup lease held, 300 iterations:
- execution_allowed(('db.scheduled_tasks',), path): min 4.9-5.9 ms, median 6.8-14.7 ms
- execution_allowed(('config',)): min 4.85 ms
- the 4-owner call: min 7.7 ms, median 10.7 ms
- cProfile: each call makes 307-493 os.open syscalls, because pinned_directory walks every path component about 15 times per call; acquire_storage accounts for about 75%
- Path-depth regression (depth 13 vs 19) gives about 0.3 ms per component, so the real ~/.config depth of 5 costs about 3-4 ms per call on a quiet machine

(2) Headless TldwCli.run_test boot trace, 3 runs. I wrapped activation.execution_scope and recorded thread, duration and call site:
- Pre-first-paint (before HomeScreen's first _display), only app.py:15017 on_mount runs: 6.7/8.5/10.9 ms
- Right after first paint comes one contiguous loop slice of 4 calls (app.py:15207, 16260, 19009, 19022): 72 / 91 / 61 ms
- Then Scheduling/scheduler/loop.py:433: 18-82 ms on the loop
- A site the finder and the first verifier both missed: app.py:17583 admitted_initialize (4 owners), run as an asyncio task on the loop for TTS and STTS on every boot, 100 ms after post-mount. It measured 257+147, 414+170 and 639+44 ms on the main thread, overlapping recorded loop stalls of 605-711 ms
- start_subscriptions_fts_backfill at app.py:16458 was 7-11 ms on main
- Steady state: each 30 s tick makes 2 calls on the loop (loop.py:463 plus the nested @_admitted_dispatch tick at loop.py:46): 10.2+6.0 ms

(3) Amplification: 8-13 threads are alive at these sites. I ran the same call on main alongside a single CPU-bound Python thread. The sched call went from about 7 ms to a median of 758 ms (p10 168 ms), and the 4-owner call to a median of 239 ms. This is the GIL convoy: each of the ~300-500 GIL-releasing os.open calls can wait out the 5 ms switch interval. That explains why boot-time sites cost 10-100x the quiet figure.

Verdict: keep P1. Boot is a common path, the post-paint burst is 15-20 ms even when quiet, and the convoy makes it much worse under real boot concurrency. The steady-state tick alone is only about 0.05% of a core, which is P2/P3. The app.py:17583 site may merit P0: it measured over 100 ms per boot, but only under host load, so re-measure it on an unloaded machine before escalating. Fix note: the fix plan must include app.py:17583. The scheduler fix must also cover the nested loop.py:46 scope, not just loop.py:463. Passing retained= removes only acquire_storage; activation_permission still does pinned_directory walks on the loop.

For the scheduler, acquire the tick's lease through to_thread and pass it as `retained=` to execution_scope. F1 makes each call microseconds regardless.

For the scheduler, acquiring the lease in a thread and passing retained= removes only the acquire half. execution_scope still runs execution_context, _source_scope_admitted and activation_permission (disk reads) on the loop, so either run the whole scope check off-loop or rely on F1/PERF-08 amortization. title: Inside a transaction every get_connection() re-resolves and stats the DB path twice
known_task: TASK-33267 (PERF-08 appendix row, 'unverified'; on origin/dev, filed after the pin)
trigger: Yes. Any execute_query, get_connection or nested transaction() issued while an outer operation is open on the same thread. The chatbook importer's per-message loop inside one immediate transaction is a real bulk path. Console persistence helpers pay it a handful of times per turn (negligible).
cost:
Isolated probe (sandbox path 14 components deep, loaded machine):
- execute_query SELECT 1: 0.028 ms outside a transaction, 0.200 ms inside one
- nested transaction()+execute inside a transaction: 0.293 ms
That is about 170 µs of overhead per in-transaction statement here. A real path is about 6 components deep, so estimate 60–100 µs, or about 1–2 s extra for a 10k-message import at 2 or more get_connection calls per message.
fix: When `selected == self.path` and this operation has already passed a full check on this thread, check only the provenance, pause and hold fields. Alternatively, verify the parent against a held O_DIRECTORY fd via one fstat instead of `Path.resolve()`, and cache `lexical_path(path)` on the participant. A full re-resolve is then needed only at the operation boundary.
fix_notes: Caching lexical_path(path) on the participant is safe. Skipping the full re-resolve after the operation's first check on this thread is safe only if parent-swap detection survives. Today it uses a path-based os.stat(self.path.parent) compared with the recorded identity, which does detect a swap. Replacing that with fstat of a held O_DIRECTORY fd would miss a path-level swap, since the held fd still points at the old inode. Keep one path-based stat of the parent and drop only the per-component resolve(). Any change here is ADR-126 territory and needs the backup owner's review.

    selected = lexical_path(path)
    parent = os.stat(self.path.parent)
    if (selected != self.path
        or selected.resolve() != self.resolved_path   # realpath = lstat per component
reason: Confirmed on the pin. _Operation.check(path) at storage_admission.py:79-85 does lexical_path, os.stat(parent) and selected.resolve() (an lstat per component). Inside an operation, ChaChaNotes _get_thread_connection is @_core_getter (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3424). That runs `_check_operation(previous, previous.path)` (participants.py:580). The function body then calls _core_access (:3451), which calls `_check_operation(operation, participant.path)` (participants.py:411). On origin/dev this finding is an 'unverified' P2 row under PERF-08 (TASK-33267) with no task text or AC covering it, so this verification adds evidence. P2 is right: the cost only matters for bulk data and less frequent paths (import, FTS backfill).

title: Backup and restore re-hash whole archives 9–13 times per operation; verify_sealed does 2 full passes per call
trigger: User-initiated backup (start_backup via the backup-create-start thread worker) and restore review/start (summary, preview_restore, start_restore via thread workers). Each restore phase calls verify_sealed again.
cost: Estimated, not re-measured here. The pass counts are verified from the code. At roughly 2 GB/s for hashlib SHA-256 on this machine class, a 5 GB profile costs about 15–30 s of extra hashing CPU plus 35–55 GB of extra reads. The per-chunk statvfs is about 80k calls per 5 GB, a few hundred ms, and minor.
fix: Hash during the copy in copy_capture_file and in acquire's input copy, and return the digest. For process-owned private staging files, detect changes by comparing the `_identity` fstat tuple (dev, ino, size, mtime_ns, ctime_ns, already captured) instead of re-hashing, keeping one authenticated hash per artifact. verify_sealed should do an identity check plus a manifest re-read, re-hashing only when the identity changed. Drop `_space` from _inspect's read loop. Pick ZIP_STORED for high-ratio members during the first package pass instead of re-packaging everything.
fix_notes: The repeated hashes are deliberate TOCTOU defences in the ADR-126 design (for example, verify_sealed's contract is to invalidate the preview if the completed bytes changed). Replacing them with an fstat identity tuple weakens that: mtime is settable with utime, and the change detector relies on ctime granularity. Treat that part as security-review territory, not low risk. Zero-risk wins first: (1) hash during copy_capture_file and return the digest, which saves 1N; (2) drop _space() from _inspect's read-only member loop, or check once up front. Medium risk: reuse acquire's digest of its private copy instead of the writer's pre- and post-acquire _hash passes. For plaintext, verified.digest equals the output digest; for encrypted, the ciphertext digest is carried in encrypted_source. Re-packaging for >100× members is rare and cannot be decided before compressing, so it is low value. The verify_sealed double-hash needs a design decision, not a mechanical change.

title: Raw-CLI output sanitizer walks every output character in Python, and keeps doing so after the preview and record caps are exhausted
trigger: Any raw-CLI command with large output (user `!cmd` or approved model raw_cli). The parent thread runs for as long as the command streams.
cost: Measured on a loaded machine: sanitizer 141 ms per 1 MiB; accumulator 155 ms per first MiB and 85 ms per MiB after both budgets are full, with still only 5 events emitted. The finder's 54 ms/MB is on the low side, so 100 MB of output means about 5-15 s of GIL-held CPU in the app process. The loop still gets 5 ms switch-interval slices, so this slows the UI rather than freezing it.
fix: In consume(): once the preview budget and the record budget are exhausted and truncation has been reported for that stream, only add len(payload) to _raw_bytes and return (skip decode and sanitize). In feed(): add a fast path: if state is 'text', no pending CR, and one precompiled regex finds no C0/C1/ESC/CR characters in the chunk, return the text unchanged at C speed.
fix_notes: The budget short-circuit in consume() is safe only once truncation has been reported for that stream (_reported_truncation), and _raw_bytes must still be incremented so total_bytes stays exact. The incremental decoder state can be abandoned once the budgets are gone, because finish() output is also discarded then. The regex fast path must also require self._state == 'text' and not _pending_cr at chunk entry, and it must treat \r, ESC, C0 and 0x7F-0x9F as slow-path triggers (\x9b/\x9d/\x9c fall in C1).
reason: raw_cli_executor.py:575 _StreamSanitizer.feed is a per-character Python state machine. _OutputAccumulator.consume (679) always runs decode plus feed, and _accept then runs _utf8_prefix, which encodes the whole text again twice and builds an f-string record, even after MAX_RAW_PREVIEW_BYTES (32 KiB) and the record budget are both exhausted. consume is called from the parent-side loop (line 1386), inside RawShellExecutor.execute, which runs in a thread worker in the TUI process, so it competes for the GIL with the Textual loop. The worker's _drain_pipe forwards every byte in 8 KiB chunks with no output cap, so the parent processes all output. No open task covers it.

title: web_fetch and robots checks build a new httpx.Client (fresh SSLContext) per call, even on a warm cache hit, and never pool connections
trigger: Agent web_fetch calls (worker thread) and web_deep_search per-result robots checks (executor).
cost: Not re-measured. The finder's figure (about 10 ms httpx.Client() vs 0.6 ms with a reused SSLContext) matches the standard httpx cost. The loss that matters most is on cache hits, which otherwise take under 1 ms; also note _validate_hop does live DNS on every cache hit.

Cache httpx_verify()'s result or the SSLContext per ssl_verify setting in Utils/tls_trust.py, which also benefits every other build_httpx_client caller. Optionally keep one module-level client per UA with trust_env=False and follow_redirects=False.

A module-level shared client must keep trust_env=False and follow_redirects=False, and it must be safe across threads (httpx.Client is), but a pooled keep-alive connection could reuse a socket to an IP validated on an earlier hop. The SSRF guard validates per hop via DNS, so reusing connections across calls needs care. Caching the SSLContext per verify setting in tls_trust is the lowest-risk win.
reason: web_tool_impls.py:1050 builds _new_web_fetch_client() on a warm cache hit whenever respect_robots is on, which is the default, even if the robots parser for that host is already cached. title: Every Console sync tick force-relayouts the screen: left_rail.sync_model_recovery calls Static.update unconditionally and re-runs the rail allocation reconcile
trigger: Every Console sync tick at 5 Hz while any session has a run in flight. One caveat: while text is actively streaming, the transcript's own growth already forces a relayout in the same refresh cycle, and Textual coalesces them. The marginal whole-screen relayout therefore lands mostly on non-streaming ticks, while the reconcile CPU is paid on every tick.

Isolated headless boots (boot_probe3 and boot_probe4, 532-widget Console, loaded machine).

cost:

Per unchanged tick (10 ticks):
- refresh_if_scope_changed: median 377 ms wall, 2.1 helper-process spawns and 3,016 open() calls per tick, with nothing changed.
- Awaiting it pushed the tick's transcript-sync start from a median of 353 ms to 778 ms.
- It runs off the loop: loop lag was p50 0.4 ms during run_owned_db_call.

- The capture_scope shape (2 x run_owned_db_call) costs 2 spawns, 1,628 opens, 260-405 ms wall and ~95 ms child CPU.
- The same read on a retained worker connection costs 26-42 ms with 0 spawns; raw SQL is 0.011 ms.

- recomposes ConsoleCharacterContext twice;
- rebuilds _current_console_rail_state() twice on the loop (wiring.py:223): 480-700 ms loop CPU (11,947 opens), max loop lag 400-640 ms.

Skip the before/after double read unless the first read differs from the cached fingerprint. Use a plain asyncio.to_thread on a retained connection, or a dedicated single reader thread, instead of run_owned_db_call for these tiny metadata reads. Keep groups and state equal when rows are unchanged so a revision bump alone does not recompose.

Replacement triggers must cover the DB swap, character switch, store persistence completion and section open, or the display goes stale. 2. Cheapest safe steps: do the before and after reads inside ONE thread hop (one connection, one helper spawn); cache get_local_authority_id per DB instance; stop awaiting it ahead of the transcript sync (fire-and-forget it, fenced by a generation); skip it while the Character section is not rendered. 3.
