title: Every ChaChaNotes/AgentRuns transaction pays the storage-admission handshake (~245 open() calls), and run_owned_db_call reconnects through the helper process on each call
trigger: Every ChaChaNotes and AgentRuns transaction app-wide. Hot instances in this slice: F3 (on the loop, per tick), F4 (per tick), F5 (per keystroke), F7 (on the loop, per tick while drilled in).
fix: Amortise admission per thread or per operation scope: cache the verified parent-directory fds or identity and revalidate only on generation or pause changes (the same fix TASK-32804.1 AC#2 asks for, applied in storage_admission rather than only in config). For run_owned_db_call, keep one registered reader connection per executor thread, or use a dedicated DB executor, instead of connecting and closing per call.
fix_notes: High risk. The admission path enforces backup-recovery pause and generation fencing and ADR-029 private-path trust. Any cache of verified directory identity must be invalidated on generation, pause and selector changes, and must still refuse during maintenance. run_owned_db_call retires connections deliberately, so that maintenance quiescence can drain handles and cancelled awaiters do not leak them. A retained per-executor-thread connection must be registered with the quiescence registry and closed on maintenance. A dedicated single DB reader thread with one registered connection is the safer shape. Separately, spawning a helper process per connection open is the dominant constant; skipping the helper prepare when the path identity is unchanged since the last verified open would need a security review.

title: Raw CLI streaming creates a new OS thread (threading.Timer) for every 50 ms repaint window
trigger: Yes. Every stdout or stderr event of a running `/raw` (or `! `) CLI command; at most one live Timer thread at a time, recreated per 50 ms window.

fix_notes: A pure monotonic-timestamp throttle inside on_event loses the trailing flush. If output bursts and then goes quiet mid-run, the last chunk would not repaint until the next event or the end of the run. The replacement must keep a trailing flush: one long-lived per-invocation flusher thread waiting on a Condition or Event with a 0.05 s timeout, or marshal a single loop-side `set_timer` through `_marshal_to_ui`. Keep `cancel_repaint`'s terminal semantics, so no repaint after finalize.

title: Draft spend refresh debounces by destroying and recreating a Textual Timer on every keystroke, then runs the full settings-summary sync
trigger: Yes. Every composer draft mutation while the active session has no run in an active status. refresh fires once per 0.2 s typing pause.
cost: Estimated: about 20-60 µs per keystroke for Timer construction plus task create and cancel, which is noise against the ~0.37 ms per-key baseline. The pause-time refresh cost is out of scope here (F2).

A one-shot `set_timer` task ends after firing, and `stop()` sets `_task=None`, so reset() on a fired or stopped timer never fires again. The fix must be 'reset() if the timer is pending, else set_timer()', tracking pending state via the existing `self.timer = None` in refresh. Alternatively, keep a monotonic deadline and let a single timer re-arm itself if the deadline moved. The benefit is marginal, so this is optional hygiene.

cost:

- 211x44: 21.5-22.2 ms
- 235x52: 29.8 ms

view_state snapshots every session. At 211x44 it costs 22.3 ms with one session, 44.7 ms with two and 67.4 ms with three. The selected_session_id property costs 0.12 µs.

Per keystroke, today's cost is the view_state in send_key plus the view_state in the echo _refresh, so 2N snapshots:

| Size | Sessions | Per key | Wasted |
|---|---|---|---|
| 211x44 | 1 | 44.7 ms | 23 ms |
| 211x44 | 2 | 89 ms | 67 ms |
| 211x44 | 3 | 135 ms | 113 ms |
| 235x52 | 1 | 59 ms | 30 ms |
| 80x24 | 1 | 9.3 ms | 4.6 ms |

The wasted work is the send_key view_state plus the non-selected snapshots.

Caller trace:

- The sync @on handler at chat_screen.py:2403-2409 calls send_key.

For view_state itself, either make TerminalSessionView.screen optional for non-selected sessions (audit its consumers), or cache each session's snapshot keyed on model._generation. That cache is sound only if every mutation bumps _generation; feed does (screen_model.py:658), and so does line 608, which is probably resize. title: Terminal manager notifications use blocking call_from_thread per parser turn, coupling PTY I/O to UI-loop latency
trigger: Every parser turn of every attached session while the Terminal workspace view is attached. Keystroke delivery and PTY reads stall for the whole time the loop is busy.

The generation guards already make a late or dropped callback harmless.
reason: Code matches the finding. _marshal_terminal_to_ui (wiring.py:635-640) calls screen.app.call_from_thread(callback) from off-loop threads. In the installed Textual 8.2.8, App.call_from_thread does run_coroutine_threadsafe(...) and then future.result(), so the calling thread blocks until the loop runs the callback. The calling thread is the per-session runtime thread: _run_runtime (session_manager.py:1328-1373) does take_input and _write_runtime_input, then process_output. process_output calls _notify_subscribers (session_manager.py:598, 1596-1603), which runs ConsoleTerminalController._manager_changed (terminal.py:441-444), then _marshal_to_ui. After that the same thread reads PTY output. The callback only runs _queue_refresh, which is already coalesced by _frame_pending, so the blocking round-trip buys nothing. It chains the terminal's input and output pump to loop latency, which includes F2's 19 ms-per-session snapshots in the resulting _refresh frame. No open task covers it.

That is harmless for a deleted id, but it is a semantic change. Safer: keep a separate absent-id set stamped with the same cache_at/TTL, test `wanted <= set(cached_map) | absent`, and clear it wherever the map cache is cleared (the appearance-write invalidation). Alternatively, fix the root state by unbinding or closing the native session on soft-delete, but that is a behaviour change outside a perf fix.

title: Every arrow key on the Tools, Permissions or Audit tables does a guarded profile-inventory read plus a permission-store load and an inspector remount
trigger: Every arrow key (or click) on the focused Tools, Permissions or Audit table -> RowHighlighted -> the forwarded selection -> the workbench's async handler on the loop. Holding an arrow key queues one handler run per row.
cost:
Same headless bench. The handler ran once per key press: 12 of 12 Down presses in the Tools table and 10 of 10 in the Permissions matrix. This confirms DataTableClickSelectMixin (table_click_select.py:151) forwards every highlight with no debounce.
- Tools arrow key: 2 main-thread guarded ops (read_profile_inventory_snapshot + list_tool_arg_rules), plus 61-69 ms of non-store main-thread CPU (inspector remount and repaint).
- Permissions arrow key: 1-2 ops, plus 27-43 ms non-store.
At the realistic per-op cost of 6-17 ms (depth-scaled, see F1), that is about 75-100 ms per Tools key and 35-75 ms per Permissions key. Measured today under filesystem contention, the max stall was 341-413 ms per Tools key and 145-294 ms per Permissions key. Also verified that MCPAuditMode and MCPServersMode use the same mixin (mcp_audit_mode.py:322, mcp_servers_mode.py:276). The audit handler at mcp_workbench.py:4856 does the validate read per key. This is a per-keystroke cost of 10-20 ms or more, on a secondary screen, so P1 stands.
fix:
1. Read-only display paths should compare the captured context against the cached `self._tool_policy_profile_context` (selector generation plus profile id) instead of re-reading the store. Writes already carry expected_profile_digest and expected_revision, so the store rejects a stale write anyway.
2. Fetch arg rules off the loop (asyncio.to_thread), or derive them from the payload already loaded in the last pass.
3. Debounce highlight-driven selection by about 100 ms with a cancellable timer (the browser-search debounce pattern), so scrolling a list does not remount the inspector on every row.
fix_notes: Option 1 is safe for display: compare against the cached _tool_policy_profile_context (profile id + selector generation). Every mutating path still validates server-side with expected_profile_digest and expected_revision, and the write buttons re-validate. Keep the fresh-read validate on the write handlers. A debounce of about 100 ms must preserve the mixin's arrow-then-Enter dedup (_pending_activation_key), and must not drop the final row the user lands on. Cancel and re-arm the timer; do not throttle.
evidence:
DataTableClickSelectMixin.on_data_table_row_highlighted -> handler(DataTable.RowSelected(...))  # arrow key == selection
async def on_mcp_tools_mode_tool_selected(...):
    context = self._validate_profile_context(self._tool_policy_profile_context)  # read_profile_inventory_snapshot + digests
    arg_rules = self._arg_rules_for_row(tool, context.profile_id)  # list_tool_arg_rules -> store.load()
    await inspector.show_tool(tool, ...)  # 2x remove_children + mount_all
reason:
DataTableClickSelectMixin.on_data_table_row_highlighted (UI/Widgets/table_click_select.py) forwards every focused, user-driven RowHighlighted to the pane's on_data_table_row_selected. The only dedup is a repeat of the same row; programmatic rebuilds are suppressed by repopulating_table. MCPToolsMode, MCPPermissionsMode and MCPAuditMode all use the mixin. The workbench handlers each re-read the store on the loop:
- on_mcp_tools_mode_tool_selected (4614): _validate_profile_context -> read_profile_inventory_snapshot, then _arg_rules_for_row -> list_tool_arg_rules -> store.load (permission_store.py:1773), then inspector.show_tool (remove+mount)
- Permissions row selected (4762): the same validate + arg rules
- Audit entry (4856): validate only
_session_approvals_for_row is in-memory under a lock, so it is fine. There is no debounce and no open task (grepped backlog for _arg_rules_for_row, _validate_profile_context and debounce).

title: Monolithic _sync_children: every interaction re-reads the stores, re-derives the whole catalog and rebuilds all five DataTables, including hidden canvases, in one ~100 ms non-yielding block
known_task: TASK-32804.7 (Done, config reads only); task-261 (Done, declined diffing); umbrella TASK-32804
trigger: A rail click (button) or a servers-table row selection -> _select_server_key -> a full pass. Each lifecycle action runs two passes. Save completions, source switches and 'r' each run a pass. All on the event loop.
cost:
Headless bench.
- A direct _sync_children pass does 5 main-thread guarded ops (inventory x2, load, kill switch, read_recent(200); read_recent is about a quarter of a load, measured at 1,460 vs 6,066 opens) plus 109-113 ms of non-store main-thread CPU. That is about 135-195 ms per pass at realistic op cost; the measured max stall today was 967-1120 ms.
- A rail click (_select_server_key on the same key) does the same 5 ops plus 244-293 ms non-store, about 270-380 ms realistic.
Exhaustive call-site list, untruncated: 14 awaited call sites in mcp_workbench.py (reload 1161, _record_mcp_recovery_review 3470, _apply_view_state 3962, _switch_source 3990, _select_server_key 4055, _refresh_server_discovery 4262, _observe_local_master_save 4422, _observe_workspace_root_save 4515, _save_builtin_flag 6207, _save_tool_gate 6254, _delete_local_profile 6303, _save_local_profile 6398, _run_server_mutation 6483, _apply_import 6641). There is 1 more in _observe_lifecycle at 6756, plus the optimistic run_worker(self._sync_children) coroutine at about 6721, which is not a thread. No caller outside the module. New scope: MCPServersMode also uses the click-select mixin. Its ServerRowSelected goes to on_mcp_servers_mode_server_row_selected (4100), then _select_server_key, which ends in an unconditional _sync_children. So every arrow key in the Servers table, the landing mode, runs a full pass. It stays P1 only because the MCP hub is not a common path.
fix:
Split each pass into a data phase and a render phase.
1. Data phase: one asyncio.to_thread hop that returns (tools, effective, inventory, kill_switch, audit_entries, selected-tool arg rules), deduping reads within the pass.
2. Render phase: render only the ACTIVE canvas. Mark the others dirty and render them in set_mode. This keeps the documented 'never stale when switched to' invariant that task-261 cited when it declined diffing.
3. Give the selection, CHECKING-badge and save paths scoped syncs (rail, overview and inspector only) rather than the full pipeline.
4. Skip remounting callouts, toolbar and toggles when their widget spec is unchanged.
fix_notes: The data phase in a thread must not touch widgets, and must snapshot self._source, _snapshots, _catalog_records and the profile id/generation first. local_hub_tools builds providers whose character and watchlists services are lazy, so no SQLite handle is created in hub_tools(). Still, TASK-32804.12 warns that control-plane local services carry thread-affine SQLite: audit get_inventory before threading it. Rendering only the active canvas conflicts with the documented 'hidden canvas never stale when switched to' invariant that task-261 relied on, so the dirty flag must be rendered in set_mode before the switcher shows the canvas. The recovery_token re-checks after each await must be preserved. The risk is high, as the finder says.
evidence:

self._last_hub_tools = tools
effective, policy_inventory = self._capture_permission_render_state(tools)  # inv + load + inv

await self._sync_permissions_mode(effective, ...)  # get_kill_switch load + matrix rebuild
await self._refresh_selected_tool()  # inventory + arg-rules reads
await self._sync_audit_mode()       # log.read_recent(200) + 200-row rebuild

Read _sync_children (1493-1609). Under _sync_children_lock it runs, in order:
- rail.sync_state
- update_overview (servers table rebuild), with _active_target_label -> target_store.list_targets; that path has no source check, so it can fire under the local source when the service remembers an active target

All of it is on the loop: the callers are async handlers or run_worker(coroutine) with no thread. There are 51 textual mentions and about 15 real call sites, including _select_server_key (4055), _switch_source, _apply_view_state, lifecycle (optimistic plus completion passes, 6711-6721), and the save observers. task-261 (Done) declined rebuild diffing and pointed to task-236 for store loads. task-236 (Done) fixed only get_external_servers N+1. TASK-32804.7 fixed only the config reads.

title: Every warm MCP visit runs two full _sync_children passes: reload(), then an unconditional pass from the restored view state
trigger: Every MCP visit after the first, in the same process (the screen-state store keeps the snapshot).
cost:
This is now measured end to end, no longer estimated. The headless bench restores the saved view state exactly as MCPScreen.compose does (mcp_screen.py:151 set_initial_view_state; app.py:13519-13522 restore_state; save_state at mcp_screen.py:320 always writes mcp_hub_view_state).

| Visit | _sync_children passes | Main-thread guarded ops | Non-store main CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold | 1 | 9 | 1206 / 1320 ms (two runs) |
| Warm, servers | 2 | 14 | 1443 ms |
| Warm, permissions | 2 | 15 (extra inventory read from select_tool_policy_profile) | 1718 ms |

The second pass comes from reload() (1161), then _consume_pending_view_state, then the unconditional `await self._sync_children()` at the end of _apply_view_state (3962). The extra cost per warm visit is one full pass: about 5 guarded ops plus about 110 ms+ of rendering, roughly 135-195 ms of loop time at a realistic op cost. It is a per-screen-visit cost on a secondary screen, so P1.
fix: Apply the pending view state (source, mode, selected key, scope, profile) BEFORE reload()'s single _sync_children. Alternatively, have _apply_view_state resync only when the restore actually changed state that the reload did not already render (compare get_view_state() before and after).
fix_notes: The lower-risk variant is the finder's second option: compare state before and after _apply_view_state and skip the trailing pass when source, selected_server_key, scope, scope_ref and the profile id are unchanged. Include _hold_canvas_overview in the comparison, because _apply_view_state clears it and that changes the Servers canvas render. Hidden canvases are already rendered by reload's pass, so set_mode alone needs no resync. Moving the restore before reload's pass is riskier. TASK-1320 documents a mode-chip/ModeChanged ordering trap, and _apply_view_state needs _snapshots (for selected_server_key validation) and the deferred canvases mounted by _sync_children.
evidence:
# mcp_screen.compose: self.workbench.set_initial_view_state(self._initial_view_state())  # stashed pre-mount
# reload():
    await self._sync_children()
    ...
await self._consume_pending_view_state()   # -> _apply_view_state(state)
# _apply_view_state(): set_mode(...); maybe select_tool_policy_profile(...)
    await self._sync_children()   # unconditional second full pass
reason:
MCP route is not reusable (screen_registry.py:143, reusable defaults to False), so every visit builds a fresh MCPScreen. On a non-first visit:
1. app.py:13514-13522 restores the saved snapshot via restore_state before mount. self.workbench is still None at that point, so only state_data is set.
2. compose_content (mcp_screen.py:151) calls set_initial_view_state(state_data['mcp_hub_view_state']). The workbench is not mounted yet, so the state is stashed in _pending_view_state.
3. on_mount -> _start_initial_load -> reload() -> _sync_children() (1161).
4. _consume_pending_view_state() (1171) -> _apply_view_state -> set_mode and so on, ending with an unconditional `await self._sync_children()` (3962).
save_state (323) always writes mcp_hub_view_state, so the stash is present on every warm visit. In permissions mode, select_tool_policy_profile adds one more inventory read. There is no open task: TASK-1320 moved reload into a worker but did not dedupe the passes.

title: 4 Hz save-status poll calls Static.update unconditionally, forcing 4 full-screen relayouts per second while the MCP screen is visible
trigger: A 4 Hz timer while the MCP screen is mounted, with no user action. It fires with no save ever submitted: the owner is None, so the default text is re-projected.
cost:
Headless bench with the real workbench (142 widgets, 211x44), idle in Servers mode for a 10 s window:
- Timer running: 40 screen relayouts and 305.9 ms of main-thread CPU, or 3.06% of a core.
- Timer paused: 0 relayouts, 0.1 ms, or 0.0%.
- Earlier runs: 2.67% (the previous run of this bench) and 1.12% (the first verifier).
- The _sync_local_config_save_status callback alone costs 2.6-2.8 ms per tick. The rest is the relayout that Static.update forces: Textual 8.2.8 _static.py update() calls refresh(layout=True) unconditionally. That is reached through mcp_tools_mode.py:687 and mcp_servers_mode.py:1398, plus the Button label setters.

The code path is confirmed: set_interval(0.25) at mcp_workbench.py:986, then _sync_master_save_status (4381) with no stamp dedup. It is not always on. Navigation uses switch_screen (app.py:13595), which replaces the non-reusable MCPScreen, so the timer dies when the user leaves the screen. It keeps running only while MCP is visible, including under modals pushed on top. That rules out P0 and keeps P1.
fix:
1. Add the same stamp dedup that _sync_root_save_status uses: owner revision, completion_revision, current_config_identity() and config_file_revision. Skip the projection when the stamp is unchanged.
2. Make project_local_master and set_local_config_status skip Static.update() when the text is unchanged.
3. Better still, arm the interval only while a save is pending (state.result is None) and stop it once the save settles. _observe_local_master_save already resyncs on completion.
fix_notes: The smallest safe change: in set_local_config_status and project_local_master, skip Static.update and the label assignment when (message, error) is unchanged. That removes the relayouts, and the leftover tick cost (one stat plus queries) is negligible. A stamp dedup must also include _master_catalog_failure and the get_cli_setting value, or a catalog-failure suffix could be missed. Arming the interval only while a save is pending is the cleanest option. It still needs a kick when a save is submitted from another screen instance, because the owner lives on the app and survives screen recreation.
evidence:
self.set_interval(0.25, self._sync_local_config_save_status)
...
def _sync_master_save_status(self):
    canvases = [c for t in (MCPToolsMode, MCPServersMode) for c in self.query(t) if ...]
    enabled, text, error = self._master_save_projection()  # get_cli_setting + stat(config)
    for canvas in canvases: canvas.project_local_master(enabled, text, ...)
# -> set_local_config_status -> status.update(message)  # Static.update => refresh(layout=True) every tick
reason:
on_mount arms set_interval(0.25, self._sync_local_config_save_status) at mcp_workbench.py:986, for the widget's lifetime. The MCP screen is non-reusable, so the timer ends on navigation away; it keeps running under pushed modals. Every tick, _sync_master_save_status (4381):

- calls project_local_master on each canvas
- MCPToolsMode.set_local_config_status then calls Static.update(message) unconditionally

title: Filter inputs on Tools, Permissions and Audit rebuild the whole DataTable per keystroke with no debounce; Tools also rebuilds with auto-height rows and recomputes every row's cells
trigger: Input.Changed on #mcp-tools-filter-text, #mcp-perm-filter-text or #mcp-audit-filter-text, once per keystroke, synchronously on the loop.
cost:
DOWNGRADE from P1 to P2. The mechanism is confirmed: none of the 3 on_input_changed handlers debounce, and each keystroke rebuilds the table. At realistic scale the cost is moderate, and it is on a rarely used screen.

Real MCPWorkbench at 211x44, with real bound stores and the default catalog (74 Tools rows, 81 Permissions rows). Typing 'read' then 4 backspaces, loadavg 42-50 (bench_f6wb.py). Per-keystroke main-thread CPU medians:
- Tools: 47.5 ms, vs 26.1 ms with _apply_filter stubbed, so about +21 ms is attributable. First character +32 ms, clearing to empty +35 ms.
- Permissions: 48.3 vs 23.1 ms, so +25 ms.
- Loop-stall median: +20 ms (Tools) and +10 ms (Permissions).

Standalone canvases (bench_f6.py):
- Tools at 74 tools: +19 ms median.
- Tools at 150 tools: +21 ms median; first character +39 ms, clear +85 ms.
- Permissions at 155 rows: +21 ms.
- Audit at 200 entries: +25.5 ms; clear +81 ms.

There are zero guarded MCP store operations while typing, so F8 does not compound this.

On an unloaded machine this is likely about 12-17 ms attributable per keystroke. That stays under the visible-lag threshold at typing speed, on a rarely used Hub filter rather than a hot path, so P2 fits the "less frequent path" rule better than P1.

Fix-plan corrections:
- _apply_filter's own Python takes only 1.7 ms per full-catalog call (measured directly), so precomputing cells saves at most 1.7 ms.
- height=1 saved 0-4 ms at 74 tools, 150 tools and 155 permission rows.
- The cost is Textual's deferred re-measure and re-render of the whole cleared table (clear(columns=True) plus MCPToolsTable._clear_caches).
- So debouncing, and not rebuilding columns, is the only lever that matters.
fix:
1. Debounce the three filter inputs (about 120-150 ms set_timer; cancel the previous timer).
2. Precompute per-tool render cells (server_cell, schema_cell, state_cell, name width) once in update_tools/update_states rather than per keystroke.
3. Use height=1 when _tool_column_width is None (nothing wraps) and keep auto-height only when the Tool column actually wraps.
4. Clear rows only, not columns=True, when the column set is unchanged.
fix_notes: height=1 when _tool_column_width is None is safe only if no other cell wraps. The Server cell is ellipsized to _SERVER_CELL_BUDGET and Tags is joined text that could still be wider than its column, so verify that no column width is capped. Otherwise keep height=None. The debounce timer must be cancelled on unmount, and select_tool_row's filter clear must flush synchronously; it already calls _apply_filter directly. Clearing rows only (not columns) is valid only when the Tags on/off tuple and the Tool width are unchanged.
evidence:
def on_input_changed(self, event):  # every keystroke
    self._filter_text = event.value
    self._apply_filter()
# _apply_filter: table.clear(columns=True); self._measured_tool_width(table)  # Text(...).cell_len over ALL tools
#   per row: _ellipsize(Text(...).truncate) + parse_schema(...) + state_text(...)
    table.add_row(*row_cells, key=tool.tool_id, height=None)  # auto-height: renders every cell to measure
# MCPToolsTable._update_dimensions -> self._clear_caches()
reason:
All three filter handlers are synchronous and have no debounce or timer:
- mcp_tools_mode.py:943-956 on_input_changed -> _apply_filter
- mcp_permissions_mode.py:~1147
- mcp_audit_mode.py:828-832
Tools _apply_filter (807-904) does table.clear(columns=True), recomputes _measured_tool_width over all tools (Text.cell_len), and runs parse_schema, _ellipsize and state_text per row. It uses add_row(..., height=None) (auto-height), and MCPToolsTable._update_dimensions calls _clear_caches. Permissions uses the same pattern (add_row height=None at 1060). Audit rebuilds up to 200 rows with columns. Library's verified-fine note concerns DB search, not this. No open task.

title: _capture_permission_render_state holds the permission store's process-wide RLock on the event loop across 2-3 guarded file reads
corrected: tldw_chatbook/UI/MCP_Modules/mcp_workbench.py:2174-2179 (fence around capture); tldw_chatbook/MCP/permission_store.py:976-980 (mutation_fence), :192 (_resolved_path_lock), :773 (load already takes the same fence); callers mcp_workbench.py:1589, :2697, :2717
trigger: Every full _sync_children pass (51 call sites: reload, source/server select, lifecycle completion, save observers) and standalone _sync_permissions_mode (Space-cycle, kill switch, re-allow, profile select). Real loop-side contention needs a concurrent worker-thread store write, such as a Console always-allow approval or mark_config_changed from an agent-side resolution, during an MCP-hub sync pass. That is plausible but rare.
cost: Estimated, not measured. The loop blocks for at most one concurrent atomic JSON write (~13 ms, per the task-32804.7 figure), and only when the overlap happens. The inner store.load() already exposes the loop to the same lock, so the extra exposure from the outer fence covers only the 1-2 extra inventory snapshot reads. The 39 ms capture cost itself belongs to F1/F3 (the on-loop capture), not to this finding.
fix: Falls out of F1/F3: run capture() inside asyncio.to_thread so the fence is never taken on the loop thread.
fix_notes: The fix is the same change as F1/F3, so file it together with them rather than as a separate task. Do NOT drop the fence. It keeps the before/after inventory generation comparison coherent, so capture() can never show a mixed actionable render. Move the whole fenced block (fence inside the thread) into asyncio.to_thread. Before offloading, snapshot the widget state that capture reads (self._tool_policy_profile_id, self._tool_policy_selector_generation via _tool_policy_inventory) on the loop, so the worker never reads mutable widget attributes. Also check that no callee inside capture touches the DOM or app.notify: _resolve_effective_states only logs, which is fine. Dropping only the outer fence would not remove loop contention, because load() and the setters take the same RLock.
evidence:
store = getattr(service, "permission_store", None)
mutation_fence = getattr(store, "mutation_fence", None)
if callable(mutation_fence):
    with mutation_fence():      # threading.RLock shared per resolved path
        return capture()        # inventory + effective_tool_states(store.load) + inventory, ~39 ms
reason: The code matches the finding. mcp_workbench.py:2174-2179 does `store = getattr(service, 'permission_store', None)`, then `mutation_fence = getattr(store, 'mutation_fence', None)` and `with mutation_fence(): return capture()`. permission_store.py:976-980 `mutation_fence` holds `self._path_lock`, which is the process-wide RLock per resolved path from `_resolved_path_lock` at :192. capture() is sync and runs directly on the loop. It is reached from the `async def` `_sync_children` (:1589) and from `_sync_permissions_mode` (:2697 standalone and :2717 profile fallback). Both are awaited on the loop with no to_thread; _sync_children has 51 call sites and _sync_permissions_mode has 28. Inside the fence, capture runs `_tool_policy_inventory` (read_profile_inventory_snapshot/read_snapshot_strict, a file read plus json plus sha256). It then runs `_resolve_effective_states` -> `UnifiedMCPControlPlaneService.effective_tool_states` (unified_control_plane_service.py:5219), which does `store.load()` and possibly `mark_config_changed` (a write). A second inventory read follows, and a third on drift. Other threads do contend for the lock. BuiltinToolGate._load_payload (builtin_tool_gate.py:308) does `store.load()` on agent worker threads once per turn, the MCP gate reads at unified_control_plane_service.py:5456/5546/5597 do the same, and the Console's offloaded setters take the fence too. The finding overstates the extra cost the outer fence adds. `load()` (:773) and every setter already take the same lock, so the loop could already block on a worker's write inside `effective_tool_states` without this fence. The fence only widens the loop-side hold window from the single load() to the whole 2-3-read capture. Contention needs a worker-thread write (a Console always-allow approval or a rug-pull mark) that overlaps an MCP-hub sync pass. That coincidence is rare, the worker side waits on a background thread (harmless), and the loop-side wait is bounded by one small JSON atomic write (~13 ms per the task-32804.7 measurement). The workbench's own `_call_profile_scoped_off_loop` writes are awaited before the resync, so the widget cannot contend with itself. The ~39 ms hold is the on-loop capture cost itself, which is F1/F3's loop-blocking finding and not new cost from this finding. P3 is right: this is a real but narrow widening of an existing lock contention, with no independent hot trigger. No open task covers it. TASK-32804.7 (Done) offloaded the permission-store writes and config reads but left capture() on the loop.

title: Immutable snapshot diffs are never cached, and every turn-file-card mount builds a fresh provider on the loop that re-reads config and re-spawns git
trigger: Every ConsoleTurnFileCard mount (conversation load or session switch re-mint) and every Review open or file revisit. Card git runs off-thread.

Invalidate it on shadow-repo retention reset. Read the diff cap once (module-level lazy) or pass it from the bridge; cache ShadowRepo per canonical root.

The changed_files raise -> snapshots_pruned -> 'history … was pruned by retention' banner path would stop firing, and the review would show diffs for snapshots that can no longer be reverted. Invalidate the cache on retention reset, or re-probe has_snapshot cheaply. Bound it (lru_cache maxsize), because diff_text payloads can be large. The in-screen revisit cost is better fixed by F2's bounded per-generation memo than by a module-global cache.

title: Video card specs do sync storage admission + filesystem checks (and, with a recovered-media catalog, full RecoveredMedia construction + 2 SQLite connections) per video row on every transcript sync
trigger: Every transcript sync: the 0.2 s tick during runs, plus send, stop, session switch, resume and image-prep completion. The cost applies only when the viewed conversation has generated-video messages, and the severe branch requires a restored backup catalog.
cost:
MEASURED in an isolated scratch profile. HOME, XDG_* and TLDW_CONFIG_PATH pointed at scratch, bootstrap.default_bootstrap_root was pointed at scratch the same way the Tests local_root fixture does it, and storage.admit_startup() was held as in the running app. The measured code has no test-mode branches (I grepped private_sqlite*, storage_admission and bootstrap). The benchmark called VideoStore.resolve_state, the per-row call in _build_video_card_specs. Scripts are in scratch/slice49-F3-lens2/{bench,prof,depth,count}.py.

(1) NO catalog (any user with generated videos), per video row per sync. Median 19-34 ms at the scratch path depth of 12 components, for both the ready and expired cases. Cost grows about 2 ms per extra path component (depth sweep: 12 to 24 components took 34 to 58 ms and 28 to 44 ms). Extrapolated to the real profile depth of about 6-7 components (~/.local/share/tldw_cli/<user>/generated_videos), that is roughly 10-20 ms per row. The machine was at load average 28-50, so the unloaded cost is probably lower, but still well above 10 ms. cProfile shows the cost is not stat/resolve work, as the first pass assumed ('0.3-2 ms'). It is 2 acquire_storage admissions per row (80 participant.operation / 40 acquire_storage per 20 calls). Each admission runs admission_authority, startup_permission and _scope, re-walking the bootstrap registry and pinned directories. At 12 components that is about 458 open, 474 fstat, 454 close, 123 lstat, 66 stat and 20 listdir per row. At real depth it would still be about 1,000 syscalls per row.

(2) Catalog present (catalog.sqlite3 in recovered_media, which exists only after restoring a backup that captured TTL generated images or videos; prepare_temporary_capture skips profiles with no sources). Measured 196-310 ms per video row per sync, even for a row with no ref in the catalog. That cost is paid by every video row, including newly generated videos, because RecoveredMedia is constructed before refs are checked. Breakdown: RecoveredMedia(root) constructor 110-150 ms, resolve_reference 55-74 ms. The first verifier attributed the cost to the SHA-256. The measured dominant cost is actually 3 connect_private_sqlite calls per row: the constructor's migrate connection, recover(), and resolve_reference. Each launches a fresh `sys.executable -I -S private_sqlite_helper_entry.py` subprocess (HelperLease.start, private_sqlite_process.py:366) and blocks on kqueue for its reply. The profile shows 60 helper starts per 20 calls. A ready recovered video adds the full-payload read and SHA-256 on top, about 1.2 ms/MB (1 MB 219 ms, 10 MB 232 ms, 50 MB 282 ms), which reaches seconds for files near the 512 MB cap.

TRACE (exhaustive; the grep of _sync_native_console_transcript found 2 call sites, both awaited coroutines):
- chat_screen.py:18768 inside _sync_native_console_chat_ui. That coroutine is awaited directly by the set_interval(0.2, _poll_transcript) timer at chat_screen.py:18947, which runs while the run status is active, in-flight runs > 0, a wake delivery is pending or a review is pending. It is also scheduled via run_worker(coro) with no thread, on send, stop, switch and resume.
- chat_screen.py:23268, after the review-notes modal.
Nothing is offloaded or cached upstream. The only gates before line 18379 are teardown, maintenance-pause and the in-progress coalescing flag, and none of them skips a normal tick. _build_video_card_specs (video.py:184) has no memo and iterates the full projected transcript: it is not bounded the way _recent_console_image_messages is. The refresh_key gate comes after the specs are built. The other resolve_state callers (video.py:1283 and 1344) are one-shot actions.

VERDICT: keep at P1. In any conversation containing one generated video, each 5 Hz tick during streaming costs about 10-20 ms of loop time, which meets the rubric's per-tick threshold. It scales linearly with the number of video messages, so about 5 videos means per-tick stalls of 50-100 ms or more. The restored-catalog branch is P0-grade for the users it affects: about 200-300 ms per video row per tick, a saturated loop, and about 15 Python subprocess spawns per second per video. It stays out of P0 only because it needs a restored backup that included generated media.

Resolve states once, off the loop with asyncio.to_thread, keyed on the (message id, slug, ext) set, and invalidate the result on save or expiry. No open task covers this; TASK-21109 and TASK-3401.5 are unrelated.

At minimum, construct RecoveredMedia once (not per call) and never run migrate/recover on the read path.

A cheaper first step is to skip the whole push when the session's display_projection_revision and the streaming buffer length are unchanged, which helps settled ticks. title: Chunking Lab sample editor publishes an undebounced whole-sample session edit per keystroke (O(sample) joins on the loop, hash/model_dump/prune in a thread, full refresh with ~25 query_one)

That keeps drain_edits' snapshot guarantees for Run/Save/export. If a debounce is added, drain_edits must flush it, or Run could snapshot a stale sample. Comparing a stored last-loaded hash instead of editor.text is fine, but the prevent(TextArea.Changed) guard around load_text must stay.

title: Canvas compiler source locator is quadratic (prefix slice + count per element), about 50% of compile time
trigger: Every compile: canvas tool create/update, interactive import (import_html_async prepare), and every /api/plan frame load (resolve_render_plan).

fix_notes: Precompute newline offsets once and use bisect: line = bisect_right(nl, start) + 1, and column = start + 1 if idx == 0 else start - nl[idx-1]. This gives output identical to the current formula, so the diagnostics tests stay green. Keep the per-tag search offset logic unchanged. The low fix_risk is fair.

title: Render plans for immutable revisions are recompiled on every frame load; import then plan compiles the same source twice
trigger: Every canvas frame load: open, navigate or select, and each follow reload after a new revision. Open-in-Canvas always compiles twice.
cost: Compile measured at 8.3 ms (13 KB), 78 ms (210 KB) and 124 ms (444 KB). ADR-121 itself records 84-125 ms at the combined ceilings. The work is off-loop in the default executor but contends for the GIL, and it only runs while Canvas is in use, which fits P2.
fix: Revisions and plans are immutable. Keep a small OrderedDict LRU (about 8 entries) on NativeConsoleCanvasAuthority / CanvasCompilation keyed by (content_sha256, runtime_profile, snapshot.build_id), and seed it from the import path's prepared plan.
fix_notes: This design constraint is deliberate. ADR-121 ('Interactive compilation ownership') says 'No extra executor, source cache, database owner, or revision writer is introduced' and 'A completed prepared plan remains operation-local'. compilation.py's module docstring repeats 'without owning ... source caches'. A plan LRU therefore needs an ADR amendment first. ADR-124 requires cache identity to include compiler/security policy as well as exact source and profile manifest, so key on (content_sha256, runtime_profile, snapshot build/manifest id, compiler policy version), not just sha and profile. Plans are derived from source, so a bounded LRU retains source-derived data in memory. The fix_risk is medium, not low.
reason: NativeConsoleCanvasAuthority.resolve_render_plan (native_authority.py:731-762) recompiles the immutable revision source through compile_canvas_document on every /api/plan request (gateway._plan:1940/1962). import_html_async compiles via _prepare_import (line 489), and the browser's follow-up /api/plan compiles the same source again. The served parent (serve.py:202-222) does the same per plan. No plan cache exists anywhere in Canvas (grep: no lru_cache or plan_cache). CanvasCompilation is a 2-slot non-queueing admission (compilation.py:103-134), so overlapping loads can raise canvas_compilation_busy.

Static URLs already embed shell_incarnation_id (gateway.py:1582), so any cache reuse is per shell incarnation only. Verify in Chromium that a sandboxed/opaque-origin frame and a data:-URL worker actually hit the cache before investing. Otherwise the gain is Firefox/Safari only.
reason: Code verified. _security_headers_middleware (gateway.py:1615) sets Cache-Control: no-store on every response, including /static/. _static_asset (2372-2389) serves the runtime inventory (quickjs-runtime.js is 737,944 bytes; worker and renderer are 53-85 KB each). The served-mode public_runtime_asset sets no-store explicitly (gateway.py:2405). The renderer builds the worker from a data: URL bootstrap that dynamically imports canvas_runtime_worker*.js (canvas_renderer.js:1265-1268), which imports quickjs-runtime.js. So each frame load re-transfers about 0.9 MB. Downgraded to P3 for three reasons. (1) The TUI-loop cost is only aiohttp writing about 1 MB over loopback, roughly 1-3 ms per frame load. The heavy part, JS parse and WASM instantiate, happens in the browser, not on the scarce Textual loop. (2) Frame loads come from boot, navigation and follow reloads after agent revisions, not a per-key or per-tick path. (3) The proposed fix probably does nothing in Chromium. The renderer runs in an opaque-origin sandbox (CSP 'sandbox allow-scripts' at gateway.py:123, iframe sandbox='allow-scripts'), and the worker is a data: URL. Under Chrome's split HTTP cache, requests from opaque-origin frames get a transient network isolation key and are not cached whatever the headers say. Firefox and Safari, which partition by top-level site, would benefit. No open task covers it.

title: ConsoleCanvasController holds a threading.RLock across SQLite service calls that UI-loop paths also take
trigger: A worker-thread canvas update_canvas/create_canvas holds the lock during DB reads while the loop enters list_session_canvases/read_session_canvas (gateway handlers) or capture_selected_scope (the start of another session's agent reply).
cost: Estimated. The loop waits up to the worker's remaining lock-hold time: about 3 point or ancestor-path reads plus a sha256 of up to 512 KiB in validate(), so a few ms to tens of ms at large path lengths. It happens only under concurrency.
fix: Take the lock only to snapshot or mutate stage state, and do the _service_call I/O outside it, revalidating the generation after. Once F4 moves UI-side calls off the loop, the loop no longer waits on this lock.
fix_notes: Moving the _service_call I/O outside the lock is risky. The lock currently makes the stale-parent check and the sequence allocation atomic against concurrent updates to the same canvas and against run commit/discard, so revalidation after reacquiring needs careful generation fencing. The safer, smaller fix is to move the loop-side callers off the loop instead (asyncio.to_thread around capture_selected_scope in _run_agent_reply, and around the sync authority calls in the native gateway handlers). The loop then never contends on this lock.
evidence:
with self._lock:
    ...
    read = self._service_call("read_canvas", scope, canvas_id)       # DB under lock
    ...
    sequence=self._next_sequence(stage, canvas_id, parent),          # 2 more DB calls under lock
# list_session_canvases / read_session_canvas: with self._lock: self._service_call(...)
reason: Verified: ConsoleCanvasController._lock is a threading.RLock (console_canvas_controller.py:374). _update_canvas holds it across _service_call('read_canvas') at 1153 and _next_sequence, which does next_revision_sequence (1854) and list_canvases (1861), all under the same 'with self._lock' at 1109. read_canvas at 572-582 also does DB I/O under the lock, and update_canvas takes that path between the preflight and the final acquisition. _service_call (1711-1727) runs the durable service method synchronously. Loop-side waiters exist. console_chat_controller.py:28369 is inside async _run_agent_reply (not threaded), and it calls capture_selected_scope, which takes the controller lock and then, through native_authority._capture_selected_scope, calls _read_exact -> read_session_canvas (lock plus DB, 1011-1013). Native gateway handlers call the sync authority through _maybe_await on the loop (list_session_canvases 988/994, read_session_canvas 1011), for example /api/state and /api/plan after a follow event. Canvas tool calls run on the agent worker thread. So the loop can block on the RLock while another session's worker holds it across up to about 3 DB calls. This requires concurrency (a fleet or a parallel session's canvas tool, or browser access during a tool call), so P3 stands.

title: Browser shell polls /api/events every 350 ms per open canvas tab for as long as the tab stays open
trigger: While any Canvas browser tab is open: about 2.9 req/s per tab, forever. Background-tab timer throttling lowers the rate but does not stop it.
cost: Estimated at about 0.3-0.5 ms of aiohttp handling per poll, about 1-1.5 ms/s of loop time per open tab (about 0.1-0.15% core), plus loop wakeups. That is below the P0 idle-tax threshold of ~1% core, so P3.
fix: Long-poll: hold /api/events on an asyncio.Event per (session, canvas) that _publish sets, with about a 25 s timeout. The client loop stays the same apart from dropping the 350 ms delay.
fix_notes: Long-poll needs matching changes in the served-mode parent-to-child control protocol, cancellation on close, revoke and dispose, and re-running the selection_epoch and _session_is_current checks after the wait. A lower-risk first step: stop or slow polling while document.hidden, and back off exponentially (350 ms up to about 5 s) when polls return no events, resetting after user actions.
reason: Verified at canvas_shell.js:821: 'if (!closed) pollTimer = window.setTimeout(pollEvents, 350)'. It re-arms unconditionally in finally. grep finds no visibilitychange or document.hidden gating in canvas_shell.js. Each poll hits gateway._events (gateway.py:1993): _require_session plus authority.read_events plus json_response. read_events (native_authority.py:964) is a sync dict/tuple copy. The native gateway's aiohttp site is started on the Textual loop (chat_screen.py:21386 -> open_canvas_with_textual), so polls are handled on the UI loop. No open task covers canvas event polling.

title: NativeConsoleCanvasAuthority._events grows for the process lifetime and is fully copied on each poll
trigger: Every canvas publication appends an event that is never evicted. Every 350 ms browser poll copies the per-key list.
cost: Estimated at about 0.5-1 KB per event. Even hundreds of revisions stay in the hundreds of KB, and the per-poll tuple copy and scan costs microseconds. Hygiene only.
fix: Use collections.deque(maxlen=64) per key. The client already treats an unknown cursor as 'last event only' (read_events returns events[-1:]).
fix_notes: deque(maxlen=64) is compatible with the existing uses: setdefault(...).append, the prior_events[-1] check and pop() in gateway_scope, and tuple() in read_events. All three setdefault(..., []) sites must change to deque. When a cursor is evicted, read_events returns events[-1:], which the shell already handles as follow-latest. Optionally also drop keys for disposed or deleted conversations. Low risk.
reason: Verified: NativeConsoleCanvasAuthority._events (native_authority.py:203) is appended to at 395 (via _publish per revision), 642, 946 and 1255 (_publish). The only trimming is gateway_scope popping one trailing 'disconnected' event (703-707) and dispose() clearing everything (274). read_events (964-973) tuple-copies the whole per-key list and scans it linearly for the cursor on every poll. Growth is proportional to canvas publications (revisions, imports, selection changes), not to time, and each event is small, so this is not a meaningful long-session leak.

title: Turn-commit canvas batch validation walks the ancestor chain with one SELECT per message inside the write transaction
trigger: Once per assistant turn (or temporary-session promotion) that commits canvas revisions, inside the Console persistence write transaction.
cost: Measured with an in-memory SQLite micro-benchmark (PK lookups, 50k noise rows): 1.9 ms for a 1000-message path and 6.4 ms for 4096. That excludes the per-statement quiescence tax (TASK-31502), which adds to each of the N statements. It extends write-lock hold on a rare path, so P3.
fix: Use one recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE path(id, parent, conv, deleted, depth) ... LIMIT 4097) and validate in Python, as _require_durable_active_path already does with a single IN query.
fix_notes: A WITH RECURSIVE walk keyed on messages.id with a depth column and LIMIT 4097 must keep three checks: cycle detection (a recursive CTE with UNION ALL loops on a cycle until the LIMIT, so detect a repeated id or depth > cap in Python), the conversation_id match, and the deleted=0 check on every row. Ideally also rejecting at the first bad row, as the loop does. Capture a query plan per the repo's index-plan rule if any index assumptions change.
reason: Verified at repository.py:921-935. _validate_append_batch walks parent_message_id with one 'SELECT parent_message_id, conversation_id, deleted FROM messages WHERE id = ?' per ancestor, capped at MAX_CANVAS_DURABLE_ACTIVE_PATH_MESSAGES = 4096 (limits.py:26). It runs inside the write transaction through append_batch_in_transaction (832/856) <- console_transaction_contribution.py:178 <- console_canvas_controller.py:198 (turn contribution write). Only turns that staged canvas revisions reach it. The same module already validates a path with a single IN query (_require_durable_active_path, 1303-1348), and a recursive-CTE precedent exists (console_dispatch_repository.py:92).

title: Ingest registry listener does O(queue) work per notification and remounts the whole queue panel per job transition, making folder submit O(N^2) and every tick a full queue remount
trigger: Yes. Clicking Start on the Import canvas runs the synchronous per-file submit loop, which fires the listener N times on the UI thread with the Import canvas selected. Each later mark_parsing, mark_writing, mark_done and mark_failed arrives through call_from_thread and fires it again. Up to 500 persisted jobs are restored across restarts (app.py:2403), so the queue the listener walks and renders includes history.
cost:
All numbers are main-thread CPU (thread_time). Runs used the isolated env; scripts are in scratch/l2-slice50-ui4/ (f1_state.py, f1_panel2.py). The host was heavily loaded (load average 18-50 on 18 cores), so wall-clock figures are inflated. A calibration loop held at 6.1-6.3 ms before and after the runs, so the CPU figures are not.

(A) Per-notify listener work on the real LibraryIngestJobRegistry and real build_library_ingest_state. This is a lower bound: jobs() copy + analyze_skipped_ids + state build + counts/count_duplicate_done + the attention jobs() copy. Cost: 2.4 / 7.0 / 12.7 / 26.2 ms at 100 / 300 / 500 / 1,000 jobs.

(B) Synchronous folder-submit loop with that listener attached: 120 ms at 100 files, 1,075 ms at 300, and 12,948 ms at 1,000 files. 1,000 is the default library.ingest_directory_scan_limit (app.py:3061). The same loop without the listener takes 7.2 ms for 1,000 files. With 500 restored history jobs (the _MAX_PERSISTED_INGEST_JOBS cap, whose DONE rows stay visible): 1,634 ms at 100 files and 5,634 ms at 300. This is the path the Start button takes: @on(Button.Pressed, '#library-ingest-start') (library_screen.py:28715) -> _submit_library_ingest_form -> _do_submit_ingest -> _enqueue_library_ingest_snapshot -> app.submit_library_ingest_job, which loops over the expanded folder files (app.py:3233). The Import canvas is selected throughout, so every notify rebuilds the state. This contradicts TASK-32804.5 (In Progress), whose AC#1 'a 1,000-file folder import does not block the UI for more than a fraction of a second' is checked. Its fix covered only the app listener.

(C) Real LibraryIngestQueuePanel in a headless App at 211x44 with the real tldw_cli_modular.tcss. Per job transition, the listener does state build + panel.state + refresh(recompose=True). Figures are recompose / recompose+layout+render / longest loop block (1 ms ticker):

- 100 DONE rows (426 nodes): 468 / 733 / 338 ms
- 300 DONE rows (1,226 nodes): 1,679 / 2,153 / 2,004 ms
- 500 DONE rows (2,026 nodes): 2,984 / 3,799 / 3,451 ms
Without app CSS: 17/48, 136/327, 655/1,075 and 1,210/1,922 ms.

The cost grows superlinearly with row count. DONE rows carry an actions Horizontal plus buttons and never group, because _GROUPABLE_ROW_STATES is FAILED/SKIPPED/CANCELLED only. update_progress uses a separate progress-listener channel, so only mark_* transitions recompose. Transitions that land in the same loop turn coalesce into one recompose, but each still pays the O(N) state build.

Conclusion: a common gesture (a folder import with the Import canvas open) freezes the loop for hundreds of ms per transition and for seconds on submit. P0 stands.

(2) Use the non-copying registry.iter_jobs_for_listeners() (added by TASK-32804.5) in _build_library_ingest_state and _library_landing_attention_action, and skip the attention computation unless the landing is visible and not suspended. Keep the per-notification batch-settle baseline and active-count crossing logic synchronous: it depends on seeing each crossing, and the counts are O(N) but cheap. Note that refresh(recompose=True) already coalesces within a loop turn; the quadratic cost is the state build and the copies. (2) iter_jobs_for_listeners yields live registry objects. It is safe for the attention computation, but build_library_ingest_state must not keep live job references in LibraryIngestCanvasState, or the old_state/new_state structural comparison can alias. Materialise the rows from it rather than storing jobs. (3) Keyed row diffing has to respect the task-32231 group collapse, the in-place progress patching by #library-ingest-progress-{job_id}, and focus restore (TASK-31583). Bounding the rendered history ('Show N older') is the lower-risk first step.

Whole-screen arm (screen_recomposes=1; the rail widget identity was lost on every such switch), CPU / longest block:

- conversations -> media: 1,777 / 1,819 ms
- media -> prompts: 1,661 / 1,587 ms

Mixed display booleans must become class toggles. Extending residency route by route (Conversations, Prompts, Skills, Collections shells) is safer than a generic 'rebuild only #library-shell-grid', because the header, rail and footer registration still have to be re-applied, as swap_library_browse_route does. title: refresh() override rebuilds the full footer shortcut model on every plain screen refresh and on focus changes, including uncached focus_chain walks and full-DOM row queries
trigger: Partly. The triggers are resize frames (rare for a full-screen user), screen switches (once per visit) and focus changes inside the media viewer. It is not every focus change app-wide.
cost: Estimated only; nothing was measured. focus_chain is O(widgets) and uncached in Textual 8.2.8, which puts it on the order of 0.2-0.7 ms at 100-400 widgets. The whole footer build is plausibly around 1 ms.

Elsewhere, memoize the computed shortcut tuple on a cheap signature (selected row, relevant view flags, focused widget id, width bucket, lifecycle, compose generation) and skip the rebuild when it is unchanged. Cache _library_slash_would_land per (focused, compose_generation) instead of rebuilding focus_chain. Read media neighbours from browse-controller state instead of querying `.library-media-row`.

Resize-driven compact transitions also change hide_ancillary. Memoising on a signature is the only safe variant, and the signature must include compact state, focused widget, select/sort flags and emergency stage. Caching _library_slash_would_land per (focused, compose generation) is reasonable.

trigger: Yes, but low frequency. It runs once per presentation-changing snapshot: a visit resume, a completed ingest job, or a note save.

title: _run_library_service_call(isolate_in_worker=True) creates and tears down a fresh asyncio event loop per call
trigger: Yes, but off the UI loop. The calls happen a few times per visit and per item open.
cost: Measured in a worker thread: asyncio.run() median 0.22 ms, p95 0.47 ms, against 0.045 ms for a reused asyncio.Runner. This is about 1 ms of worker latency per visit and adds nothing to the event loop.
fix: Call a sync twin of these scope methods directly in the worker. Alternatively, drive the coroutine with a cached per-thread asyncio.Runner instead of asyncio.run per call.
fix_notes: A per-thread cached Runner on to_thread's default executor threads keeps one event loop alive per pool thread across calls. Any service coroutine that creates loop-bound primitives (asyncio.Lock, clients cached on the loop) would then leak state between calls. It would also bypass run_finite_local_worker's per-call finiteness contract unless the Runner is created inside it. Calling a sync twin of the scope methods directly is cleaner, but it duplicates the policy-enforcement path (_enforce_policy) the async methods run. Low value; hygiene only.
reason: _run_library_service_call (library_screen.py:12995-13024) is confirmed: with isolate_in_worker=True it runs invoke_service_in_worker through asyncio.to_thread, and that calls asyncio.run() once per call whenever the service returns an awaitable. The code marks this with a deliberate 'policy-exception: worker-thread loop' comment. There are 26 isolate_in_worker=True sites in library_screen.py and 49 in Library_Modules. The per-call sqlite connection close is the separate, already-known TASK-24457 (8 fresh connections per visit).

title: Roleplay library remounts every row on each debounced search keystroke, page, sort and refresh; Dictionaries/Lore are unpaged
trigger: Per Roleplay visit (initial load), per mode switch, per debounced search pause, per page/sort/tag change, and after character mutations. All run on the event loop through awaited mounts.
cost:
Benchmark: scratch/second-lens-s51-5/bench_f1.py. It mounts the REAL PersonasLibraryPane in a minimal Textual 8.2.8 app at 211x44, with about 150 filler Statics standing in for the rest of the screen. It loads the app's real CSS trio: the screen-scoped sheet, the 20,382-line tldw_cli_modular.tcss, and the screen-self sheet, the same CSS_PATH order as app.py:7538. I measured CPU (process_time) for `await pane.update_rows(...)` plus a pilot.pause, then subtracted a baseline pause with no work. Character rows carry meta, so each row is ListItem+Vertical+2 Static (4 widgets).

Results with the real stylesheet (medians):
- 10 rows: update_rows 39 ms, update+paint net ~64 ms.
- 50 rows (PERSONAS_LIBRARY_PAGE_SIZE): update_rows 100 ms (90-158), update+paint net ~180 ms (raw 141-214).
- 200 rows (unpaged Dictionaries/Lore scale): net ~906 ms. That is superlinear, not 4x the 50-row cost.

Without any stylesheet, 50 rows costs ~93 ms net. The first verifier's 50-100 ms figure therefore undercounts by about 2x, because the real bundle roughly doubles the cost.

Re-rendering an IDENTICAL rows tuple costs the same (~226 ms at 50 rows), so a tuple-equality short-circuit would save all of it. update_rows (personas_library_pane.py:419 `await list_view.clear()`, :482 `await list_view.extend(items)`) has no short-circuit.

Trigger re-verified:
- Per visit: on_mount -> _load_after_mount -> refresh_character_list -> refresh_character_library_list -> _render_library_rows -> _reload_character_page. The DB reads run through asyncio.to_thread, then _display_character_page:3690 calls update_rows on the loop.
- Per debounced search pause: PERSONAS_SEARCH_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS=0.2 set_timer at :4072, then an exclusive async worker (not a thread) -> _render_search_query.
- Per page, sort, tag or mode change: _on_page_changed_delta, _cycle_sort, _apply_tag_filter -> _reload_active_library / _reload_character_page.
- Dictionaries (:4327) and Lore (:4409) pass all filtered rows with no page_size.

With a full 50-row page this is at or above 100 ms per visit or search pause, which borders on P0. With typical libraries under 50 characters it is 60-100 ms, and it runs only once per typing pause, so P1 stands.
fix: Stop remounting. Keep PERSONAS_LIBRARY_PAGE_SIZE row widgets and update their Static text, classes and ids in place, or diff by dom_id (remove only the missing rows, mount only the new ones). Short-circuit when the new rows tuple equals the last one rendered. Page the Dictionaries/Lore modes like Characters, and filter the cached _dictionaries_cache/_lore_books_cache in memory for search.
fix_notes: Textual forbids changing a widget's id once set (dom.py raises "Node 'id' attribute may not be changed once set"). The suggested 'update ids in place' is therefore impossible. Use fixed slot ids (row-0..row-49) with _row_lookup keyed by slot, or diff by dom_id (remove missing, mount new, move_child to reorder). Preserve _marked_ids pruning, mark_active_row, the ListView index/highlight, and the recovery/empty-row branches. The cheapest first step is a short-circuit when the rows tuple and pagebar args equal the last render. Filtering _dictionaries_cache/_lore_books_cache in memory on search is safe, since only mutations need a re-fetch.

title: vLLM setup calls get_api_key, and therefore a ~13 ms load_settings() admission handshake, on every keystroke and 4 Hz during probes
trigger: Every accepted keystroke in any vLLM setup text field, and every 0.25 s during a vLLM launch probe.
cost:
Benchmark: scratch/second-lens-s51-5/bench_f2b.py, run in an isolated profile. I asserted that HOME and TLDW_CONFIG_PATH resolve under scratch, and confirmed profile_paths derives from $HOME.

The chain is confirmed:
- vllm_setup_view.py:1589 @on(Input.Changed) -> _change_draft/_change_numeric_lexeme -> DraftChanged.
- llm_screen.py:3310 -> _apply_vllm_view_state -> exactly ONE get_api_key('vllm') at :2837. That is the only config read in llm_screen.py and vllm_setup_view.py; refresh_lab_status/read_server_rows only call Popen.poll().
- config.py:1862 @_config_participants.guarded wraps load_settings, so even a warm _cache_hit enters operation(): 2 lock acquires plus raw._scope.

Measured warm on a heavily loaded host (loadavg 24-48): load_settings ~25-41 ms and get_api_key('vllm') ~25-38 ms median. The finder saw 13 ms on a lighter host. get_cli_setting takes 0.0015 ms.

An audit-hook open counter shows why the cost depends on the profile: 608 opens per get_api_key at HOME depth 10 and 998 at depth 20. That is ~39 opens per path component plus ~218 fixed, because _open_verified_parent walks every directory component.

The real profile is shallower. $HOME=/Users/<u> puts the config at depth 4 and the data at depth 6. The scratch paths were at depth 11 and 14, so a real profile does about 300 opens, half the benchmarked count. Scaling the finder's unloaded 13 ms gives about 6-7 ms per keystroke on macOS, and less on Linux. That is under the 16 ms frame budget and under the P1 per-keystroke bar of 10-20 ms.

The surface is the Lab > Models > vLLM setup form, a rare setup flow. The probe loop at :4044 (0.25 s sleep, 30 s window) costs about 2.5% of a core, and only while a vLLM launch is being probed.

The local instance is P2. The root cause is still real and belongs with TASK-32804.1: a warm load_settings hit pays full admission across about 103 call sites. The fix is to serve _cache_hit before the guard and keep @guarded on _load_settings_uncached. It should be sized from the hottest of those call sites, not from this form.
fix: In this slice: compute credential_configured once, after profiles load or on a config-changed event, and cache it on the screen. Alternatively, derive it from app_instance.app_config['api_settings']['vllm'] plus the env var through resolve_provider_api_key, so apply_state stays cheap. Root fix (config.py): serve load_settings' _cache_hit before entering @_config_participants.guarded, the same way TASK-32804.1's _warm_config_cache_hit does for load_cli_config_and_ensure_existence, so only _load_settings_uncached pays admission. TASK-32804.1 left load_settings guarded on the hit path, so this is new scope.
fix_notes: The root fix mirrors 32804.1. Do not rebind load_settings, because guarded's wrapper checks `getattr(source, name) is wrapped` and 'load_settings' is in its allowed set. Instead, drop @guarded from load_settings, serve _cache_hit() first, and keep the guard on _load_settings_uncached (already in the allowed set), or add a guarded inner. Also check the TASK-32804.1 pin test and the storage-admission tests. The local fix (caching credential_configured on the screen) risks stale readiness after a key is saved in Settings or an env change, so invalidate it on config-publish or on screen resume.

def _on_vllm_draft_changed(self, event): ... self._apply_vllm_view_state(focus=False)

    credential_configured=bool(get_api_key("vllm")),

In vllm_setup_view.py (tldw_chatbook/UI/LLM_Management/, not UI/Screens), @on(Input.Changed) at :1589 maps every vLLM field to _change_draft (:1472) or _change_numeric_lexeme (:1484). Both post DraftChanged (:1482/:1499). LLMScreen._on_vllm_draft_changed (llm_screen.py:3310) then runs _apply_vllm_view_state, which calls `credential_configured=bool(get_api_key("vllm"))` at :2837. get_api_key (config.py:9319) calls load_settings() at :9345. load_settings is decorated with @_config_participants.guarded (config.py:1862), and its `_cache_hit()` check is INSIDE the guarded body. guarded's wrapper (config_participants.py:400-420) always enters operation(). title: Meetings transcript repaints the whole RichLog on every relabelled segment: O(n^2) per meeting, with bursts at Stop
trigger: Only with live_diarization enabled. One full repaint per diarizer-assigned segment while recording, a burst of k repaints at Stop (the batch diarize relabel), and one per rename.
cost: Re-measured RichLog(wrap=True) clear plus rewrite at 211x44 with ~110-char lines: 100 lines 6-13 ms, 360 lines 22-33 ms, 720 lines 47-64 ms. During recording that is one 20-60 ms hitch per segment late in a long meeting. A Stop pass relabelling hundreds of segments serializes roughly k x 30-60 ms of loop work, i.e. seconds of sluggish UI.
fix: Coalesce repaints. In _render_segment, set a dirty flag and schedule one _repaint_log through call_after_refresh or set_timer(0.1) if none is pending, so each frame gets at most one repaint. Have the Stop pass emit a single batch ('segments') event instead of one per segment. Longer term, render lines as per-line Statics in a VerticalScroll (update only the changed one) or cap RichLog history.
fix_notes: Coalescing is the low-risk fix: set a dirty flag and schedule one _repaint_log via call_after_refresh or set_timer if none is pending. rendered_lines stays authoritative, so the _rendered_transcript_text test hook is unaffected. A batch 'segments' event changes the session emit and sink contract (the sinks persist per seq), so it is a medium-risk change; keep it separate.
reason: Code verified. meetings_screen.py:836-843: when a re-delivered segment's line changes, _render_segment calls _repaint_log, which does `log.clear()` and then rewrites every line of rendered_lines (:846-850). meeting_session.py:889 emits each segment, and :924 re-emits it after _diarizer.assign sets speaker_id; the label changes from coarse to 'Speaker N', so each assigned segment costs a full repaint. The Stop pass re-emits every relabelled segment one at a time (:791-793). Each emit goes through _on_session_event, then a blocking app.call_from_thread(_apply_event), then a full repaint, so the cost is O(k*n). _rerender_transcript (:996) repaints for renames and self-match. BUT the whole path needs self._diarizer, which exists only when `[meetings] live_diarization` is on, and that defaults to false (config.py:5540; meeting_owner.py:174/560). The claim that _attach_if_running replays segments into repaints is overstated: replayed lines that are unchanged hit neither branch, and new ones append. Downgraded from P1: this is an opt-in feature, and the cost only scales with long meetings.

title: Lore list counts entries with an N+1 query that loads every entry's content, repeated per search keystroke and per entry edit
trigger: Lore mode entry, each debounced lore search pause, and every lore book/entry mutation (11 _render_lore_rows call sites).
cost: Estimated, off the event loop. It costs 1+B transactions (each taxed by the TASK-31502 quiescence registry) plus a full decode of every entry of every book. That is negligible for typical data (a few books) and tens of ms of worker time with GIL contention for about 50 books x 100 entries. This is a data-scaling N+1 on a less-frequent path, so P2.
fix: Get the counts in one statement: a LEFT JOIN or GROUP BY in list_world_books (SELECT world_book_id, COUNT(*) FROM world_book_entries WHERE deleted=0 GROUP BY world_book_id), or a count_world_book_entries() helper. For search, filter the cached _lore_books_cache/_dictionaries_cache in memory; only mutations need a re-fetch.
fix_notes: The proposed SQL is wrong: world_book_entries has NO `deleted` column (schema in ChaChaNotes_DB.py:1824 and recovery_core_schema.py:348). Use `SELECT world_book_id, COUNT(*) FROM world_book_entries GROUP BY world_book_id` (idx_world_book_entries_book exists), or a LEFT JOIN count in list_world_books. Per CLAUDE.md, capture a query plan without sqlite_stat1 if the query shape changes. The in-memory search filter over _lore_books_cache is safe.
reason: personas_screen.py:4354-4359: _list_world_books_with_counts calls manager.list_world_books(True), then runs `len(manager.get_world_book_entries(book['id']))` per book. world_book_manager.py:538-586: each call is its own db.transaction() with SELECT keys, content, ... and 3 json.loads per entry, only for len(). It runs off-loop via asyncio.to_thread (:4381). It is called from _render_lore_rows, which always re-fetches, including on a debounced search (:4209). _lore_books_cache is written but not used for filtering. It also runs after lore entry reload (:6607) and 11 call sites in total. No open task covers it.

title: One character selection reads the same SELECT * character_cards row (with image BLOB) 5 times over serial thread hops
trigger: Every local character selection in Roleplay (click/Enter, first-paint auto-select, restore, CharacterCardChanged reload).
cost: Estimated. Each read copies the portrait BLOB (a 1-2 MB memcpy is about 0.1-0.2 ms) and deserializes the JSON fields, which is larger when a card embeds a lorebook. That is about 1-3 ms per read, so roughly 5-15 ms of redundant worker time per selection, plus 3 serial thread hops of added latency. It does not freeze the UI.

title: Model install progress sends one UI event per 1 MiB chunk with no throttle, flooding the loop during pre-verify hashing
trigger: Every curated or remote model install. The pre-verify phase posts one message per MiB at hashing speed. The fetch phase posts at download speed, which is benign.
cost: Estimated. About 10 query_one plus 4 Static.update and 2 ProgressBar.update per event, roughly 0.3-1 ms. Hashing a page-cached file runs at about 0.5-2 GB/s, so 500-2000 events/s: loop saturation for the duration of pre-verify of a multi-GB model, plus backlog drain. Per-install, less-frequent path, so P2.
fix: Throttle in deliver(): forward only on a phase or file change, on the final byte, or when at least 100 ms have passed since the last forwarded event, and keep the latest progress in _model_install_last_progress for hydration. Use post_message or call_soon_threadsafe rather than blocking call_from_thread for progress.

Always forward the terminal event of each phase, and keep _model_install_last_progress updated for hydration. For audio_cpp, keep the cancel-event and is_attached check. Swapping call_from_thread for a non-blocking post is fine because post_message is already thread-safe, but preserve the deliver_current ownership check. Also note that the worker loop's to_thread completion is queued behind every pending progress callback.

title: Roleplay screen is not a reusable route: every visit re-composes it and re-runs the full initial load and auto-select
trigger: Every navigation to the personas and ccp routes: fresh construct, compose, mount, _load_after_mount, restore or auto-select, and an async on_unmount drain on leave. Reached through handle_screen_navigation on the App pump.
cost:
Exhaustive trace on 840ed2ca58.

Routes:
- ScreenRoute.reusable defaults to False (screen_registry.py:35).
- Only home (:82), chat (:99) and library (:114) set it; grep finds exactly 3 `reusable=True`.
- Both entry routes are non-reusable: 'personas' (:116-121) and 'ccp' (:161-163, which also maps to PersonasScreen).

Navigation (app.py:13471-13500):

- personas_screen.py has 0 on_screen_resume/on_screen_suspend references.

Per-visit work on the loop:
- on_mount:1926 arms set_interval(0.25) and launches _load_after_mount as an async worker, not a thread.

- Then _reload_character_page (count and page via to_thread) and update_rows. I measured that step in F1 at ~64 ms (10 rows) to ~180 ms (50 rows) of loop CPU with the real stylesheet.
- Then the deep-link/restore/_auto_select fan-out.

Precedent: TASK-24452 recorded -80% (Chat) and -95% (Library) switch CPU from reuse. It also found Home gained nothing because Home was cheap and outgoing teardown dominates. Personas is the opposite case: expensive to build AND to tear down.

No open task enables Personas reuse; I grepped backlog/tasks for personas combined with reusable/on_screen_resume/instance reuse. Deep links are the main fix hazard: _pending_character_conversation_link is consumed only in _load_after_mount (:2070) or the :2226 refresh path. P1 kept; it stays below P0 because reuse only helps warm re-visits.

Snapshot-restore is skipped on a reuse hit, so the _restored_from_saved_state/_pending_restore path goes dormant; confirm that nothing else relies on it. The 0.25 s poll early-returns when not is_active but still wakes at 4 Hz; stop it in suspend and re-arm it on resume. Cancel the search debounce in suspend.
