(1) _attach_stream_usage -> store.record_trajectory_timing(flush=True) -> write_trajectory_rows -> db.upsert_trajectory_rows, which is a transaction(immediate=True). (2) store.mark_message_complete (27275) -> _persist_existing_terminal/_persist_existing_message -> persistence.update_message_content (chat_persistence_service.py:2873, transaction(immediate=True)). That is at least 2 depth-0 transactions per send on the loop, plus feedback, trace and usage writes. Extra evidence: the second _scope pass (the one with file I/O) runs inside `with _lock:` on the process-wide RLock, so off-loop DB work (F5 discovery, pooled workers) contends with on-loop transactions. Not covered by an open task. TASK-31502 measures the quiescence locks at about 23 us per transaction. TASK-32804.1 fixed the same handshake only for config reads, by serving warm hits ahead of the guard, not by amortizing admission. The scratch path has about 11 components against about 6 in production, so production is probably about 4-5 ms per transaction, about 8-15 ms per send. That is still P1 per-send.

title: Scope service retires its worker SQLite connection after every call; each new connection spawns a Python helper subprocess (~65 ms), so every Library conversations page, Console resume and Home snapshot pays it again
trigger: Library conversations tab (every page, search submit and visit), Console resume of a saved conversation, the Home content snapshot and the STTS conversation list. Each lands on an asyncio.to_thread worker whose connection the previous call closed.
cost:
Script: scratch/lens2-s7c1/f2_scope.py, run in an isolated profile under loadavg about 50. The setup is a real ChatConversationScopeService over a real ChatConversationService and ChaChaNotes DB, with 3,000 conversations of 4 messages each. The call shapes match production: the Library page is list_conversations(mode=local, scope_type=all, limit=20, offset), and Console resume is get_conversation_tree. I ran 15 calls per cell, with the close-per-call and kept-connection cells interleaved twice. An audit hook counted Popen calls.

Results (median):
- Library page: 247-280 ms with close-per-call vs 35-36 ms with the connection kept. 1.0 Popen per call and 53-56 ms of helper child CPU per call.
- Console resume tree: 120-126 ms vs 1.0-2.2 ms. 0.93 Popen per call and 46-47 ms child CPU.
- Library search: 470-481 ms vs 268-349 ms. The FTS query itself is heavy, but it still pays 1 spawn per call.

For comparison, the quieter-machine figures were 56.5 vs 6.9 ms (finder) and 85.6 vs 8.2 ms (verifier). The earlier depth sweep in scratch/second-lens-patdb shows the helper child's CPU stays at 45-51 ms regardless of path depth, so a production path does not remove the roughly 50-60 ms per call. Loop lag showed no consistent difference, so the cost is off-loop: latency, CPU and one Python child process per call.

Caller trace: I listed every consumer of `chat_conversation_scope_service` with an untruncated grep. The list_conversations and get_conversation_tree callers that go through the close-per-call path are:
- library_conversations_controller.py:1213, every page, search and visit
- library_screen.py:13263 _list_local_source_snapshot (Library visit, called from :11421)
- home_screen.py:482, the Home snapshot
- STTS_Window.py:726/735
- Console workspace rail: workspace.py:2094 _fetch_workspace_rows (tree pages), plus :3462 and :7125
- the scope service's own get_library_user_content_evidence, about line 269
- console_conversation_hydration.py:339/349 get_conversation_tree, i.e. Console resume

None of these callers caches the connection or sends the call to a long-lived thread, so every call reconnects. The locate_conversation_page and reader paths use other methods and are not affected.

This stays P1 because it is a per-visit, per-page and per-resume latency of about 50-80 ms. It overlaps TASK-24457, but it adds a new site and shows that the helper spawn is what dominates connection cost. The verifier's constraints on the fix still apply: TASK-31993.5 AC#3 forbids a new thread framework, and caching the prepare verdict is a security decision.
fix: Keep the TASK-31993.5 retirement guarantee without paying it per call. Route local conversation reads through one dedicated single-thread executor per CharactersRAGDB that owns a long-lived connection, and close it only from the recovery pause/retire hook (participant.retiring_threads / storage pause). Alternatively, cache the helper's prepare verdict per (st_dev, st_ino, mode) for the process lifetime and re-run it only on an identity change, so reopening a thread-local connection no longer spawns a subprocess.
fix_notes: The close-per-call is intentional (TASK-31993.5 AC#1). Recovery drain cannot close another thread's cached handle, because _core_closing refuses a foreign-thread close. TASK-31993.5 AC#3 also says 'no new general thread framework', so a dedicated per-DB executor contradicts a recorded constraint and needs an explicit decision. It must also let the pause hook submit the close onto that executor's own thread. Caching the helper's prepare verdict per (st_dev, st_ino, mode) weakens what the out-of-process helper exists to do: verify and prepare private file modes and identity at open time, a TOCTOU/symlink boundary. Treat it as a security review, not a perf tweak. Fixing it in the helper would also speed up every other connection-churn site (Subscriptions/db_offload.py has the same close-per-call pattern, and TASK-24457's 8 per-visit connections).
reason: chat_conversation_scope_service.py:189 (list_and_close) and :399 (read_local_tree) call db.close_connection() after every to_thread call. The next call on a pooled worker therefore opens a new thread-local connection through ChaChaNotes _get_thread_connection -> connect_private_sqlite (private_sqlite.py:1878). On non-Windows that path calls prepare_in_helper -> HelperLease.start, which runs subprocess.Popen([sys.executable,'-I','-S',helper]) at private_sqlite_process.py:366. Re-measured in isolation, counting Popen calls: list_conversations on a pooled thread costs 85.6 ms median (71.0 min) with 1.0 Popen per call when closing after each call, against 8.2 ms (6.4 min) and 0.08 Popen per call when the connection is kept. A fresh-thread get_connection alone costs 67.8 ms. Callers verified: library_conversations_controller._load_library_conversation_page (line 1204) uses app.chat_conversation_scope_service.list_conversations for each page and search. console_conversation_hydration (line 340) uses get_conversation_tree for Console resume. home_screen:501 and STTS_Window:735 call list_conversations. The work is off-loop but adds about 60-80 ms of user-visible latency, plus a Python child process, on every Library conversations page and every Console resume. TASK-24457 (Library opens 8 fresh connections per visit) is related, but it attributes the cost to PRAGMAs and screen re-instantiation. This finding adds a new site (the scope service's deliberate close-per-call) and new evidence: the helper subprocess spawn dominates connection cost, which applies to every connection-churn finding.

title: Citation pydantic cluster (~15.5k lines, off by default) costs 45-60 ms at boot and first paint; consumers only need an enum, an exception and a constant
trigger: Every boot (app.py module-scope import) and the Console first paint (chat_screen, console_chat_store and console_chat_controller import the cluster at module scope).
cost:
Script: scratch/lens2-s7c1/f3_imp.py, run in isolation. It first imports every dependency outside the citation cluster (pydantic, config, ChaChaNotes_DB, chat_conversation_service and so on), then times the import of the entry modules. That pulls in exactly 11 citation modules and no other modules. It then replays the app's boot wiring: build_local_citation_conversation_service plus the ownership coordinator. I ran 6 interleaved A/B rounds. In the B arm, pydantic's global default is patched to defer_build=True after the dependencies load, so only the citation models are affected.

Results (loadavg about 45):
- Baseline import: 42-73 ms (median about 51).
- With defer_build: 26-64 ms (median about 29).
- Deferred schema work paid later at wiring: only about +1 ms (1.0-1.3 ms vs 0.2-0.3 ms).
Net saving: about 20-22 ms once per boot under load, probably about 12-15 ms on a quiet machine.

The rest of the cost cannot be removed by the fix as proposed, because its premise is false. The consumers do not "only need an enum, an exception and a constant":
1. TldwCli.__init__ (app.py:7738) calls _wire_chat_conversation_services() at app.py:8223, pre-paint. That calls build_local_citation_conversation_service (app.py:9700), which constructs a CitationTraceRepository at boot. title: write_trajectory_rows retries with time.sleep backoff (5 attempts, each able to wait the 15 s busy timeout); some callers are on the event loop

title: ConsoleActivityReceiptService holds its RLock across DB I/O that loop-side readers wait on; publish_ordinary re-reads all unseen receipts on the loop

trigger: publish_ordinary runs synchronously on the event loop for each inactive/hidden-session COMPLETED/FAILED/STOPPED transition, via _set_run_state called from async controller methods. The drain thread holds the RLock across DB writes while the switcher's 5 Hz poll and the workspace/buddy renders read it on the loop.
cost: The finder's figure is about 9 ms per background completion on the loop (not re-measured here), growing with the unseen count because of the full paged reload. Worst case is bounded by busy_timeout=5000 ms under AgentRuns write contention. Lock contention with hydration is a rare, roughly 16 ms, one-shot window.

fix_notes: Lock-free readers are safe only if generation, snapshot and state are published as ONE immutable tuple in a single attribute assignment. Separate atomic fields let a reader pair a new generation with an old snapshot. Writers must still serialize the marks reconcile. Replacing the post-publish reload with an append is risky. publish can supersede an earlier revision of the same logical_outcome_id (superseded_at/transition_revision), and the reload also picks up acknowledgements made by other connections. An append would have to remove superseded rows and keep the created_at DESC order, so keep the reload and just move it off-loop. publish_ordinary's return value is ignored by _publish_inactive_outcome, so fire-and-forget via to_thread works. Ordering against acknowledge and publish_fleet_drain is still kept by the RLock, but a background publish must not run after runtime dispose (check the authority token as ensure_activity_hydration does).

The Console fork path is on the loop. _fork_lineage_entry (console_chat_store.py:7323) calls get_console_fork_source_message once per prefix message, in both issue_fork_fence (called synchronously from request_console_chat_fork, session.py:2199) and validate_fork_fence (async _run_console_chat_fork, session.py:2451). That is 2N point reads on the loop, each copying the row's image BLOB. One correction: update_message_content on stream finalize targets assistant rows, which normally have NULL image_data, so the per-send cost is roughly zero. The BLOB cost applies to edits of image-bearing messages and to forks. P3 is right: these are rare, user-initiated actions whose cost scales with image bytes.

title: Chat/__init__.py eagerly imports six service modules (Library, Backup_Recovery, runtime_policy bootstrap to config)
trigger: Any non-TUI process importing any tldw_chatbook.Chat.* submodule, such as the MCP stdio server on its first chat tool, scripts or test workers. The TUI boot already imports the same modules, so the marginal cost there is zero.
cost: Measured: 541-734 ms warm for the Chat package __init__ closure (config 249-363 ms of that). The real marginal saving is smaller for importers of Chat_Functions, which need config anyway.
fix: Turn the package __init__ into a PEP 562 lazy __getattr__ facade, following the Local_Ingestion template.
fix_notes: A PEP 562 __getattr__ facade (the Local_Ingestion/TTS template) keeps `from tldw_chatbook.Chat import X` and mock.patch('tldw_chatbook.Chat.X') working, since patch uses getattr/setattr. Backup_Recovery/chat_source_participants._classes() looks up classes via sys.modules.get and still works, because any live instance implies its module is imported. Add a subprocess import-closure guard, as TASK-22503's AC does, so it cannot creep back. The payoff is modest because config is on almost every non-trivial path anyway.

from .chat_conversation_scope_service import ChatConversationScopeService   # -> Library -> Library_Collections_DB
from .chat_conversation_service import ChatConversationService              # -> Backup_Recovery.chat_source_participants
from .server_chat_conversation_service import ServerChatConversationService  # -> runtime_policy.bootstrap -> config

The TUI pays nothing extra: app.py:123-146 already imports these services at module scope. The non-app consumers are the MCP server, which imports Chat lazily inside its tool handlers (MCP/server.py:428, 606, so the stdio process pays on its first chat tool call), helper scripts and every test worker. title: Attachment pipeline is async def around purely synchronous PIL and file work; callers spin a fresh event loop per attachment
trigger: Each Console file attach, drag-drop path and clipboard image paste (user action; up to 5 per message) creates one event loop, and for PDF/doc/ebook files one executor thread.
cost: About 0.3-2 ms of loop, and possibly executor, setup and teardown per attachment. Negligible next to the PIL or parse work itself. Estimated.
fix: Make load_processed_file, process_attachment_path and process_attachment_bytes (and prepare_image_payload) plain sync functions, and call them with asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) directly.
fix_notes: Making the pipeline 'plain sync' is bigger than stated. It cascades into FileHandlerRegistry.process_file and all 10 or so FileHandler.process() implementations, _extract_local_ingest_text's internal to_thread, ChatImageHandler.process_image_file and prepare_image_payload, and the legacy _process_image_data adapter, whose async signature its docstring says is pinned by tests. Given the tiny payoff, the lazy option is to leave it, or add a one-line sync wrapper used by both chat_screen sites. Converting to sync only pays off if an on-loop caller ever appears.

)
# process_attachment_bytes: PILImage.open(...).verify() and ChatImageHandler.prepare_image_payload (sync PIL resize/save) behind 'async def'

I grepped every caller untruncated. The ONLY production callers of process_attachment_path, process_attachment_bytes, load_processed_file and file_handler_registry.process_file are those two chat_screen sites, both already off-loop. prepare_image_payload's other callers are inside chat_image_events and are reached only through the same path. So no loop-blocking exists today; the risk is latent. One more detail the finder missed: the PDF/document/ebook handlers await asyncio.to_thread internally (Utils/file_handlers.py:65). title: Terminal re-projects every cell of every session on the UI thread per frame and at least twice per keystroke
trigger: Every keystroke runs this on the UI loop. chat_screen.py:2403-2409 on_console_terminal_input_requested -> ConsoleTerminalController.send_key -> _selected_session_id -> view_state, which snapshots all sessions. The echo comes back on the runtime thread: process_output (session_manager.py:598) -> _notify_subscribers -> _manager_changed (terminal.py:441) -> call_from_thread -> _queue_refresh -> screen.call_after_refresh(_refresh) -> view_state again. That is at least 2 all-session snapshots per keystroke. While output streams it is one per frame, coalesced by _frame_pending. This happens only while the Terminal workspace is open: the subscription is added in open_workspace and removed in detach_workspace (chat_screen.py:2327/2388/17114).
cost: Measured on pin 840ed2ca58 in an isolated env with the real TerminalScreenModel (sl70-hotmisc-lens2/bench_term.py). Load average was 20-50, so these are min-of-40 values. snapshot() for a prompt screen (a few lines, mostly blank) costs 3.3 ms at 80x24, 10.7-11.3 ms at 160x40, 14.5-15.8 ms at 200x45 and 19.1-20.7 ms at 235x50. A full colored ls screen costs 4.5, 13.5-14.0, 18.1-19.3 and 23.2-25.6 ms at the same sizes. cProfile of 20 snapshots at 200x45 shows 180,200 _safe_style calls (one per cell) and 360,400 regex fullmatch calls; _safe_style accounts for 1.07 of 1.95 s cumulative (55%). Exhaustive caller trace of view_state/_selected_session_id in tldw_chatbook (untruncated grep): terminal.py:250 _session_view, :350 send_key, :371 send_paste, :388 request_resize, :462 _refresh, :508 _resize_generation, and :517/:536, the two bodies that call it. session_manager.send_key (914-928) only offers to the input actor and does NOT notify. So each keystroke runs exactly one all-session snapshot pass from send_key->_selected_session_id, plus at least one more from the echo: runtime thread process_output -> _notify_subscribers -> _manager_changed -> app.call_from_thread (blocking) -> _queue_refresh -> screen.call_after_refresh(_refresh) -> view_state. view_state snapshots every session with a model (up to MAX_SESSION_RECORDS=4), but only the selected screen is consumed. Per keystroke on the loop, one session costs 22-41 ms at 160x40-235x50, and each extra open session adds 11-20 ms per pass, twice. P0 (>=100 ms) needs 3+ full-width sessions in an opt-in, armed feature, so P1 stands. Fix check: a right-to-left last-column scan using default_char plus a style-tuple memo reproduced the current output exactly (asserted equal on an ls+prompt screen). With it, prompt snapshots drop from 10.7 to 0.63 ms at 160x40 and from 19.8 to 1.04 ms at 235x50, and full ls snapshots from 25.0 to 9.1 ms. Fix (a), reading runtime.selected_session_id in _selected_session_id, is safe: runtime.send_key validates the view through _input_actor_for_view_locked.
fix: (a) Make _selected_session_id() read the existing cheap property runtime.selected_session_id (session_manager.py:634) and not build a view_state. (b) Have view_state snapshot only the selected session's screen; the other sessions need only projection metadata. (c) In _project_line, detect blank cells with `character == screen.default_char` and memoize _safe_style on the pyte style tuple (fg, bg, bold, ...), keeping a small dict. (d) Cache projected rows and invalidate them by an accumulated dirty-row set. Today dirty is cleared per feed; accumulate it until the next snapshot, so a keystroke echo re-projects about 1 row instead of rows x cols cells.
fix_notes: (a) is trivially safe. runtime.selected_session_id exists (session_manager.py:634), and runtime.send_key/send_paste/resize_session already validate the view token through _input_actor_for_view_locked/_valid_view_locked, so the view check is not lost. (b) is safe because only the selected session's screen is consumed (console_terminal_workspace.py:601) and focus_session notifies on a switch. (c) `character == screen.default_char` is only a sufficient fast path: keep the full _safe_style comparison as the fallback, because unsafe colors normalize to 'default'. A memo keyed on the (fg, bg, bold, italics, underscore, strikethrough, reverse, blink) tuple is pure and safe. (d) The dirty-row cache is medium risk. pyte and the custom _BoundedScreen mark rows dirty, and resize/alt-screen/reset mark all rows, but dirty is cleared per feed (_feed_parser:651), so it must accumulate until the next snapshot. The custom draw path must also keep adding rows (for example _clear_intersecting_wide_cells). Do (a)+(b)+(c) first; they remove most of the cost.
evidence:

# _project_line: _safe_style (dataclass + 2 regex) on EVERY blank cell
character.data != " " or _safe_style(character) != SafeTerminalStyle()
# session_manager.view_state: snapshots ALL sessions

TerminalScreenModel.snapshot (screen_model.py:610) projects every row, and _project_line (680-688) calls _safe_style on every column to find the last non-blank cell. TerminalSessionManager.view_state (session_manager.py:654-703) snapshots every session that has a model, up to MAX_SESSION_RECORDS=4. terminal.py:531 _selected_session_id builds a full view_state only to read selected_session_id, and send_key (348), send_paste (369), request_resize (386) and _resize_generation (508) all go through it. title: Terminal output parse re-projects every scrolled line cell by cell, capping throughput at 0.19 MB/s while holding the GIL and model_lock
trigger: The daemon thread terminal-runtime-<id> (session_manager._run_runtime, started in _start_runtime_locked) calls process_output whenever output_actor.pending_bytes > 0, that is, for every chunk the shell prints. It runs off the loop but holds the GIL and model_lock, so it contends with the Textual loop thread (switch interval 5 ms) and blocks the UI's view_state snapshot.
cost: Measured isolated on the pin (bench_term.py f2, bench_slice.py, bench_fix2.py). Parse throughput is capped at about 1,200-2,450 lines/s at 160-200 columns whatever the line length. That is 0.15-0.19 MB/s for ls output, 0.16 MB/s for 80-byte build lines, and 0.03-0.04 MB/s for 15-byte lines. With scrollback projection stubbed out, throughput rises to 0.35-0.74 MB/s, so projection is 69-90% of parse CPU. The finder understated the loop impact. process_output holds model_lock for a whole parser turn, and the 8 ms turn budget (io_actors.py:619-624) is checked only between 1 KiB slices. Measured model_lock hold per 1 KiB slice, min/median: short lines 19.2/23.8 ms at 160x40, 24.6/30.2 ms at 200x45 and 28.8/34.2 ms at 235x50; build lines 5-8 ms; ls 4-5 ms. So for short-line output one turn is 3-4x the budget. The loop's view_state (`with model_lock: model.snapshot()`) waits for up to one full turn every frame while output streams. The wait is bounded, not starved, because the runtime thread makes a blocking app.call_from_thread after every turn: Textual 8.2.8 app.py:1834-1837 returns future.result(). On top of that wait the frame pays its own 11-20 ms snapshot (F1). That is a per-streamed-frame loop stall of about 30-55 ms while the Terminal is open, so P1 stands. Background sessions keep parsing at full cost even with the workspace closed (_run_runtime runs regardless of view), which adds GIL contention: a UI-thread CPU task's p95 went from 4.65 to 9.25 ms. Fix: the same right-to-left scan plus style memo as F1, checked equivalent, raises short-line throughput from 1,525 to 10,214 lines/s. That brings a 1 KiB slice from 44.8 to 6.7 ms, under the 8 ms budget; build lines go from 1,175 to 2,365 lines/s. Lazy scrollback is not needed; the shared cheap projection is enough. Merge F2's fix into F1's.
fix: Reuse F1's memoized projection: a default-char fast path plus a style memo makes the per-line cost scale with non-blank cells. Better still, retain scrollback lazily: keep a compact copy of the pyte row (or its (data, style-key) runs) and project only when the history view needs it. Optionally add a gate fast path that scans runs of printable bytes with bytes.translate or a regex, not per-byte method dispatch.
fix_notes: The shared blank-cell fast path and style memo from F1 give the largest win with the smallest diff: short lines stop paying for 200 columns. Lazy scrollback (keeping raw pyte rows or compact runs) interacts with the byte accounting in _retain_scrollback_line (accounted_bytes drives the MAX_SCROLLBACK_BYTES eviction), so the accounting must still be computed eagerly or approximated conservatively. Mutable pyte row dicts must not be retained by reference, because pyte reuses and moves buffer rows on scroll; copy them. The protocol-gate bulk-scan change is optional and low value (under 10% of the profile).
reason: The code matches. _BoundedScreen.index (screen_model.py:186-195) calls _on_scroll(self.buffer[top]) on every full-viewport scroll. _retain_scrollback_line (660) calls _project_line (680), which runs _safe_style (a dataclass plus 2 regex fullmatch calls) on every column, including trailing blanks, because the last-non-blank scan styles each cell. process_output (session_manager.py:570-598) runs the parser turn under model_lock, the same lock view_state takes for the UI snapshot. The 8 ms turn budget (io_actors.py process_parser_turn) is checked only between 1 KiB slices (MAX_PARSER_SLICE_BYTES=1024), so one slice with many newlines can run past it.

title: Terminal visible-refresh coalescing is dead: every parser turn (hidden sessions included) does a blocking call_from_thread into the UI loop
corrected: tldw_chatbook/UI/Console_Modules/terminal.py:441-444 (_manager_changed -> _marshal_to_ui) and terminal.py:456-462 (_refresh -> view_state); terminal.py:422 is jump_live and is not related.
trigger: The runtime thread of every RUNNING session notifies after every parser turn, hidden sessions included, while the Terminal workspace is open (the subscriber is ConsoleTerminalController._manager_changed). A hidden session's output triggers _refresh -> view_state, which snapshots all sessions (F1 cost), and the fingerprint then equals the last one, so the work is discarded.
cost: Estimated. The blocking round trip ties the runtime thread to loop latency, and each loop iteration can take a 20-27 ms snapshot at full width (F1, measured). A busy hidden session (for example a build) keeps triggering all-session snapshots on the loop at frame rate with no visible change.
fix: Honor ParserTurnResult.refresh_requested: notify only for visible-session turns that newly request a refresh. Call actor.acknowledge_visible_refresh() from terminal._refresh after projecting. Replace call_from_thread with a non-blocking handoff (loop.call_soon_threadsafe, or post_message); the callback's result is unused.
fix_notes: Fix risk is medium rather than low. If refresh_requested is honored, the acknowledge must run on every _refresh exit path, including the early returns on an unchanged fingerprint, a non-TerminalViewState value, and NoMatches. Otherwise _refresh_pending stays set and the visible terminal stops repainting. Acknowledging needs a new manager method, because the controller has no actor access. Replacing call_from_thread with non-blocking screen.call_later / post_message is safe: Textual's post_message detects a foreign thread and uses loop.call_soon_threadsafe. But without the refresh_requested gate that would enqueue one Callback per parser turn (about 125/s), so land both changes together. Lifecycle, rename and focus changes keep their own _notify_subscribers calls, so skipping notifications for hidden-session output does not lose metadata updates.
evidence:
# io_actors: computes refresh_requested / _refresh_pending ...
if processed_bytes and visible and not self._refresh_pending:
    self._refresh_pending = True; refresh_requested = True
# ...but process_output ignores result.refresh_requested:
self._queue_model_replies(session_id, model, replies)
self._notify_subscribers()
# acknowledge_visible_refresh() has zero callers; wiring.py:
screen.app.call_from_thread(callback)   # blocks runtime thread
reason: The code matches. process_parser_turn computes refresh_requested (io_actors.py:645-655), but process_output (session_manager.py:570-599) ignores it and calls _notify_subscribers unconditionally. acknowledge_visible_refresh (io_actors.py:658) has no production callers: an untruncated repo-wide grep finds only Tests/Terminal/test_io_actors.py. _marshal_terminal_to_ui (wiring.py:635-640) uses screen.app.call_from_thread, which on Textual 8.2.8 is run_coroutine_threadsafe followed by future.result() (verified from the installed source), so the runtime thread blocks until the loop runs the callback. No deadlock is possible: model_lock and the manager _lock are both released before _notify_subscribers.

title: Each terminal session runs a 200 Hz runtime-bridge poll and a 100 Hz input-flush poll while idle (on top of the known 50 Hz monitor)
known_task: TASK-31503 (adjacent: covers only the 50 Hz monitor thread, not these two loops)
trigger: Both threads are always on for every RUNNING session, even at an idle prompt and even when the Terminal workspace is closed. The runtime thread is started in _start_runtime_locked and the flusher in posix_backend._start_owner_workers (948-958), alongside the TASK-31503 monitor.
cost: Measured on a structural replica on this machine (PTY master, O_NONBLOCK, RLock x4, Event.wait(0), then stop.wait(0.005)): 0.64% of a core for the runtime bridge and 0.21% for the input flusher. That is about 0.85% per idle session, a lower bound because the real loop also runs record validation. Together with TASK-31503's about 1.5%, one idle session costs about 2.4% of a core. Kept at P2 because the feature is opt-in and each thread alone is under the 1% P0 bar.
fix: Runtime bridge: block in select()/poll() on the PTY master fd plus a self-pipe signalled by send_key/offer_* and stop, not a 5 ms sleep loop. Input flusher: use `self._input_pending.wait()` with no timeout, since close() already sets it (posix_backend.py:625). Land this in the same PR as TASK-31503 (monitor cadence).
fix_notes: The input flusher fix is a one-line change to self._input_pending.wait() with no timeout, safe as verified above. Keep the 10 ms EAGAIN backoff at lines 993-994. A select/poll-based runtime bridge is medium risk: _read_master also serves _output_buffer and the post-reap EOF scan (lines 1038-1054), which are not fd-readable events, and take_input/offer_reply need a wake source. A smaller interim fix: add a wake Event set by send_key/send_paste/offer_reply/stop, and back off idle waits from 5 ms up to about 50 ms after N idle passes. Output latency after an idle period then rises at most to the backoff cap, while input wakes immediately.
evidence:
_RUNTIME_POLL_SECONDS = 0.005
# _run_runtime loop: take_input (lock) + _runtime_output_state (lock)
# + _read_runtime_output (lock + os.read -> BlockingIOError) + _poll_runtime_exit (lock)
if not worked:
    stop.wait(_RUNTIME_POLL_SECONDS)
# posix_backend._flush_pending_input:
if not self._input_pending.wait(_PROCESS_POLL_SECONDS):  # 10 ms
    continue   # close() already sets _input_pending (line 625)

Each pass takes the manager RLock 4 times (take_input, _runtime_output_state, _read_runtime_output with os.read -> BlockingIOError, _poll_runtime_exit with wait_for_shell_exit(0)) and also evaluates self.permitted, a cheap app_config lookup. posix_backend._flush_pending_input (974-994) loops on _input_pending.wait(0.01). _close_requested is set only in request_priority_close (line 621), which also sets _input_pending (625), and finalize_shutdown goes through request_priority_close. So a wait() with no timeout cannot miss the close signal.

trigger: This runs in server mode only, on each server API call. Key it on (runtime_context.snapshot() revision, credential-store read generation, target-store write generation or file (st_ino, st_mtime_ns, st_size)). That calls resolve_target (637-639) -> ConfiguredServerTargetStore.get_target (server_target_store.py:84), which is @mcp_sources.guarded and goes through the nested list_targets/load -> _read_payload -> mcp_sources.reader under raw_participants._scope (acquisition plus pinned private-path walks). title: Cross-slice: every core-repository connection()/transaction() pays storage admission (~245 open() syscalls, 4-7 ms), versus 0.02 ms raw, a regression since 2026-09-16
trigger: Every `with db.transaction()` on ChaChaNotes and every connection()/transaction() on the other participant repositories, on the loop or on workers. Loop examples verified in this slice: the MainNavigationBar.on_mount recompute (F7) and the EventObserver store calls (F8).
cost: Per operation, measured isolated with the real import path (tldw_chatbook.config -> admit_startup; enrollment held as bootstrap.unbound), file-backed DBs, audit-hook guard on the real profile and network (bench_adm2.py). At DB path depth 16, an empty ChaChaNotes transaction costs min 4.3-5.4 ms / median 5.3-6.1 ms, and ClientNotificationsDB list_notifications(20) and get_settings cost 4.9-5.6 ms min. execute_query('SELECT 1') costs 0.01-0.02 ms. Each transaction makes 265 open(), 10 listdir and 7 flock calls, and acquire_storage accounts for 91-94% of the time. Adding 8 path components adds 128 open() calls and 1.5-1.9 ms, a slope of 16 open() per component. A real profile is about 8 components shallower (/Users/<u>/.local/share/tldw_cli/...), which extrapolates to about 137 open() and about 2.7-3.8 ms per operation, roughly 150x the raw cost. Only transaction() pays this on ChaChaNotes: common reads such as get_conversation_by_id, get_messages_for_conversation and list_character_cards use execute_query and skip admission. Census from a real isolated TldwCli boot at 235x52, fresh profile, network blocked, wrapping sa._acquire_storage and classifying calls by a _repository_operation frame (census.py/census.out). On-loop repository admissions per phase: boot 29 (subagent_counts x5, get_active_workspace x3, list_console_unseen_marks x3, list_workspaces x2, library collections __init__ x2, scheduled_tasks x3, and others), plus 80 off-loop; cold Library visit 5 (get_active_workspace x4, unseen marks x1); warm Library 2; Console visit 4 (list_console_unseen_marks x2, subagent_counts, get_active_workspace); Personas 1; Settings 1; 10 s idle 0. A peer census (sl23-lib2/send_adm.out) found 3 on-loop repository operations per steady send (write_trajectory_rows x2, settle_with_assistant). At real depth that is about 10-15 ms per visit or send and about 90 ms spread across boot on the loop, with no single freeze of 100 ms or more, so P1 is right and P0 is not. Fix-plan correction: repository operations are a small minority of on-loop admissions. In the same census a Console visit made 118-122 other acquire_storage calls through load_settings from chat_screen.py:7700 _provider_readiness_app_config (about 0.7-1.2 s of loop time at scratch depth). title: Install progress posts one UI message per MiB with no coalescing; the 1 MiB pre-verify hash step can flood the event loop
trigger: During every managed model install (Library Parakeet, first-run wizard speech/OmniVoice, Lab curated installs), one message per MiB reaches the Textual loop. In the pre-verify phase, events arrive at hash speed (roughly 0.5-2 GB/s, so 500-2000 events/s) for the length of the hash.

title: DuckDuckGo search pages with up to 5 bare requests.post calls, a new TCP/TLS handshake per page, while the create_session() helper is dead
trigger: Every duckduckgo-backend perform_websearch call (agent web_search tool, deep-search fan-out per sub-query) that needs more than one results page. Typically 0 extra pages at result_count<=10, occasionally 1.
cost: Estimated one extra TCP+TLS handshake (~100-300 ms) per additional page on a worker thread. Typical is 0-300 ms per search, not ~1 s. Deep search multiplies this by the number of sub-queries. No event-loop impact.
fix: `with requests.Session() as s:` around the pagination loop (or reuse `create_session()`), keeping the same timeout and verify arguments.
fix_notes: Prefer a plain `with requests.Session() as s:` (or the TASK-19830 shared default-timeout session factory) around the loop, keeping timeout and verify. Do NOT simply reuse create_session(). It mounts Retry(total=5, status_forcelist=[429, ...]), which would add silent retries on 429 against an anti-bot-sensitive endpoint and raise worst-case latency. Delete create_session() as dead code instead.
evidence:
for _ in range(5):
    response = requests.post("https://html.duckduckgo.com/html", data=payload, timeout=SEARCH_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_S, verify=requests_verify())
...
def create_session() -> requests.Session:   # never called
reason: Code is as quoted. WebSearch_APIs.py:3201 calls bare `requests.post("https://html.duckduckgo.com/html", ...)` inside `for _ in range(5)`, which builds and discards a Session on every page, so no keep-alive. `create_session()` at :3151 is defined and never called: a full untruncated grep of Web_Scraping/ finds only the def. The tests patch `searx_create_session`, which is a different function. There is one real caller, perform_websearch at :2182, reached from Tools/web_tool_impls.py:1328 (agent web_search), Tools/web_search_tool.py:84, deep search at WebSearch_APIs.py:607, and search_backend_settings.py:276. These run on tool or worker threads, not the event loop (web_tool_impls guards its cache with a threading lock for 'concurrent tool threads'), so this is wall-clock latency, not UI blocking. The finder overstates frequency. Pagination continues only when page 1 returns fewer than max_results after ad and dedupe filtering. result_count is capped at 10 (SEARCH_MAX_RESULT_COUNT=10, and web_search_tool clamps to at most 10), and deep search defaults to 10. So a typical search makes 1 request, sometimes 2; 5 is only the worst case. search_backend_settings passes 1. title: Article extractor launches a fresh Playwright driver and Chromium per URL per retry, and leaks per-thread event loops

Separately, `_default_url_article_scraper` (local_media_reading_service.py:4484-4490) calls future.result() on a fresh ThreadPoolExecutor when a loop is running. That would block the loop if ever called from it, which is worth a check by whoever touches this path.
evidence:

    browser = await p.chromium.launch(headless=True)      # per URL, per retry
_thread_local.loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()             # never closed
scraping_semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_SCRAPERS)  # module-global, shared across loops
reason: The cited code exists (Article_Extractor_Lib.py:485-486 launches Chromium inside the per-attempt retry loop), but no production path reaches it on this pin. `load_and_log_configs()` (:201-202) returns `{}`, and fetch_html evaluates `loaded_config["web_scraper"]` (:461) before the retry loop. That covers every caller: the Library URL ingest (local_media_reading_service.py:4364 -> `_default_url_article_scraper` -> scrape_article_sync -> run_async_function), deep search (WebSearch_APIs.py:1457), subscriptions (Subscriptions/scrapers/generic_scraper.py:132), scrape_urls_batch and scrape_and_summarize_multiple. title: Academic provider lanes build a fresh httpx.Client per call (no pooling across queries/iterations)
trigger: Research run (Research window or Console deep research) -> per round, up to 5 sequential search_papers calls -> up to 10 concurrent provider lanes on to_thread workers, each constructing and closing its own httpx.Client. It is never on the event loop.

Estimated: one TCP+TLS handshake per provider per query (about 100-300 ms wall, overlapped across concurrent lanes). Only queries 2-5 of a round within the 5 s keepalive could reuse connections, so the saving is at most about 1 s wall per round in a minutes-long LLM-bound run.

To get any reuse, use one lazily created module- or engine-scoped client, closed at engine shutdown. Security risk: do NOT give the shared client follow_redirects=True just because OSF needs it. Semantic Scholar sends an x-api-key header, and a redirect-following shared client would reopen the cross-origin header leak that task-19557 closed. Pass follow_redirects=True per request for OSF only. A client shared across concurrent to_thread lanes relies on httpx/httpcore pool thread-safety, which works in practice. Keep per-request timeouts as they are (_request_with_retries passes timeout=). Low value overall; bundle it with other research-lane work instead of fixing it alone.

title: themes.py pins AA text colours on all 91 themes at import time (about 20 ms every boot, pre-paint)
trigger: import tldw_chatbook.app (the boot path) -> module-scope import of css.Themes.themes -> 91 x ensure_readable_text_hues, every launch, pre-paint. App.__init__ registers BUILTIN_THEMES and only one theme is active at boot.
cost:
All runs were isolated (scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, TLDW_TEST_MODE=1, audit tree 840ed2ca58). The app was not imported, and the real-profile mtimes were unchanged afterwards. Scripts are in scratch/l2-themes-f1/.

(1) A/B test of the module body (bench_ab.py). Each run was a fresh process with textual pre-imported, executing the themes.py code with and without the two module-scope loops at :2142 and :2153. With 15 runs per arm: WITH the loops it took 31.2-59.4 ms (median 35.8 ms, min 31.2). WITHOUT them it took 1.40-2.36 ms (median 1.48). The two loops therefore cost about 30-34 ms per launch.

(2) Cost split (bench_split.py, 7 fresh processes). Pinning ONE theme (textual-dark, first call including warm-up) took 0.35-0.46 ms, which is the residual cost after a lazy fix. generate() alone over the other 90 themes took 27.6-30.6 ms, and pinning those 90 took 28.6-34.9 ms. So Theme.to_color_system().generate() at about 0.31 ms per theme is nearly all of the cost; the blend loop is minor. 40 of the 91 themes actually receive pins. Re-pinning all 91 already-pinned themes still took 26.1-29.9 ms. That confirms the first verifier: there is no short-circuit, and the finding's claim that it 'already memoizes via _tldw_pinned_text_hues' is wrong. A lazy get_theme or current_theme hook needs an early `if hasattr(theme, _PINNED_ATTR): return theme`.

(3) Trigger trace. The console script tldw-cli points to cli.py:main_cli_runner. cli.py:88 imports tldw_chatbook.app synchronously on the main thread before App.run. app.py:187 then imports ALL_THEMES at module scope, which runs themes.py:2142-2155. So the cost is paid pre-paint on every launch (also before the splash), and a .pyc cannot help because it is module-body execution.

Nothing at boot needs the pins of more than one theme. on_mount (app.py:14979) only calls register_theme(), which in Textual 8.2.8 is a plain dict store. Only `self.theme = default_theme` resolves one theme. The command-palette provider (app.py:1136-1150) and theme_catalog use only names. Runtime consumers of pins run later: settings_theme_editor.py:625 pinned_text_hues and Tests/UI/test_theme_contrast.py. load_user_themes calls create_theme_from_dict, which pins each saved theme; that cost is small and scales with the user's saved themes.

No open task covers this. Matching tasks are TASK-31429 and TASK-32940 (both Done) and TASK-33003.6 (To Do); 33003.6 would add another per-theme pass with the same shape (ensure_visible_rules is not in the code yet).

About 30 ms of boot pre-paint work meets the P1 rubric line (first paint or boot at about 10-20 ms or more) and is larger than the first pass's ~20 ms. Moving to one theme at boot would save about 29-33 ms. A generated literal table would bring the boot cost to about 0.

Register the themes unpinned, then call ensure_readable_text_hues (it already memoizes via _tldw_pinned_text_hues) in a TldwCli.get_theme()/register_theme hook, or wherever a theme is resolved for use: the boot default, a switch, or an editor load. Boot then pays for one theme (about 0.2 ms). Alternative: precompute the pinned values into a generated literal table gated by Tests/UI/test_theme_contrast.py. Route TASK-33003.6's new pass through the same hook.

Add an early `if hasattr(theme, _PINNED_ATTR): return theme` before any lazy hook. That early return matters because Textual's App.current_theme calls get_theme() often, so a get_theme hook must be O(1) after the first pin. Pin before Textual first builds CSS variables for the theme. Consumers that assume shipped themes are already pinned also need the hook: settings_theme_editor.py:625 reads pinned_text_hues(theme), and Tests/UI/test_theme_contrast.py parametrizes over ALL_THEMES. The picker's _COLOURS_CACHE previews also need it if they show text-* hues. A generated literal table avoids the ordering risk but needs a regeneration gate.

title: File-picker DirectoryNavigation keeps a 33 Hz poll timer running until the dialog unmounts, even after the scan and hydration finish
trigger: Any open FileOpen, FileSave or SelectDirectory fspicker modal, at 33 Hz for the whole time it is open, including idle time after the listing and hydration are complete. It is on the event loop but bounded to the dialog's lifetime.

title: EmbeddingFactory holds one global lock across model build and whole-batch inference, so query embeds queue behind ingestion batches
trigger: A RAG search (a Console RAG-enabled send or a Library RAG answer) issued while post-ingest indexing or a backfill is embedding a document. "Ingest a document, then ask about it" is a natural workflow. The work is off the event loop (asyncio.to_thread), so the cost is send/search latency, not a UI freeze.
cost: Estimated. A one-text query embed (~10-50 ms on its own) waits for the entire in-flight document embed. That is seconds for a typical document on a CPU model and tens of seconds for a large book (hundreds of chunks at batch_size 32). With a remote embedder it can wait up to about 135 s of timeouts and backoff. A first-use model load (_build, seconds) also blocks every other embed. I upgraded it from P3 to P2: the cost on the less frequent concurrent path is large (multi-second).
fix: Use a per-model lock with an in-use refcount, and evict only at refcount 0. Build models outside the global lock with a per-model single-flight. Optionally split large ingestion batches so short query embeds can interleave.
fix_notes: A per-model lock with a refcount does NOT fix the main case, because ingestion and query use the same default model. Same-model calls must stay serialized for HF models: HF fast tokenizers raise 'RuntimeError: Already borrowed' under concurrent use from threads, and model_recovery.recovered_encode already holds a per-borrower RLock (item[4]) for local-path models. The effective fix is to hold the lock per internal sub-batch, not per call, so a query can interleave between the batch_size chunks, and protect eviction with a refcount. Move the OpenAI HTTP call and its retry sleeps outside the lock (look up rec under the lock, then call). Note that requests.Session sharing across threads is not formally thread-safe. Building outside the global lock needs a per-model single-flight, otherwise two threads can load a multi-GB model twice. Risk is medium: the existing lock deliberately prevents use-after-free on eviction.

            ...
                rec = self._build(model_id_to_use)   # download/load, seconds
            ...
            result = embed_fn(texts, as_list=as_list)   # entire batch under the global lock
reason: The code is at the cited lines. Embeddings_Lib.py:798 takes `with self._lock:`, line 825 builds the model with `rec = self._build(...)` under it, and line 845 runs `result = embed_fn(texts, ...)` under it. The comment there admits it serializes all embedding calls. I traced the sharing: ingestion_indexing.py keeps ONE process-wide shared RAG service ("shared with search", _shared_service). search_service.py:84 and library_local_rag_search_service.py:1092 fetch it via get_shared_rag_service, so ingestion indexing and query search use the same EmbeddingsServiceWrapper, EmbeddingFactory and _lock. The ingestion side, rag_service.py:973, calls create_embeddings_async(chunk_texts) with EVERY chunk of the document in one call. _HuggingFaceEmbedder.embed then loops over sub-batches of batch_size inside that single locked call. The query side, rag_service.py:1587, calls create_embeddings_async([query]) against the same lock. The ingestion indexer runs on its own background thread and loop (ingestion_indexing.py:1110), so the two really are concurrent. title: Local feedback/grammar stores: each mutation does 2 whole-store deepcopies, a full indented JSON rewrite and an fsync on the event loop; rows are never purged
trigger: No current trigger. The only reachers are direct test construction and the backup participant machinery. The finding becomes loop-blocking only if a future UI handler awaits these methods without offloading.
cost: Measured in the isolated env: submit_feedback took 55.9 ms at record 1, 58.2 ms at 2, 41.1 ms at 100 and 62.8 ms at 300 (200-char notes), on a loaded machine. This matches the finder's 27-72 ms order of magnitude. The base cost is admission syscalls plus fsync, and it grows with store size.
fix: Only if the stores are kept (F1). Run the mutation bodies via asyncio.to_thread. Skip the inner deepcopy when a guarded operation is already active for the same source (or snapshot with a shallow list copy, since records are replaced, not mutated in place). Write compact JSON (no indent/sort_keys). Purge deleted rows on persist. Longer term, an append-only JSONL or a table in an existing DB.
fix_notes: The proposed 'shallow list copy, since records are replaced, not mutated in place' is WRONG. update_feedback mutates the record dict in place (record['issues']/['user_notes']/['updated_at']), and so does delete_feedback (record['deleted']). The grammar update/delete paths do the same. A shallow snapshot would therefore not roll back a failed mutation, and the deepcopy is the rollback contract of the backup/recovery guarded mutation. Skipping only the inner, nested deepcopy when the same source already holds an active guarded op is the safe variant. Moving bodies to asyncio.to_thread must keep the whole guarded scope, wrapper plus body, on one thread: _State records threading.current_thread() and storage._task_identity(), and _local.operation is thread-local. Purging tombstones is safe for the idempotency lookup, which already skips deleted rows. The whole finding is moot if F1 retires the stores.

title: Each from_config server service owns a private API client and httpx pool; first use builds a new SSLContext on the loop and none are closed

As a separate cross-cutting fix, cache one SSLContext in Utils/tls_trust.httpx_verify() so no httpx client construction pays the ~10 ms certifi parse. TASK-1538 (Done) listed the provider-wide from_config migration as unfiled follow-up work.

It also changes semantics: it follows the active-server switch (arguably the correct behavior) and raises differently when no profile is configured, so app.py's try/except ValueError fallbacks become moot. For the cross-cutting SSLContext cache in httpx_verify(), key the cache on the resolved TLS setting (verify flag plus custom CA path) and invalidate it when those settings change. title: ACP start_session always busy-polls for the full startup timeout (2 s) even when the process started fine
trigger: Manual Launch/Restart button on the ACP screen. It runs in a thread worker and is rare.
cost: About 200 thread wakeups per launch. The 2 s latency is intrinsic to the readiness heuristic, and the proposed fix does not remove it.
fix: Use `self._process.wait(timeout=startup_timeout)` inside try/except TimeoutExpired (one blocking wait with no 10 ms spin), or lower the default grace. The "didn't exit within N s" readiness heuristic itself can stay.
fix_notes: Popen.wait(timeout) plus TimeoutExpired is fine as tidy-up, but it does not reduce ready latency. Real latency reduction needs a readiness signal from the ACP runtime, such as a handshake on stdio, and that is a feature change.

deadline = time.monotonic() + max(0.05, self.config.startup_timeout_seconds)
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    return_code = self._process.poll()
    if return_code is not None: ... return FAILED
    time.sleep(0.01)
self._status = ACPRuntimeProcessStatus.RUNNING
reason: The code is as quoted (runtime_process.py:228-241). It runs only from a user click via @work(thread=True) _launch_acp_runtime_worker (acp_screen.py:445-465), so it never touches the event loop. The 2 s wait is not waste. It is the method's readiness heuristic: 'did not exit within startup_timeout_seconds' means RUNNING, because there is no readiness probe. The proposed fix, Popen.wait(timeout=...), returns early only when the process EXITS, so a successful launch still takes the full 2 s. The latency the title describes would not change. The only real saving is about 200 10-ms sleep/poll wakeups on a worker thread, once per manual launch or restart. That is negligible, below even P3 micro-inefficiency, and a 10 ms sleep loop is not a busy-wait. Lowering the default grace is a behaviour and reliability trade-off, not an efficiency fix.

title: Planning/label sanitizers do per-character Python generator scans (31 us per 200-char summary) and re-resolve the display cap per step
trigger: Once per proven model round during conversation resume (on the loop, through F2), and per live step on the agent worker thread (off the loop).
cost: Micro-benchmark (isolated, loaded machine): the full safe_intermediate_thinking_summary took 51-110 us on a 200-char summary. The any() control-char scan alone was 29.3 us, against 0.49 us for a compiled regex. _sanitize_task_marker_label was 9.4 us, each of the three regexes about 3.4-4 us, and display_cap 2.2-2.5 us per call. The per-character scan is the largest single component, so the fix removes roughly half the cost. At about 100 rounds that is ~3-5 ms; only large conversations reach ~100 ms.
fix: Module-level _CTRL_RE = re.compile(r"[\x00-\x09\x0b-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]") for the reject check. Build _CTRL_TABLE = {c: ' ' for c in C0/C1} and use " ".join(text.splitlines())[:N].translate(_CTRL_TABLE) (truncate first, keep the exact 200-char semantics). Pass the resolved cap into format_agent_step_marker / _truncate_step_text from the resume loop. Keep the existing privacy tests as the regression pin.
fix_notes: Truncating first is equivalent here because each replaced character maps to exactly one space. The reject class [\x00-\x09\x0b-\x1f\x7f-\x9f] correctly exempts \n. The three regexes remain (~11 us), so expect about a 2x gain, not 30x. Passing a resolved cap down is safe; the live path must still read fresh per run so a Settings change takes effect.

The better fix is making _literal_terminal_text C-speed (str.translate with a precomputed control-char table, or a re.sub over [\x00-\x08\x0b-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]). A ~100 ms bridge-side throttle is fine if the result and settle paths always flush, but it only halves an already 20 Hz-capped rate. Keep the flush in _settle_raw_shell_marker so the terminal state is never dropped.
evidence:
# :10286 _append_raw_shell_preview
used = len(stdout.encode("utf-8")) + len(stderr.encode("utf-8"))
# :10457-10493 raw_shell_progress_sink, per RawCliStreamEvent, under _raw_shell_marker_lock:
#   state.stdout, state.stderr, clipped = self._append_raw_shell_preview(...)
#   self._update_raw_shell_marker(state)  -> format_raw_cli_content(whole preview) + store.update_tool_marker(...)
reason: The code matches: bridge :10286 re-encodes stdout and stderr, and raw_shell_progress_sink :10457-10493 calls _update_raw_shell_marker for every RawCliStreamEvent under _raw_shell_marker_lock. Two of the finding's premises are wrong, though. (a) 'No coalescing' is false: the producer (raw_cli_executor.py:90-92, 772-818 _CoalescingOutput) batches pipe reads into ≤8 KiB chunks flushed at most every 50 ms per stream. The executor's own _accept (:713-754) also caps the shared preview at 32 KiB and stops emitting text events after that. So the event rate is ≤~20/s per stream and the total is bounded. (b) The re-encode is negligible (measured 0.57 µs at 32 KiB). The real per-event cost is format_raw_cli_content -> _literal_terminal_text (console_raw_cli.py:73-80), a per-character Python generator join over the whole preview. Each event also runs store.update_tool_marker -> _recompute_active_path (console_chat_store.py:12044, :22020), an O(transcript) rebuild that bumps the display revision. It all runs on the executor or sink thread, off the loop; the loop only picks up changes on the 0.2 s poll, so loop-side cost is bounded at 5 Hz. The real residual is GIL-competing CPU during slow-trickling shell output.

title: Three independent full-hydration derivations of the same agent history run on the loop for one conversation open
trigger: Opening or resuming a saved conversation that has agent history: the resume path (workspace.py:6420), the next transcript sync (chat_screen.py:18284, on a revision-key miss) and the next rail sync (agent.py:~1250, on a historical-cache miss). All run on the event loop.
cost: MEASURED in an isolated env (scratch/f12-second/{bench,split,floor,scope}.py). File-backed AgentRunsDB in WAL mode with the real storage-admission path active. Counted acquire_storage calls per derivation: A=4, B=2, C=2. Synthetic history: N primary turns x S steps (~600 B tool results), a 12-step subagent every 5th turn, and a change snapshot every 2nd turn. The box was heavily loaded (loadavg 44-52 on 18 cores), so figures are min/median. PER OPEN, A+B+C as shipped: 30x8 116/142 ms; 100x8 165/218; 100x24 191/467; 300x8 184/261; 300x24 426/709. SAME WITH ADMISSION NO-OP'D (SQL+JSON+marker CPU only): 6/12, 21/35, 61/81, 77/129, 298/478. One-statement floor (latest_primary_run_metadata): min 5.8, p10 8.9, median 14.1 ms, vs 0.024 ms with admission no-op'd. cProfile shows ~245 posix.open calls per statement. So at 100 turns or fewer, 70-95% of the per-open cost is the 8 storage-admission floors (F7's mechanism), not hydration. Hydration dominates only at 300x24 (~70%). Unloaded estimate (floor ~6 ms): ~55 ms at 30x8, ~70 at 100x8, ~110 at 100x24, ~125 at 300x8. The cost scales with agent history on a common path, so P1 stands. It is not P0: unloaded it stays under 100 ms until roughly 100 rich turns, and most of it is F7's cost. CHEAP FIXES, MEASURED: (1) One outer `with db.connection():` scope hits the _repository_operation reuse path and cuts 8 admissions to 1: 127->20 ms (30x8), 129->36 (100x8), 195->88 (100x24), mins. The three derivations run at different call sites, so per-method scoping gives 8->3. (2) Metadata-only primary query for B: 0.31 vs 5.2 ms intrinsic at 100x8 and 1.0 vs 18 at 300x8. (3) latest_primary_run plus children-of-primary for C: 0.14 vs 5.0 at 100x8. (4) A's intrinsic cost is unavoidable hydration plus building 1550 ConsoleChatMessage markers at 100x24 (31-39 ms). It can only be offloaded; its caller is async, so asyncio.to_thread fits. A shared AgentHistoryView cache is not needed to get most of the win. TRACE ADDITIONS (full grep, untruncated): A has exactly one caller, agent.py:2290 <- workspace.py:6420, inside async _resume_console_workspace_conversation (awaited from workspace.py:5292, chat_screen.py:24783, archive.py:302 and wiring.py:1541, all on the loop, none offloaded). A runs once per resume of a conversation that is not already open. B's only caller is transcript.py:131 <- chat_screen.py:18284 (async _sync_native_console_transcript). Its cache is SINGLE-SLOT, keyed (conversation_id, revision), so it misses on every Console session-tab switch. It also misses on EVERY completed agent turn: console_chat_controller.py:29065/29080/29091 -> _record_run_assistant_message -> bridge.record_run_assistant_message (:9754) -> publication_signal.anchor_published() bumps the revision, and so does completed(published=True) per change-review window. So B (list_runs over ALL kinds, hydrated) is per-turn and per-tab-switch as well as per-open, which the finding under-counted. B is gated on git being available (console_runtime.py:3559). C's only caller is agent.py:1248, reached from chat_screen.py:16357 (compose_content, i.e. first paint) and :9508 (rail sync). It is cached per conversation in a dict, so it runs once per conversation per process.
fix: Introduce one per-conversation AgentHistoryView built off the loop (asyncio.to_thread) from metadata-first queries: primary anchors, last-N steps and count, direct children, change snapshots, and delivered notes, each read once. Cache it on the bridge keyed by (conversation_id, publication revision, run generation), and serve resume markers, change-review markers and the historical rail from it. This subsumes F1, F2, F4 and F9 in one PR.
fix_notes: resume_marker_messages genuinely needs every primary run's steps to rebuild markers, so a 'metadata-first' view cannot remove that hydration. It can only move it off the loop (the caller is already async, so wrap the DB read in asyncio.to_thread) and share it. Cheap independent wins: switch change_review_marker_messages to a metadata-only primary query (it never reads steps and currently hydrates subagents too), and make _derive_historical_snapshot use latest_primary_run plus a children-of-primary query. A single cached AgentHistoryView is medium risk: the three consumers invalidate differently (change-review publication revision, historical cache invalidated on in-process run start/finish, resume at open only), so a shared key can serve stale rail or markers. Folding F9 into the same PR is scope creep: F9 is a worker-thread send-path fix, not a conversation-open path.

change_review_marker_messages -> list_runs(ALL kinds, hydrated) + change_snapshots_for_conversation (again)

title: Every send re-audits every local skill's trust (dir scans + manifest HMAC + storage admission) on the event loop
trigger: Every manual send (async prompt_queue.dispatch -> sync _admit_console_turn_to_runtime on the loop), every queue add/edit, retry/regenerate/continue/edit/summarize via resolve_turn_configuration_snapshot, and fleet wakes. No thread offload anywhere on the chain.
cost:
Setup: real LocalSkillsService plus SkillTrustService at the app's own store location (default_local_skills_store_dir(get_user_data_dir())), using the 14-skill obra/superpowers corpus. Scratch profile at data-dir depth 15 and depth 23. Box load was 29-54 on 18 cores, so the ms figures below are min CPU (process_time); call and open counts do not depend on load. Script: scratch/sl-s9/bench.py; results in sweep_{0,8}.jsonl and qos_{0,8}.jsonl.

capture_skill_context_maximum, min CPU at d15:
- K=0 user skills: 0.43-0.50 ms, 0 opens. Built-ins skip trust.
- Trusted K=1: 80-113 ms (63.5k Python calls, 2,835 os.open, 9 acquire_storage).
- Trusted K=5: 423-570 ms (308k calls, 14,175 opens, 45 acquire_storage).
- Trusted K=14: 1.05-1.54 s (873k calls, 39,690 opens, 126 acquire_storage).
- Trust never set up (no manifest, all skills blocked) still costs 58-85 ms at K=1, 249-439 ms at K=5 and 0.94-1.24 s at K=14.

Cost is linear in K at about 61k calls per skill. The finder's O(S^2) manifest term is negligible.

Counts grow exactly linearly with path depth (d15 vs d23, e.g. K=5: 14,175 to 21,135 opens). Extrapolated to a real ~/.local/share/tldw_cli/<user> path (depth 6) and converted with the call-ratio/open-ratio bracket: K=1 about 36-76 ms, K=5 about 190-380 ms, K=14 about 0.55-1.0 s per snapshot.

Split per trusted skill: status_for_skill is 59-76 ms (6 acquire_storage) and current_fingerprint_digest is 16-25 ms (3 acquire_storage). So fix (b), reusing the scan, saves only about 25%. The lever is the per-call storage admission (acquire_storage and pinned-directory walks), not the scan: a raw scan costs about 0.2 ms.

Caller trace (full, untruncated grep) finds 2 call sites:
- session.py:3603 via _build_console_turn_execution_context. Reached from wiring.py:271 (_admit_console_turn_to_runtime, sync, from prompt_queue._launch_chain:996 on every manual send, via async dispatch awaited in chat_screen:19262) and from wiring.py:2208 (queue/edit capture, prompt_queue:732/932/984).
- console_chat_controller.py:22581, reached from retry/regenerate/continue/edit via resolve_turn_configuration_snapshot and from fleet wake at console_runtime:2372.

Nothing on either path offloads or caches. TASK-32921 (Done) only removed the per-skill keyring reads; the admission cost remains. P0 applies to users with 3 or more user skills; users with no user skills pay about 0.
fix: (a) Cache the catalog snapshot per app, keyed on the index file mtime/generation, the trust-manifest generation and the builtin-disabled set; invalidate on skill mutations and trust changes. (b) Stop computing definition_digest for every skill at capture time. Compute it lazily in ensure_frozen_definition for the mentioned skill only, or reuse the fingerprints status_for_skill already scanned so each skill is scanned once, not twice. (c) Run the capture inside asyncio.to_thread from the async send and queue paths so a cache miss cannot freeze the UI. (d) Load the manifest once per capture instead of once per skill, which is O(S^2) today.
fix_notes: (a) A cache keyed only on index mtime + manifest generation misses out-of-band edits to skill files. The re-scan exists to detect tampering, so the key must include per-skill-dir stat (mtime_ns/ino/size of each file, or at least the dir tree), or the catalog must accept a stale verdict and rely on the execute-time ensure_skill_trusted/pin checks. State which. (b) Reusing the status scan's fingerprints for definition_digest is the cheapest, lowest-risk win: it halves the scans. (d) Loading the manifest once per capture is safe. (c) Offloading is riskier than stated. _admit_console_turn_to_runtime is deliberately synchronous (custody ordering), and the rest of the snapshot reads non-thread-safe store/session objects. Offload only the skill-trust file work, e.g. pre-capture via asyncio.to_thread in the async dispatch before calling the sync admission. The biggest lever is F8: the per-skill admission handshake itself.
reason: Code matches the pin: capture_skill_context_maximum (console_chat_controller.py:1300-1332) walks local._visible_records(), which re-reads the index JSON and the builtin SKILL.md. For each user skill it calls _summary_for_record -> _trust_fields_for_record -> trust_service.status_for_skill (skill_trust_service.py:477). That runs _execution_scope (acquire_storage per source path, execution_scope, local_content_lifetime.operation), then _load_valid_manifest (a full HMAC manifest load per skill, so O(S^2)), then _scan_skill. It then calls current_fingerprint_digest (@content_call admission plus a second _scan_skill). Nothing caches any of this. The app comment at app.py:8783 even says the loader 'runs on every skills read, including the Console's per-send capture'. Trigger traced: prompt_queue.dispatch (async, awaited from chat_screen._dispatch_console_draft_send) -> _stage_normal_chain -> _launch_chain (prompt_queue:996) -> wiring._admit_console_turn_to_runtime (sync, wiring:256-271) -> session._build_console_turn_execution_context (session:3603). It is also reached via _capture_configuration on queue/edit (prompt_queue:732/932/984) and via controller.resolve_runtime_turn_configuration_snapshot (22581) on retry/regenerate/continue/edit and fleet wake (console_runtime:2372). None of it is offloaded. Built-ins skip trust, so with zero user skills the cost is negligible. It scales linearly with user skills, with an O(S^2) manifest term. Not covered by any open task (grepped backlog for capture_skill_context/skill_context_maximum/_execution_scope: none). Extra detail: when trust is locked and a key cache exists, _try_cached_unlock also attempts a keyring read per status call. That read is mitigated by _cached_keyring_read's TTL cache.

title: Rest of the per-send turn snapshot does sync MCP-store, DB and manifest work on the loop, and two builders implement it
trigger: Same snapshot path as F1 (every send/queue/retry/regenerate/edit/wake), plus _compose_mcp_provider once per agent run (agent_runtime defaults to true; default Console sends compose MCP). All sync on the event loop.
cost:
Setup: the real app wiring. LocalMCPStore(get_user_data_dir()/'local_mcp_store.json') -> LocalMCPControlService -> UnifiedMCPControlPlaneService, with the permission store at its real sibling path mcp_permissions.json. This service is constructed for every user (app.py:10941).

- 404.8k Python calls, 19,517 os.open, 58 acquire_storage; min CPU 646-862 ms.
- With both JSON files present (returning user) it is slightly worse: 436.7k calls, 20,887 opens, 62 acquire_storage, 760 ms.

Parts of that snapshot:
- get_kill_switch alone: 137-153k calls, 20-22 acquire_storage, 240-294 ms.
- permission_store.load: 216-231 ms.
- get_external_servers on an empty store: 258-328 ms (21 acquire_storage).
- describe/get_inventory: only 7 ms, so memoising the manifest is irrelevant.

Per agent run, the compose-equivalent (_compose_mcp_provider's get_kill_switch, then compose_catalog's get_kill_switch, local_external_catalog, get_inventory and effective_tool_states) costs 690k calls, 33,342 opens, 99 acquire_storage and 1.30 s at d15.

Counts are linear in depth (d23: 540.6k calls / 29,093 opens for the capture). Extrapolated to real depth 6 (count-exact, CPU bracketed by the call and open ratios): capture about 290-540 ms per snapshot, plus about 585-815 ms per agent run. Even allowing about 1.5x for load inflation, a default Console send (agent_runtime defaults to true) runs about 0.5-0.9 s of synchronous MCP-store work on the loop.

Trace:
- Snapshot: same full two-site trace as F1 (session.py:3572, controller:22583).
- Per-run: _compose_mcp_provider (controller:16239 get_kill_switch, then mcp_tool_provider.py:452/490 and unified_control_plane_service.py:2407, an async def with a sync body). It is reached from _run_agent_reply:28126 on every live run, and also from the context preview (21961) and the personal-context preflight (21656).

The store has no cache: load() -> mcp_sources.guarded -> readable() admission on every call. Same root cause as F1: per-call Backup_Recovery storage admission.
fix: Read the permission store once per snapshot and pass the payload to both the kill-switch check and effective_tool_states. Memoise describe_local_mcp_capabilities, since it is a static manifest. Cache the MCP definition maximum keyed on the permission-store generation plus the external-catalog revision. Move the whole snapshot capture into asyncio.to_thread from the async send paths, keeping the thread-confined store reads on the loop. Collapse session._build_console_turn_execution_context and controller.resolve_runtime_turn_configuration_snapshot into one builder so each fix lands once. Reuse the snapshot's kill-switch and definition hashes in _compose_mcp_provider instead of re-reading.
fix_notes: The kill switch is security-sensitive. Do not reuse the snapshot's kill-switch value in _compose_mcp_provider: the fresh re-read there exists so a switch flipped between capture and dispatch takes effect. Make the read cheap instead (a stat-validated cache). The permission file is also written by other processes (mcp-unified stdio server, MCP hub), so a cache key must be the file's (st_mtime_ns, st_ino, st_size) plus the recovery selection, not an in-process generation counter. Loading the store once and passing the payload to both the kill-switch check and effective_tool_states is safe and immediate, as is memoising describe_local_mcp_capabilities (static). Moving the whole snapshot to to_thread conflicts with the synchronous custody-admission design and with non-thread-safe store/session reads, so offload only the MCP/skill file work. Collapsing the two builders is worthwhile but they differ (rag_defaults source_types, direct_library_tools source), so reconcile carefully. The dominant cost is the F8 admission handshake.

title: Capture-On trace-provenance admission runs a BEGIN IMMEDIATE write txn with N point reads on the event loop every send
trigger: Every MANUAL/QUEUED send with capture on (the default), and prepared continuations; sync inside an async method with no to_thread.
cost:
Setup: a real CharactersRAGDB file in scratch (WAL, synchronous=1, busy_timeout=15000) and a real SemanticRevisionCoordinator / ConsoleTraceRepository. Measured admit_message_provenance plus ensure_policy inside db.transaction(immediate=True), the default no-PII path.

Min CPU at d15 for N=50/200/400 history rows: 7.6 / 8.1 / 12.0 ms. At d23: 11.4 / 12.7 / 12.2 ms.

The cost is almost all fixed, and it is not this site's own work:
- An EMPTY immediate transaction costs 7.2 ms wall min, and an empty deferred read transaction 7.6 ms, against 7.5 ms for the 100-row admit (scratch/sl-s9/dbprobe.out).
- cProfile puts 15-16 of 18 ms in TransactionContextManager.__enter__ (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:24221) -> _core_operation -> storage_admission.acquire_storage: 261 posix.open, paid by every ChaChaNotes transaction app-wide.

The finding's specific mechanisms are marginal:
- Per-row _current_revision reads cost about 12 µs per row (30 Python calls per row).
- The per-send policy INSERT plus commit is sub-ms (WAL, NORMAL sync).

The finding's 9.6 to 15.9 ms growth with history does not hold: the cost is mostly flat. Extrapolated to real depth 6 (count-exact: 117 opens), a send costs about 3.4-5.6 ms at 50 rows and 5.4-10.8 ms at 400, below the per-send P1 bar. The remaining real risk is contention. With a second connection holding BEGIN IMMEDIATE for 400 ms, admit() blocked the calling thread for 487 ms (bounded only by the 15 s busy_timeout). That is conditional on a concurrent writer and short for the usual ones: the TASK-31501 1 Hz poll holds the lock for sub-ms SELECTs, because the admission tax runs before BEGIN.

Trace re-verified: the only callers are 8175 (prepared continuation) and 12168 (_accept_durable_turn); both are sync inside async with no to_thread. The existing _run_durable_db_call (11492) is used at 8294/12069/12302/12475 but not here.

Still worth the cheap re-route, but P2. The bigger lever is the per-transaction admission tax, which also dominates F4's DB leg.
fix: Run the transaction body through self._run_durable_db_call, which already handles the :memory: case and runs on a worker thread with operation_owned_connection. Compute the store.get_message(...) owner lookups and the sidecars on the loop first. Batch _current_revision into one SELECT ... WHERE live_message_id IN (...) chunked read. Reuse an existing FrozenTracePolicy row when the policy fields are unchanged instead of inserting one per send. TASK-31505 covers only the custom-PII subprocess inside this same transaction; this finding is the default no-PII path.
fix_notes: _run_durable_db_call runs the callable on a worker via _run_owned_chat_db_operation. The current transaction body calls self.store.get_message (not thread-safe) only in the pre-loop section, which is already outside the txn, so keep all store/provider_messages work on the loop and pass only ids and frozen values into the worker body. Batching _current_revision needs chunking under SQLite's variable limit. Reusing a policy row across sends changes provenance semantics (descriptors reference a per-request policy object and policy_id); confirm that trace readers and exports do not assume a unique policy per request before deduping. The PII branch (TASK-31505) must still compute redactions before the txn.

        saved = admit_message_provenance(cursor, coordinator=coordinator,

        ... per thinking-owner JOIN query ...

When capture_mode is CAPTURE_ON, it opens database.transaction(immediate=True) at 11685 on the loop. Inside: admit_message_provenance (console_trace_provenance.py:1414-1440) calls coordinator.ensure_current_revision per saved history row (one _current_revision SELECT per row at steady state); there is a JOIN query per thinking owner; and repository.ensure_policy (11733) writes a FrozenTracePolicy with a fresh new_opaque_id() every send, so every send commits. _run_durable_db_call (11492, asyncio.to_thread when offloadable) exists and is used for commit_durable_turn per TASK-22205 (Done), but not here. Capture-On is the default: [console] exchange_capture=true (config.py:3794), trace_normalized_writes=true (3798), and console_runtime supplies _LazyTraceBoundaryFactory (3453), so supports_durable_capture holds in production. TASK-31505 covers only the opt-in custom-PII subprocess inside this same transaction; the default no-PII path is new scope. TASK-31502 (quiescence registry tax) also multiplies the per-row statement cost.

title: 0.2 s transcript tick calls context_control_inputs, re-running durable snapshots, branch-memory SQL and a recovery config scope on every tick
trigger: 5 Hz tick during any active run (and every event-driven native sync); unconditional call on the loop.
cost:

- ConsoleChatController._global_context_policy_overrides: 15.4-21.7 ms (11.8k calls, 636 os.open, 2 acquire_storage). The same 9 get_cli_setting reads without the operation(config) wrapper cost 0.013 ms, so the wrapper is more than 99.9% of that cost.
- ConsoleContextRepository.load_applicable_branch_memory: 6.0-7.7 ms, flat for N=50-400 (261 opens and 1 acquire_storage, i.e. the per-transaction admission from F3).
- get_message_versions_by_ids: 0.10 / 0.34 / 0.77 ms at 50 / 200 / 400 rows.

Adding the prior verifier's roughly 2 ms snapshot copy and digests gives about 12-20 ms per tick. At 5 Hz that is about 6-10% of the event loop for the whole of every active run, plus every event-driven sync (79 _sync_native_console_chat_ui call sites, coalesced).

title: send_refusal_copy resolves get_user_data_dir() (tens of ms) on every send and message action just to locate emergency_stop.json
trigger: Every manual send and every message action (retry/regenerate/continue/edit/summarize/restore); wake attempts when autowake is on.

- get_user_data_dir itself costs the same. The fast path verified_user_data_directory returns only inside an active raw operation, and none is active on these paths.

Full caller list (grep 'send_refusal_copy(', untruncated), all sync on the loop:
- prompt_queue.py:946, in async dispatch: every manual send.
- message.py:1690/1738/1844/2685: retry/regenerate/continue/edit.
- chat_screen.py:20114/20144: summarize/restore.

A general memo of get_user_data_dir is higher risk: it doubles as a create+verify security check (secure_private_directory) and a root-selection authority, so coordinate with the Backup_Recovery owner (TASK-32562 in progress) rather than memoising it blindly.

title: Per-send pipeline re-materialises the whole transcript ~8-10x and re-encodes/re-hashes history images for fingerprints
trigger: Per send (several full-transcript passes) and once per completed turn for the cost chip; cost is O(messages) and O(image bytes).

Otherwise sidecars and trace provenance see a stale path, which is a correctness risk. A per-row fingerprint memo must key on message id + content/variant revision + attachment identity. Fingerprinting images by persisted digest changes the fingerprint format, so baselines computed before the change will report a spurious cache break once.
